posts.content_html_raw:
Just finished 'All That's Left are Stars', so...(Actual spoilers to big parts of the game, do not read unless you're done with 0.53!)

Mini Rant incoming:

Ouch. Literally wept. I felt like fucking Lestat from the Vampire Chronicles, just weeping more and more as each new fucking blow of the hammer hit... I thought I was deep in the feels after the loss of Orig Maya...I thought the faux loss at the start of Chapter 2 was hard, then her real death, etc, whatever...but holy shit I was NOT prepared. I've managed to stay like 99% spoiler free, thankfully, cause going into this blind is perhaps one of the most enthralling pieces of literature I've ever experienced.

Every single time it jumped forward two months I felt a growing horror. The game makes it clear that any situation that is too good to be true is just that...so seeing that Akira can actually BE a good person, that Ayane gets her dream come true...I knew exactly what would happen. That Himawari would show up, explain they were never meant to be there, etc etc. I fucking knew it was going to happen...

And then it did.

I had to stop playing last night once they made it to the beach, it was too late, and I was already down from THAT stuff happening, so when I picked it up tonight, I figured...couple character resets, some lore drop(And what lore it was!), and we'll move back to the story. Akira and Ayane will have a path forward...

And then..."I'm sorry" as the opening verse of "all that's left are stars" begins playing and holy fuck I was not ready. I am devastated for these poor fictional characters. What a fucking song choice. What a fucking moment.

Mild Context:

I'm an author, I've written nearly half a million words over a 5 book series...I've hurt my characters, I've killed them, I've sacrificed them, I've trapped them in a permanent timeloop. I've set the stakes so high that only the permanent ego death, the sacrifice of everything the MC is/was/could-be is enough to end the tragedy and save the lives of his loved ones....

And it wasn't until I finished "all that's left are stars" that I felt what my own readers felt. I think I owe them an apology, cause holy shit.

Himawari is really going through alot for her parents...the pain she went through stripping them of what amounts to their happiest memories, to save them from years of pain...fuck. Devastated. Akira fighting to not lose the memories? Peak. Ayane loving her daughter enough to trust her, even as she strips her of her happiness? My god....

I'm actually gonna take a few days after that before moving into 0.54. This is the kind of thing that sticks with you, and I think the moment deserves it.

And that somehow this is really only like the midpoint of the game? Insane.

Just...holy shit. I saw a few comments about 0.53 being some of the best so far...you were right.

TL;DR - Gonna nut punch Selebus one day. Donate to my GoFundMe so I can fly to Japan and do that sooner, rather than later.

I agree that with how NuMaya's past revelation mirrored Nao-chan's situation, it's almost certainly true that Nao-chan also comes from a wish; like why wouldn’t she be?

But the reason why I am still slightly on the fence about Nao-chan simply being the wishspawn of Kaori is because Nao-chan has been so much more than just Kaori simply asking for a heterochromia family member. Why is she a mute? Why is she capable of any of those unexplainable things? Why those two eye colors in particular? Unlike Maya, we met Nao-chan since the beginning and thus any of those traits are from direct manifestation of the wish in questions and not from whatever effect the loopy Kumon-mi can give anyone. If all those stem from a wish made by someone from a different world, the hell is this wish exactly?

If I have to pick the owner of the wish within a constrained pool that consists of 34 cast members, then Kaori; for sure. However, Nao-chan's existence is to a point where she feels like a combination of Kaori's cute, innocent wish plus some otherworldly being's wish that targets specifically at Akira's "survival", and that composition is like 10% to 90%, respectively.

It is doubtful that wishes come from nothing, though. Resources and gods seem limited in the Wishing Well. Maya and Nao-chan likely came from something or some things, and Nao-chan at least seems to be "[TEMPLATE9]".

The Times New Roman room is Kyoko's room. That should be clear enough. But I'm failing to connect many dots here:
  • Kyoko's Room/TNR Room has the ramen door as the entrance(?). That should mean it is connected to Tojo Ramen, right?
  • Akira goes to the upper floor of Tojo Ramen, finds something that seems related to the Upside-down House, but it isn't the room. There is a door though.
Since the room is different, there are a few questions I want to ask:
  • Is Kyoko still in the Upside-down House?
    • If so, it's weird to see Nodoka access UDH so easily. So I'm banking on the following.
    • Maybe I just haven't seen people talk about it, but judging by the fact that Shiori is free on her own, I would say...probably not?
    • It does seem contradictory that a AYHH tweet from a couple of months ago is still talking about Shiori ordinarily as if nothing happened to UDH though.
    • Who knows? Is Shiori still living with Kyoko? Is Kyoko coping?
    • This makes it all the more confusing to understand Where and How is Kyoko as we see in the latest update because it appears to me that UDH's era has all but ended. She however is mentally...still inside (unless you're telling me there's some time-fuckery going on with the AYHH postings). As we remember, the TNR Room is a mental space built up by Akira to cope with the loss of Maya/Ami (not an endorsement of any Maya=Ami theories). This is why Akira was depicted to still be stuck in the Room for a while even though he is physically outside, it's a mental symbol. A symbol of shelter from loss.
      • Selebus says TNR Room's structure doesn't mean anything specific, but that's bullshit because you don't use the same thing twice for no reason.
  • So one extra question is: What is Kyoko coping about?

  • The long paragraph above makes it appears that Kyoko's Room and the TNR Room only seem identical only because of the mental symbology.
    • Nonetheless, if you take a look at the second WORMGOD54 screenshot, it appears that Akira knows what the room behind the door is. That makes me think that the room TNR and Kyoko shares is actually the same physical space.
    • Akira was there, Kyoko is there. That however opens the door to a big question, though.
    • If you believe that both TNR and Kyoko happened in the same physical space, how did Kyoko and Akira not run into each other?

- TNR room does have the same interior as Kyoko's room, yes. This idea would resonate with what you've mentioned, a mental symbol. What reason Kyoko would have would be very much beyond me as most if not all of her past is not revealed. Maybe it's about a certain someone in UDH; maybe discovering how the world(s) work alone is enough to do it; maybe it's both then times infinity in the worst possible way. We can imagine but wouldn't know it for sure.

It would be interesting if those two places are the exact same one but I honestly don't know what that would bring. Besides, if Selly already said the room itself isn't of much significance, I will imagine that "what Kyoko is now would've been Sensei had he chosen differently during reset6", and reached one of the officially canonical yet premature endings. Sensei got out and kept on suffering in Kumon-mi while Kyoko remained inside and became...just that.

- Door sign is just "ramen" written in katakana and thus I believe this might something generic (there are plenty of prop like this in koikatsu iirc) and not something specifically related to Tojo ramen, especially no door looks like that in Tojo Ramen.

spoilers.title: guesses
spoilers.html:
- TNR room does have the same interior as Kyoko's room, yes. But for now, I only consider this to be symbolizing the fact that Sensei during TNR and Kyoko now are both hikikomori for different reasons. This idea would resonate with what you've mentioned, a mental symbol. What reason Kyoko would have would be very much beyond me as most if not all of her past is not revealed. Maybe it's about a certain someone in UDH; maybe discovering how the world(s) work alone is enough to do it; maybe it's both then times infinity in the worst possible way. We can imagine but wouldn't know it for sure.

It would be interesting if those two places are the exact same one but I honestly don't know what that would bring. Besides, if Selly already said the room itself isn't of much significance, I will imagine that "what Kyoko is now would've been Sensei had he chosen differently during reset6", and reached one of the officially canonical yet premature endings. Sensei got out and kept on suffering in Kumon-mi while Kyoko remained inside and became...just that.

- Door sign is just "ramen" written in katakana and thus I believe this might something generic (there are plenty of prop like this in koikatsu iirc) and not something specifically related to Tojo ramen, especially no door looks like that in Tojo Ramen.

- UDH: I don't think Kyoko is still in UDH and what we are seeing is all post-UDH, with reasons similar to yours; this would also explain why Kyoko who sounded like an annoying eccentric lust demon (presumably during the time of UDH) now looks like someone barely functioning.

In all honesty, however, this is a question too impossible to answer because we don't even know what Upside Down House really is. A physical place. A mental space. A hellish dimension. A memory distortedly replayed. We don't know which category UDH falls into as what we only have is some notes from Kyoko and some cringe twitter posts. Maybe UDH is Kyoko's Kumon-mi but your or anyone's guess will have the same chance as mine to be right and that chance is like only slightly above zero. You might get some indirect answers if Nodoka is willing to share how dots are connected inside her mind during the next RAS meeting. If not, you might have to just wait for LiL's sequel.

Random Addendum/Corrections
In the original post, I left the possibility of Shiori still being with Kyoko currently open. However, it seems I forgot something important from the previous update.


The proof is clear. Shiori doesn't know that Kyoko has a daughter. There is no way they live together. UDH really is dead.
There is one obvious hole in the theory that Kyoko's Room/TNR Room is in the Tojo Ramen building. If Nodoka visits her mother, which she does, she has to enter Tojo Ramen. By that logic, she should be pretty familiar with Tsuneyo. That isn't the case though.

This hole manifests itself in TNR in a different form. Let's say we take Tojo Ramen's phone number from A Life of Prizes:

That number worked! Great! Let's try doing it in TNR!

Huh, rude to hang up on a neighbour's call. Anyhow, the problem is apparent. It doesn't seem that Tsuneyo would know that she has a neighbour upstairs if Kyoko/Akira really lived there. She even has proof that the second floor isn't anything we are thinking of.

Trust me, Sensei, I don't understand either. At least I didn't. So, where is this Room supposed to be? And how is it accessed?

To answer this question, let me first introduce to you the magical powers of Doors in Lessons in Love.


In both Happy Events, clicking on Dorm 5's Door takes you to the Room with Clocks. Despite the scarcity of evidence, it can be said that there is a consistent way to access places that you normally can't, even if the means through which gets you to normal places in normal circumstances. Doors are magical.

Back in the Camping Trip, we were shown a Door that leads to a...higher world by Nao. A Door that is in the middle of nowhere. entering it takes you to a lab(?) where the shadowy figures there make observation notes on Terminals (in case you forgot T-84 is supposed to mean Terminal 84).

This one is much more revealing than the previous Doors I showed you. This one lets Ayane and Akira enter a world that is set 15 years in the future, but more importantly, transports Ayane's consciousness to an adult body.

Note that the 3rd Pic's Door is a different door from the 2nd, through which Akira entered the White Room. However, I think it is safe to assume that the two Doors in the White Room share the same design. Please focus on the material, the coloring and the Door handle positioning of the 1st Door, and compare it with the 2nd. You can see that they aren't exactly the same Doors, and the differences in between can't be explained with real life logic. This is more of a pedantic tangent, but this explains why the metal Door in WORMGOD54 can be connected to the wooden Door in TNR/Kyoko's Room.

The above shows how magical Doors are in this game. The first one transports you to a space that you can't normally access, AKA intra-world travel(?). The second one takes you to a different world, probably the Wishing Well Offices, AKA inter-world travel. The third one takes you to a different body in a different world, AKA inter-world travel with OP powers. Basically, if there's a will, there's a Door.

This is more than sufficient to explain how Nodoka could access Kyoko's Room without ever having to enter Tojo Ramen, and enough to explain how Akira can basically live in the TNR Room for god-knows-how-long without Tsuneyo realizing it.

Because the space the two of them reside in is not in Tojo Ramen. Tojo Ramen is simply connected to the White Room (and by extension the TNR Room) through Doors that ordinarily function ordinarily in ordinary circumstances, but take you to places you won't ordinarily enter in extraordinary circumstances. Nodoka, on the other hand, could enter the TNR Room through a different Door that isn't in Tojo Ramen, if that Door is magical enough.
Understanding the extent of the power of Doors opens a Door that allows us to guess the answer of my final question in the quotes:
  • If you believe that both TNR and Kyoko happened in the same physical space, how did Kyoko and Akira not run into each other?
Click to expand...
Think about this, it's possible to be transported through time and space in consciousness in this game. It is also possible for Akira to blackout in consciousness, and people around him wouldn't realize/understand what just happened with his consciousness/protection.

So what if...



(It's hard to see but the name color is Niki's)
As you can see, the 2030 Akira got transported to is more or less an organic one, with people who live their own lives apart from himself. Even if we are to say it is a pocket dimension, I think it is no less organic of a future than Himawari's.

So I am suggesting that Akira's consciousness was transported to 2030's TNR Room in a different body(?) while his real self is still in 2020, being milked by Ami. That is why he never ran into Kyoko. Because they shared the same Space, but not the same Time. By the time 2030 hit and his students (including Nodoka) left him, maybe Kyoko's already moved.

(Of course, this split self issue is tricky to tackle, the holes this opens might be too big for this theory to stand on enough legs.)

Huh, rude to hang up on a neighbour's call. Anyhow, the problem is apparent. It doesn't seem that Tsuneyo would know that she has a neighbour upstairs if Kyoko/Akira really lived there. She even has proof that the second floor isn't anything we are thinking of.

Trust me, Sensei, I don't understand either. At least I didn't. So, where is this Room supposed to be? And how is it accessed?

To answer this question, let me first introduce to you the magical powers of Doors in Lessons in Love.


In both Happy Events, clicking on Dorm 5's Door takes you to the Room with Clocks. Despite the scarcity of evidence, it can be said that there is a consistent way to access places that you normally can't, even if the means through which gets you to normal places in normal circumstances. Doors are magical.

Back in the Camping Trip, we were shown a Door that leads to a...higher world by Nao. A Door that is in the middle of nowhere. entering it takes you to a lab(?) where the shadowy figures there make observation notes on Terminals (in case you forgot T-84 is supposed to mean Terminal 84).

This one is much more revealing than the previous Doors I showed you. This one lets Ayane and Akira enter a world that is set 15 years in the future, but more importantly, transports Ayane's consciousness to an adult body.

Note that the 3rd Pic's Door is a different door from the 2nd, through which Akira entered the White Room. However, I think it is safe to assume that the two Doors in the White Room share the same design. Please focus on the material, the coloring and the Door handle positioning of the 1st Door, and compare it with the 2nd. You can see that they aren't exactly the same Doors, and the differences in between can't be explained with real life logic. This is more of a pedantic tangent, but this explains why the metal Door in WORMGOD54 can be connected to the wooden Door in TNR/Kyoko's Room.

The above shows how magical Doors are in this game. The first one transports you to a space that you can't normally access, AKA intra-world travel(?). The second one takes you to a different world, probably the Wishing Well Offices, AKA inter-world travel. The third one takes you to a different body in a different world, AKA inter-world travel with OP powers. Basically, if there's a will, there's a Door.

This is more than sufficient to explain how Nodoka could access Kyoko's Room without ever having to enter Tojo Ramen, and enough to explain how Akira can basically live in the TNR Room for god-knows-how-long without Tsuneyo realizing it.

Because the space the two of them reside in is not in Tojo Ramen. Tojo Ramen is simply connected to the White Room (and by extension the TNR Room) through Doors that ordinarily function ordinarily in ordinary circumstances, but take you to places you won't ordinarily enter in extraordinary circumstances. Nodoka, on the other hand, could enter the TNR Room through a different Door that isn't in Tojo Ramen, if that Door is magical enough.

spoilers.html:
Understanding the extent of the power of Doors opens a Door that allows us to guess the answer of my final question in the quotes:
  • If you believe that both TNR and Kyoko happened in the same physical space, how did Kyoko and Akira not run into each other?
Click to expand...
Think about this, it's possible to be transported through time and space in consciousness in this game. It is also possible for Akira to blackout in consciousness, and people around him wouldn't realize/understand what just happened with his consciousness/protection.

So what if...



(It's hard to see but the name color is Niki's)
As you can see, the 2030 Akira got transported to is more or less an organic one, with people who live their own lives apart from himself. Even if we are to say it is a pocket dimension, I think it is no less organic of a future than Himawari's.

So I am suggesting that Akira's consciousness was transported to 2030's TNR Room in a different body(?) while his real self is still in 2020, being milked by Ami. That is why he never ran into Kyoko. Because they shared the same Space, but not the same Time. By the time 2030 hit and his students (including Nodoka) left him, maybe Kyoko's already moved.

(Of course, this split self issue is tricky to tackle, the holes this opens might be too big for this theory to stand on enough legs.)

Throwing some guesses here
- TNR room does have the same interior as Kyoko's room, yes. But for now, I only consider this to be symbolizing the fact that Sensei during TNR and Kyoko now are both hikikomori for different reasons. This idea would resonate with what you've mentioned, a mental symbol. What reason Kyoko would have would be very much beyond me as most if not all of her past is not revealed. Maybe it's about a certain someone in UDH; maybe discovering how the world(s) work alone is enough to do it; maybe it's both then times infinity in the worst possible way. We can imagine but wouldn't know it for sure.

It would be interesting if those two places are the exact same one but I honestly don't know what that would bring. Besides, if Selly already said the room itself isn't of much significance, I will imagine that "what Kyoko is now would've been Sensei had he chosen differently during reset6", and reached one of the officially canonical yet premature endings. Sensei got out and kept on suffering in Kumon-mi while Kyoko remained inside and became...just that.

- Door sign is just "ramen" written in katakana and thus I believe this might something generic (there are plenty of prop like this in koikatsu iirc) and not something specifically related to Tojo ramen, especially no door looks like that in Tojo Ramen.

- UDH: I don't think Kyoko is still in UDH and what we are seeing is all post-UDH, with reasons similar to yours; this would also explain why Kyoko who sounded like an annoying eccentric lust demon (presumably during the time of UDH) now looks like someone barely functioning.

In all honesty, however, this is a question too impossible to answer because we don't even know what Upside Down House really is. A physical place. A mental space. A hellish dimension. A memory distortedly replayed. We don't know which category UDH falls into as what we only have is some notes from Kyoko and some cringe twitter posts. Maybe UDH is Kyoko's Kumon-mi but your or anyone's guess will have the same chance as mine to be right and that chance is like only slightly above zero. You might get some indirect answers if Nodoka is willing to share how dots are connected inside her mind during the next RAS meeting. If not, you might have to just wait for LiL's sequel.
Click to expand...
,
If there isn't more concrete proof, I think I'll fall back to the symbology interpretation as well. There's probably more to see if that's true in the line where the narration said that he knows what's behind the door in WORMGOD54. That could be anything though. Maybe it is the TNR Room, maybe it's something different, maybe it's UDH itself (thus the graffiti on the wall). There'd be a lot more to pry into Akira's past if it's the latter two, so it isn't something we could talk about without more info.

(then again, Il Cervo coming to mind convinces me to be more conservative in the 'symbolism being real' area)

While we are at it, previously, we have seen UDH content appear every now and then in narration. I previously assumed that Akira is related to UDH somehow. But with the help of a certain detective, I now think that it's more likely that those events are referring to the Player (Kyoko, maybe) specifically instead of Akira. Why her story is mixed with his is yet to be seen. What I said about Akira possibly knowing about UDH could be tied to this, but nothing for sure.

The Ramen Door thing seems something harder to shrug off. Like, why would someone have a door that just says Ramen in katakana on the interior of his room? Perhaps it is a good indicator of how Kyoko and Akira share the same mental/physical space, but I think there is something more here. A lot to daydream about but not much I could press if I must be certain.

Yeah I really have no idea about UDH. But at least I believe knowing this is all post-UDH might help put things in perspective. Well, if anyone is interested in re-reading the bunch of gibberish every UDH event is.

Hello, everyone. None of you know me (obviously; this is a brand-new account), though I have a pretty decent idea who most of you are, considering that I’ve spent the last week or so doing literally nothing other than reading every single post in this thread from its very beginning. For further proof of my obsession with Lessons in Love, I have replayed this game three times over the course of around a year (currently on my fourth replay) and also possess a 2500+ page text document systematically detailing every single piece of symbolism/character detail/potentially relevant information I came across (only up to version 0.51, unfortunately), so it’s fair to say that I am about as engaged in theorycrafting and trying to comprehend the intricacies of Selebus’ legendary creation as most of this thread’s regulars.

With all that being said, the thing that is much-much closer to my own heart is not theorycrafting, but rather media analysis: as in, trying to ascertain the general themes of the narrative, the thematical links between the characters, the message the story is trying to convey, etcetera. And considering how frequently the subject of various characters being “redeemable” or “irredeemable” seems to come up as of late, I would like to share an alternative thematical perspective that I haven’t really seen anyone else bring up yet:

To me, it seems fairly evident that one of the most prominent themes of Lessons in Love is “nature vs nurture”. Every single character in this story is twisted or broken in some way, and their events center around exploring whether this outcome is the result of who they are as a person or the circumstances they grew up/found themselves in. Technically, the answer is always “both”, but, with the notable exceptions of the Arakawas (all of whom swing wildly along the entire spectrum with every new revelation about them, before inevitably centering somewhere in the middle), generally every character leans strongly to just one particular side.

Uta, for example, is very clearly “nature” (she is very impulsive and never learns from her mistakes), just like Io is very clearly “nurture”. In fact, almost all of the Dorm pairs can be kinda divided like this: aside from the aforementioned two, Chika/Sana/Miku/Rin/Otoha/Yasu/Kirin are “nature” and mostly create their own problems due to who they are (through their beliefs, desires or actions), while Yumi/Ayane/Makoto/Futaba/Nodoka/Touka/Noriko are “nurture”, and so the sources of their unhappiness are environmental and/or caused by others (yes, Futaba is “nurture”, since her self-image issues that could have been at least partially resolved through diet/going to the gym fundamentally cannot be fixed due to how Resets work, negating all of that progress). Dorm 5 intentionally stands out in this regard, as Ami is an Arakawa (and therefore an exception) and Maya is both “nature” AND “nurture”: she started as “nature” (Nu Maya, literally created by Akira to be his perfect girl) and then eventually became “nurture” (Maya Prime, jaded and broken after living through countless cycles). And the same dichotomy can be also applied to everyone else.

I bring all of this up because, since another main theme of Lessons in Love is redemption/healing from trauma, some people seem to equate all potentially “irredeemable” characters with being badly written or even outright pointless, since they openly go against that theme – or, to put it another way, that “redemption” is fundamentally the only direction all of these character arcs CAN go, and anything that deviates from that is a mistake on Selebus’ part. I disagree, obviously, believing that even the characters who won’t necessarily become better people by the end of the story can still be meaningful within the “nature-nurture” thematical framework, and as an example of what I’m talking about I would like to point to a certain someone who got her share of spotlight in 0.54 update:
Haruka.

The entire point of Haruka’s character is that she is all “nature”, no “nurture”. There is no twist, no hidden trauma to potentially explain her behavior like there is with Akira or Sekai – she is *just* a bad person, plain and simple, which makes her an important contrast to the rest of the cast. Haruka had a perfectly normal childhood, went to a perfectly normal school, had perfectly normal dreams, ended up in a perfectly normal marriage with a perfectly normal husband and is currently an owner of a semi-successful business – her life, while by no means perfect, was still VERY good (compared to everyone else, anyway), and yet she still ended up becoming a liar, a cheater and a predator… for no other reason than because such was her nature.

That’s why I don’t particularly believe that Haruka can be “redeemed” – nor that she *should* be redeemed – because it would both go against her narrative purpose as a “pure evil” of sorts, and also because the motto of “becoming a better you” that gets echoed throughout LiL just fundamentally does not apply to her like it does to everyone else. There is a “better Akira” out there somewhere who was born in a different family, just like there is a “better Ami” and a “better Sekai”, but there is no “better Haruka” – there is just Haruka who accepts who she is, or Haruka who lives her entire life in silent misery, pretending to be someone she’s not. This – albeit to a much lesser extent – also applies to all of the other “nature-aligned” characters, which is another reason why I am certain that “redemption” is not the only way the story can go for a decent number of the cast.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
"Nature x Nurture" and "Redemption".
Click to expand...
I thought it was an interesting read, but I take it as yet another way to interpret things. I think this perfectly falls into Selebus' perspective of "interpret my story as you wish". You chose to examine it through this prism and I think it makes enough sense that I don't see a point to start poking holes at it, but not enough for me to adopt it myself. I do have a few thoughts though:
Regarding Haruka herself, I've written some posts about her since the update and I'd like to add a few things. You say she has no reason to end up a liar, cheater and predator, but I beg to differ. Obviously, there is no reason that would justify her becoming a predator in terms of law or morals. But what I mean is that there is causation to her actions.

As everyone knows, Haruka had a "normal" life, no big traumas, married young, which iirc correctly was her first man, then managed to become a business owner, and enjoyed a strictly-female sexual life outside of her marriage (with her husband's approval, again, iirc).

If it was just that, sure, there'd be no real reason for her change - but Haruka had her husband go to war for years. I think you, along with some others, may have been underestimating the toil of having your pillar of support, and one partner simply be taken from you. In some regards, it can be even more distressing than them dying, because there's no finality to it. They're just a question mark. You can't move on with your life, you're constantly worrying if they're even alive, there's no communication whatsoever (in the space war case). Haruka endured this for years.

Her very first event is exactly about that. How all she had was one dude, that he's been gone for years, and that she had to deal with it all by herself and is living quite a sad life:
I included the variation where you don't have sex with Sara, because then Haruka gives out more details about herself.

Then comes Akira and takes advantage of her situation. I'm not putting the blame solely on him, but let's be real here. If Akira doesn't engage with Haruka, they just become friends. She does kiss him, but she was super drunk and lonely, and then apologises and regrets it.

Haruka further talks about her husband:
If you don't take advantage of her a second time, she has no inclination to become a predator, nor a cheater, nor anything. In the last update, she even agrees with Maki right away. There's no conflict.

I think Haruka's fall is quite realistic, she cheats because she's vulnerable and someone shows her affection, when the man she really loves has been away for years. Then she hates herself for it, and keeps doing it. The way she finds to cope is by hating herself, and self-deprecating. From then on, things keep getting darker.

If you recall, Haruka has had a sexual relationship with Maki for a long time. With a woman. She employs girls. While it is natural for her to find the girls pretty, this turns into sexualizing them because of her loneliness and desperation. Then, when Akira starts making her into a slave, it turns into actual intentions of being a predator because Akira is a predator himself. She's emulating her idea of him (because she lacks critical knowledge of his backstory) - and this idea of emulation is repeated a lot of times in her dialogue throughout the last update.

I just think that, overall, a lot of people have been comparing Haruka and Akira and reaching the conclusion of "Haruka doesn't have real justification for becoming a predator, while Akira has at least a very traumatizing backstory" - and, while it's true that Akira's backstory has a lot of depth, Haruka also has had a lot of troubles.

I really don't agree with the idea of her being "naturally evil". While what she's done recently is certainly bad, it didn't come out of nowhere, nor would she have acted in this way if they weren't part of a chain of events set in part by Akira himself.
A second point I'd like to make/question is the idea of so many characters being irredeemable. Who are these characters exactly?
Haruka is far from being irredeemable. She pushed hard on Kirin, sure. Is that irredeemable? One could argue that Akira's assault on Karin was far worse in terms of it being consensual. Same for Akira and Yumi. Nodoka and Yumi was far worse in terms of intention as well (pure malice there), the same could be said for Kirin and Ayane.

A lot of people hate/hated Otoha for assaulting Niki and her treatment of Rin. Or Osako for how callous she was towards Akira. Or Wakana for her Sekai obsession. Or Nodoka for the countless times she was Nodoka. Or Sekai for also being Sekai. And yet all of these characters have already been redeemed to various extents, or, at the very least, they have all been shown to have more depth than just being one thing.

Otoha recognizes she is trash and wants to stop being trash, enlisting Akira's help for that (wishing she could have met him earlier, and that she could have had him at her corner in the past, as Rin did). Osako is at Akira's side through his reveal of being a predator/traumatized by a predator. Wakana cares deeply for him, going out of her way to try to help him and be a support for him. Nodoka literally becomes a martyr for Akira, and almost everything she does is trying to figure things out so that she can free everyone. Even Sekai has already been shown (in "Kyoto") to having actual troubles, and been desperate to run away.

Redemption or not, all of these characters have been shown to have depth - and I think that's the way it will continue going. The question of redemption for the player and Akira are also different things, mind you. Something being irredeemable to me personally might not fit into Selebus' overall idea of how the depth of one character is enough to not make them "just evil". In that sense, yes, everyone can be either redeemable or irredeemable to each one.
I'd argue that the one character that scores close to irredeemable is Ami. But she's also the one character with the least revealed, so it's a safe bet there should be a redemption planned there somewhere (if it holds up is another matter).

Edit: Also, welcome to the thread. I echo Bingoogus' words, you're likely to fit well.

spoilers.html:
Haruka is far from being irredeemable. She pushed hard on Kirin, sure. Is that irredeemable? One could argue that Akira's assault on Karin was far worse in terms of it being consensual. Same for Akira and Yumi. Nodoka and Yumi was far worse in terms of intention as well (pure malice there), the same could be said for Kirin and Ayane.

A lot of people hate/hated Otoha for assaulting Niki and her treatment of Rin. Or Osako for how callous she was towards Akira. Or Wakana for her Sekai obsession. Or Nodoka for the countless times she was Nodoka. Or Sekai for also being Sekai. And yet all of these characters have already been redeemed to various extents, or, at the very least, they have all been shown to have more depth than just being one thing.

Otoha recognizes she is trash and wants to stop being trash, enlisting Akira's help for that (wishing she could have met him earlier, and that she could have had him at her corner in the past, as Rin did). Osako is at Akira's side through his reveal of being a predator/traumatized by a predator. Wakana cares deeply for him, going out of her way to try to help him and be a support for him. Nodoka literally becomes a martyr for Akira, and almost everything she does is trying to figure things out so that she can free everyone. Even Sekai has already been shown (in "Kyoto") to having actual troubles, and been desperate to run away.

Redemption or not, all of these characters have been shown to have depth - and I think that's the way it will continue going. The question of redemption for the player and Akira are also different things, mind you. Something being irredeemable to me personally might not fit into Selebus' overall idea of how the depth of one character is enough to not make them "just evil". In that sense, yes, everyone can be either redeemable or irredeemable to each one.

Okay, first of all, thank you for writing such a detailed reply and guiding me directly through your thought process. I am fully aware that this isn’t exactly any different from how you usually reply to everyone else, but it still helped me realize that there ended up being *quite a lot* of things in my original post that didn’t came across exactly the way I wanted them to, painting a somewhat incorrect picture of my perspective in the matter. So I’ll correct these inaccuracies first, and then go into a few more details regarding some of your finer points.

Everything that I said about Haruka was meant to come from a place of empathy and acceptance, not judgement. It wasn’t me taking the high road and blaming someone for being “too weak” and eagerly giving into temptation instead of resisting it to the bitter end “like a good wife should” – it was me gazing into the eyes of someone who voluntarily accepted the call of the abyss, and realizing that I’m looking into a mirror. I see a lot of myself in Haruka – more than in almost every other character in the game, probably, except maybe Nodoka and (partially) Akira – and so for me to truly judge her for what she did, knowing full well *why* she did it, would be nothing but pure hypocrisy. And while “green path” Haruka is, to put it bluntly, a very vile human being – which is something that she herself would openly admit, I’m sure, and I have no issue admitting it as well – I would still stand by her side at the end of the day, simply because I am a fellow weakling who knows what it feels like, if nothing else.

Now, as for the rest of your analysis: it was really good, and I even learned a few new things for myself (I never saw “red paths” for any of the characters except Rin, so I had no idea how Haruka acts if you aren’t having sex with her) – but it was, to stay on-theme, a very “concerned” perspective. Now allow me to share my own – a much more “callous” one:

When I was originally playing this game, I very quickly caught onto the fact that it is a very intentional deconstruction of the traditional dating sim, masterfully playing around with various tropes that you usually take for granted – like Chapter 1 Sensei having an “honest” mindset of an average eroge player, treating the girls only in terms of “unlocking their H-scenes”, for example, as well as many other things. And so, when Haruka was first introduced and I saw her first few events (“Invisible Worm” especially), my mind immediately interpreted her entire side of the story as a yet another subversion: this time of a very specific “three letter genre” that is *also* a staple in erotic games like this one.

The fundamentals of that entire genre (that shall remain unnamed) are inherently based on the three-way relationship between a “pure and faithful” character, their (usually barely present, non-entity) partner and some evil and corrupting outside force. So how do you subvert it? Well, one way to do it would be to make the “pure and faithful” character neither “pure” nor “faithful”, to the point where “an outside corrupting force” barely has to do anything to make them fall – which is, in my eyes, *exactly* what happens between Haruka and Sensei if you decide to take the “green path” with her.

While calling Haruka “pure evil” wasn’t exactly the best choice of words on my part, I’ll admit, the point I was trying to make is that, in my eyes, she was *always* harboring those dark thoughts and desires within her – or at least inclinations towards them – unlike pretty much all of the other characters (including Akira and Sekai), who seemingly only began to feel that way after “becoming tainted”. Like, her being very lonely and extremely sexually frustrated is one thing, sure – I don’t really blame Haruka for her relationship with Sensei, necessarily, since in her shoes I would have done it as well – but the rest of it, like the stuff with Nodoka, or Molly, or Kirin? Can you honestly tell me that if Maki/Sara had to live through the exact same set of events as Haruka they would have ended up in the same place? Crossed that same line?

I don’t think so – and *that* is the crux of it all. Haruka only needed a very small push to give in; so small, in fact, that I fully believe all of Sensei’s inner monologues in Chapter 1 in which he repeatedly calls Haruka out on her bullshit in regards to how fake her supposed “love” towards her husband truly is – say what you want about Akira, but he has proven himself to be a very good judge of character (when he actually cares, anyway). The fact that she does nothing despicable on her “red path” isn’t a point towards her virtue – it just means that, with the absence of strong enough temptations, Haruka has chosen the “silent misery” I mentioned in my original post, deciding to fully commit to wearing a mask and pretending to be a “good person”, when she truly isn’t. Speaking from experience, this is an awful way to live, which is where the true tragedy of her “green path” lies: she is much happier being true to herself and becoming a monster (the fiasco with Kirin notwithstanding), but choosing that road means that while everyone else gets to slowly walk away from the darkness and embrace the light in order to finally become “whole”, Haruka’s final destination on the path towards the same goal instead lies at the very bottom of the abyss.

Feel free to disagree with me, of course – as I said, I can easily see the validity of your interpretation of her character, as well. It’s just not how *I* see it, personally. Ultimately, like a certain someone would say, it’s all a matter of perception.

As for the whole “irredeemable” aspect of this discussion, that was just me mostly echoing the general sentiment I’ve seen repeated here a decent number of times (in relation to characters like Akira, Sekai, Ami, Nodoka, Otoha and so on), rather than my own take on the matter. As someone who doesn’t much care for redemption and would be fine with perfectly fine with either outcome for the cast, as long as their endings are narratively fitting and thematically consistent, my point was to try and show people a way to appreciate even the characters they consider “irredeemable” by changing the paradigm and looking at them from another perspective.

Okay, first of all, thank you for writing such a detailed reply and guiding me directly through your thought process. I am fully aware that this isn’t exactly any different from how you usually reply to everyone else, but it still helped me realize that there ended up being *quite a lot* of things in my original post that didn’t came across exactly the way I wanted them to, painting a somewhat incorrect picture of my perspective in the matter. So I’ll correct these inaccuracies first, and then go into a few more details regarding some of your finer points.
Spoiler:
Elaboration
Everything that I said about Haruka was meant to come from a place of empathy and acceptance, not judgement. It wasn’t me taking the high road and blaming someone for being “too weak” and eagerly giving into temptation instead of resisting it to the bitter end “like a good wife should” – it was me gazing into the eyes of someone who voluntarily accepted the call of the abyss, and realizing that I’m looking into a mirror. I see a lot of myself in Haruka – more than in almost every other character in the game, probably, except maybe Nodoka and (partially) Akira – and so for me to truly judge her for what she did, knowing full well *why* she did it, would be nothing but pure hypocrisy. And while “green path” Haruka is, to put it bluntly, a very vile human being – which is something that she herself would openly admit, I’m sure, and I have no issue admitting it as well – I would still stand by her side at the end of the day, simply because I am a fellow weakling who knows what it feels like, if nothing else.
Now, as for the rest of your analysis: it was really good, and I even learned a few new things for myself (I never saw “red paths” for any of the characters except Rin, so I had no idea how Haruka acts if you aren’t having sex with her) – but it was, to stay on-theme, a very “concerned” perspective. Now allow me to share my own – a much more “callous” one:
Spoiler:
Further analysis
When I was originally playing this game, I very quickly caught onto the fact that it is a very intentional deconstruction of the traditional dating sim, masterfully playing around with various tropes that you usually take for granted – like Chapter 1 Sensei having an “honest” mindset of an average eroge player, treating the girls only in terms of “unlocking their H-scenes”, for example, as well as many other things. And so, when Haruka was first introduced and I saw her first few events (“Invisible Worm” especially), my mind immediately interpreted her entire side of the story as a yet another subversion: this time of a very specific “three letter genre” that is *also* a staple in erotic games like this one.
The fundamentals of that entire genre (that shall remain unnamed) are inherently based on the three-way relationship between a “pure and faithful” character, their (usually barely present, non-entity) partner and some evil and corrupting outside force. So how do you subvert it? Well, one way to do it would be to make the “pure and faithful” character neither “pure” nor “faithful”, to the point where “an outside corrupting force” barely has to do anything to make them fall – which is, in my eyes, *exactly* what happens between Haruka and Sensei if you decide to take the “green path” with her.
While calling Haruka “pure evil” wasn’t exactly the best choice of words on my part, I’ll admit, the point I was trying to make is that, in my eyes, she was *always* harboring those dark thoughts and desires within her – or at least inclinations towards them – unlike pretty much all of the other characters (including Akira and Sekai), who seemingly only began to feel that way after “becoming tainted”. Like, her being very lonely and extremely sexually frustrated is one thing, sure – I don’t really blame Haruka for her relationship with Sensei, necessarily, since in her shoes I would have done it as well – but the rest of it, like the stuff with Nodoka, or Molly, or Kirin? Can you honestly tell me that if Maki/Sara had to live through the exact same set of events as Haruka they would have ended up in the same place? Crossed that same line?
I don’t think so – and *that* is the crux of it all. Haruka only needed a very small push to give in; so small, in fact, that I fully believe all of Sensei’s inner monologues in Chapter 1 in which he repeatedly calls Haruka out on her bullshit in regards to how fake her supposed “love” towards her husband truly is – say what you want about Akira, but he has proven himself to be a very good judge of character (when he actually cares, anyway). The fact that she does nothing despicable on her “red path” isn’t a point towards her virtue – it just means that, with the absence of strong enough temptations, Haruka has chosen the “silent misery” I mentioned in my original post, deciding to fully commit to wearing a mask and pretending to be a “good person”, when she truly isn’t. Speaking from experience, this is an awful way to live, which is where the true tragedy of her “green path” lies: she is much happier being true to herself and becoming a monster (the fiasco with Kirin notwithstanding), but choosing that road means that while everyone else gets to slowly walk away from the darkness and embrace the light in order to finally become “whole”, Haruka’s final destination on the path towards the same goal instead lies at the very bottom of the abyss.
Feel free to disagree with me, of course – as I said, I can easily see the validity of your interpretation of her character, as well. It’s just not how *I* see it, personally. Ultimately, like a certain someone would say, it’s all a matter of perception.
As for the whole “irredeemable” aspect of this discussion, that was just me mostly echoing the general sentiment I’ve seen repeated here a decent number of times (in relation to characters like Akira, Sekai, Ami, Nodoka, Otoha and so on), rather than my own take on the matter. As someone who doesn’t much care for redemption and would be fine with perfectly fine with either outcome for the cast, as long as their endings are narratively fitting and thematically consistent, my point was to try and show people a way to appreciate even the characters they consider “irredeemable” by changing the paradigm and looking at them from another perspective.

spoilers.title: Haruka's situation
spoilers.html:
Regarding Haruka herself, I've written some posts about her since the update and I'd like to add a few things. You say she has no reason to end up a liar, cheater and predator, but I beg to differ. Obviously, there is no reason that would justify her becoming a predator in terms of law or morals. But what I mean is that there is causation to her actions.

As everyone knows, Haruka had a "normal" life, no big traumas, married young, which iirc correctly was her first man, then managed to become a business owner, and enjoyed a strictly-female sexual life outside of her marriage (with her husband's approval, again, iirc).

If it was just that, sure, there'd be no real reason for her change - but Haruka had her husband go to war for years. I think you, along with some others, may have been underestimating the toil of having your pillar of support, and one partner simply be taken from you. In some regards, it can be even more distressing than them dying, because there's no finality to it. They're just a question mark. You can't move on with your life, you're constantly worrying if they're even alive, there's no communication whatsoever (in the space war case). Haruka endured this for years.

Her very first event is exactly about that. How all she had was one dude, that he's been gone for years, and that she had to deal with it all by herself and is living quite a sad life:

And yet all of these characters have already been redeemed to various extents, or, at the very least, they have all been shown to have more depth than just being one thing.

Otoha recognizes she is trash and wants to stop being trash, enlisting Akira's help for that (wishing she could have met him earlier, and that she could have had him at her corner in the past, as Rin did). Even Sekai has already been shown (in "Kyoto") to having actual troubles, and been desperate to run away.

Redemption or not, all of these characters have been shown to have depth - and I think that's the way it will continue going. The question of redemption for the player and Akira are also different things, mind you. Something being irredeemable to me personally might not fit into Selebus' overall idea of how the depth of one character is enough to not make them "just evil". In that sense, yes, everyone can be either redeemable or irredeemable to each one.

Haruka harbored dark thoughts all along and really just needed a small push. In her place, Maki and Sara wouldn't have done the same things.
Click to expand...
First of all, speaking as an old lady that struggles to stay alive until the end of LiL , it is refreshing to see someone identifying with Haruka because I also do, to an extent. To be fair, I much more empathize with Sara, but I have definitely lived/seen things when I was younger that were similar to the Haruka arc.

I think our conversation has already crossed the line between analysis of the game and what we get from it, so I'm not going to go back to anything we've both said in that regard. I just think that, as you point out, the topic of acting on dark impulses is quite pivotal to LiL. Haruka having these dark thoughts or not, in comparison to other people, I think is ultimately pointless - because we judge people by their actions (thoughts made manifest), rather than the thoughts themselves.

Getting quite real here right now, I have absolutely no doubt that some amount of highschool teachers find their students hot, especially if they're about to graduate and the lines between children and adults start to get messy. I'm not going to judge them for having only thoughts. Would I want my daughter to be taught by a teacher that sexualizes her in his mind? Well, no. But as long as he doesn't act on it, how would anyone know? A bit distressing to think about, but it is what it is.

What I find so interesting in this topic, especially under the Haruka light, is that so prevalent idea in the past decades that "every villain has to have a sad backstory that somewhat justifies their actions". And that's just not true. There are Akiras out there, of course, but there will also be Harukas (for the lack of a better example). People that had quite a normal life, and yet are interested in kids. Or in stealing. Or torturing. Or whatever that could be considered evil.

I don't know and, right now, don't think that's where Selebus is going with the Haruka story. But it's certainly a story with significance. When the time came in my personal life, I was a strong advocate to start teaching the kids about sexual conduct as soon as possible. Where it's wrong to be touched, what they should do, that it would never be their fault - stuff like that. All much earlier than some would consider "necessary".

My point with all of this and what I find interesting as a story theme is that evil does exist. Danger does come seemingly out of nowhere from who you least expect as well. I think it would be a good balance for a story that tries so much to make us empathize with Akira to also have just the expected idea of a predator (although I don't think that's Haruka).

Years ago, we expected that counterpoint to be Sekai - a truly evil character. But then, it started to mellow bit by bit and then "Kyoto" hit me like a truck. Recently, Ami crashed out about her last year of life as well. And now we're at a place where we just don't know enough about her either way.
Anyway, I have no point with any of this - just venting out some thoughts about the points you've raised.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Okay, first of all, thank you for writing such a detailed reply and guiding me directly through your thought process. I am fully aware that this isn’t exactly any different from how you usually reply to everyone else, but it still helped me realize that there ended up being *quite a lot* of things in my original post that didn’t came across exactly the way I wanted them to, painting a somewhat incorrect picture of my perspective in the matter. So I’ll correct these inaccuracies first, and then go into a few more details regarding some of your finer points.

Everything that I said about Haruka was meant to come from a place of empathy and acceptance, not judgement. It wasn’t me taking the high road and blaming someone for being “too weak” and eagerly giving into temptation instead of resisting it to the bitter end “like a good wife should” – it was me gazing into the eyes of someone who voluntarily accepted the call of the abyss, and realizing that I’m looking into a mirror. I see a lot of myself in Haruka – more than in almost every other character in the game, probably, except maybe Nodoka and (partially) Akira – and so for me to truly judge her for what she did, knowing full well *why* she did it, would be nothing but pure hypocrisy. And while “green path” Haruka is, to put it bluntly, a very vile human being – which is something that she herself would openly admit, I’m sure, and I have no issue admitting it as well – I would still stand by her side at the end of the day, simply because I am a fellow weakling who knows what it feels like, if nothing else.

Now, as for the rest of your analysis: it was really good, and I even learned a few new things for myself (I never saw “red paths” for any of the characters except Rin, so I had no idea how Haruka acts if you aren’t having sex with her) – but it was, to stay on-theme, a very “concerned” perspective. Now allow me to share my own – a much more “callous” one:

When I was originally playing this game, I very quickly caught onto the fact that it is a very intentional deconstruction of the traditional dating sim, masterfully playing around with various tropes that you usually take for granted – like Chapter 1 Sensei having an “honest” mindset of an average eroge player, treating the girls only in terms of “unlocking their H-scenes”, for example, as well as many other things. And so, when Haruka was first introduced and I saw her first few events (“Invisible Worm” especially), my mind immediately interpreted her entire side of the story as a yet another subversion: this time of a very specific “three letter genre” that is *also* a staple in erotic games like this one.

The fundamentals of that entire genre (that shall remain unnamed) are inherently based on the three-way relationship between a “pure and faithful” character, their (usually barely present, non-entity) partner and some evil and corrupting outside force. So how do you subvert it? Well, one way to do it would be to make the “pure and faithful” character neither “pure” nor “faithful”, to the point where “an outside corrupting force” barely has to do anything to make them fall – which is, in my eyes, *exactly* what happens between Haruka and Sensei if you decide to take the “green path” with her.

While calling Haruka “pure evil” wasn’t exactly the best choice of words on my part, I’ll admit, the point I was trying to make is that, in my eyes, she was *always* harboring those dark thoughts and desires within her – or at least inclinations towards them – unlike pretty much all of the other characters (including Akira and Sekai), who seemingly only began to feel that way after “becoming tainted”. Like, her being very lonely and extremely sexually frustrated is one thing, sure – I don’t really blame Haruka for her relationship with Sensei, necessarily, since in her shoes I would have done it as well – but the rest of it, like the stuff with Nodoka, or Molly, or Kirin? Can you honestly tell me that if Maki/Sara had to live through the exact same set of events as Haruka they would have ended up in the same place? Crossed that same line?

I don’t think so – and *that* is the crux of it all. Haruka only needed a very small push to give in; so small, in fact, that I fully believe all of Sensei’s inner monologues in Chapter 1 in which he repeatedly calls Haruka out on her bullshit in regards to how fake her supposed “love” towards her husband truly is – say what you want about Akira, but he has proven himself to be a very good judge of character (when he actually cares, anyway). The fact that she does nothing despicable on her “red path” isn’t a point towards her virtue – it just means that, with the absence of strong enough temptations, Haruka has chosen the “silent misery” I mentioned in my original post, deciding to fully commit to wearing a mask and pretending to be a “good person”, when she truly isn’t. Speaking from experience, this is an awful way to live, which is where the true tragedy of her “green path” lies: she is much happier being true to herself and becoming a monster (the fiasco with Kirin notwithstanding), but choosing that road means that while everyone else gets to slowly walk away from the darkness and embrace the light in order to finally become “whole”, Haruka’s final destination on the path towards the same goal instead lies at the very bottom of the abyss.

Feel free to disagree with me, of course – as I said, I can easily see the validity of your interpretation of her character, as well. It’s just not how *I* see it, personally. Ultimately, like a certain someone would say, it’s all a matter of perception.

As for the whole “irredeemable” aspect of this discussion, that was just me mostly echoing the general sentiment I’ve seen repeated here a decent number of times (in relation to characters like Akira, Sekai, Ami, Nodoka, Otoha and so on), rather than my own take on the matter. As someone who doesn’t much care for redemption and would be fine with perfectly fine with either outcome for the cast, as long as their endings are narratively fitting and thematically consistent, my point was to try and show people a way to appreciate even the characters they consider “irredeemable” by changing the paradigm and looking at them from another perspective.

Okay, first of all, thank you for writing such a detailed reply and guiding me directly through your thought process. I am fully aware that this isn’t exactly any different from how you usually reply to everyone else, but it still helped me realize that there ended up being *quite a lot* of things in my original post that didn’t came across exactly the way I wanted them to, painting a somewhat incorrect picture of my perspective in the matter. So I’ll correct these inaccuracies first, and then go into a few more details regarding some of your finer points.
Spoiler:
Elaboration
Everything that I said about Haruka was meant to come from a place of empathy and acceptance, not judgement. It wasn’t me taking the high road and blaming someone for being “too weak” and eagerly giving into temptation instead of resisting it to the bitter end “like a good wife should” – it was me gazing into the eyes of someone who voluntarily accepted the call of the abyss, and realizing that I’m looking into a mirror. I see a lot of myself in Haruka – more than in almost every other character in the game, probably, except maybe Nodoka and (partially) Akira – and so for me to truly judge her for what she did, knowing full well *why* she did it, would be nothing but pure hypocrisy. And while “green path” Haruka is, to put it bluntly, a very vile human being – which is something that she herself would openly admit, I’m sure, and I have no issue admitting it as well – I would still stand by her side at the end of the day, simply because I am a fellow weakling who knows what it feels like, if nothing else.
Now, as for the rest of your analysis: it was really good, and I even learned a few new things for myself (I never saw “red paths” for any of the characters except Rin, so I had no idea how Haruka acts if you aren’t having sex with her) – but it was, to stay on-theme, a very “concerned” perspective. Now allow me to share my own – a much more “callous” one:
Spoiler:
Further analysis
When I was originally playing this game, I very quickly caught onto the fact that it is a very intentional deconstruction of the traditional dating sim, masterfully playing around with various tropes that you usually take for granted – like Chapter 1 Sensei having an “honest” mindset of an average eroge player, treating the girls only in terms of “unlocking their H-scenes”, for example, as well as many other things. And so, when Haruka was first introduced and I saw her first few events (“Invisible Worm” especially), my mind immediately interpreted her entire side of the story as a yet another subversion: this time of a very specific “three letter genre” that is *also* a staple in erotic games like this one.
The fundamentals of that entire genre (that shall remain unnamed) are inherently based on the three-way relationship between a “pure and faithful” character, their (usually barely present, non-entity) partner and some evil and corrupting outside force. So how do you subvert it? Well, one way to do it would be to make the “pure and faithful” character neither “pure” nor “faithful”, to the point where “an outside corrupting force” barely has to do anything to make them fall – which is, in my eyes, *exactly* what happens between Haruka and Sensei if you decide to take the “green path” with her.
While calling Haruka “pure evil” wasn’t exactly the best choice of words on my part, I’ll admit, the point I was trying to make is that, in my eyes, she was *always* harboring those dark thoughts and desires within her – or at least inclinations towards them – unlike pretty much all of the other characters (including Akira and Sekai), who seemingly only began to feel that way after “becoming tainted”. Like, her being very lonely and extremely sexually frustrated is one thing, sure – I don’t really blame Haruka for her relationship with Sensei, necessarily, since in her shoes I would have done it as well – but the rest of it, like the stuff with Nodoka, or Molly, or Kirin? Can you honestly tell me that if Maki/Sara had to live through the exact same set of events as Haruka they would have ended up in the same place? Crossed that same line?
I don’t think so – and *that* is the crux of it all. Haruka only needed a very small push to give in; so small, in fact, that I fully believe all of Sensei’s inner monologues in Chapter 1 in which he repeatedly calls Haruka out on her bullshit in regards to how fake her supposed “love” towards her husband truly is – say what you want about Akira, but he has proven himself to be a very good judge of character (when he actually cares, anyway). The fact that she does nothing despicable on her “red path” isn’t a point towards her virtue – it just means that, with the absence of strong enough temptations, Haruka has chosen the “silent misery” I mentioned in my original post, deciding to fully commit to wearing a mask and pretending to be a “good person”, when she truly isn’t. Speaking from experience, this is an awful way to live, which is where the true tragedy of her “green path” lies: she is much happier being true to herself and becoming a monster (the fiasco with Kirin notwithstanding), but choosing that road means that while everyone else gets to slowly walk away from the darkness and embrace the light in order to finally become “whole”, Haruka’s final destination on the path towards the same goal instead lies at the very bottom of the abyss.
Feel free to disagree with me, of course – as I said, I can easily see the validity of your interpretation of her character, as well. It’s just not how *I* see it, personally. Ultimately, like a certain someone would say, it’s all a matter of perception.
As for the whole “irredeemable” aspect of this discussion, that was just me mostly echoing the general sentiment I’ve seen repeated here a decent number of times (in relation to characters like Akira, Sekai, Ami, Nodoka, Otoha and so on), rather than my own take on the matter. As someone who doesn’t much care for redemption and would be fine with perfectly fine with either outcome for the cast, as long as their endings are narratively fitting and thematically consistent, my point was to try and show people a way to appreciate even the characters they consider “irredeemable” by changing the paradigm and looking at them from another perspective.

I'm not interested in excusing Haruka's actions, but just to make an effort to lay it out here, as someone who's been in the position of hurting others for selfish reasons while fancying themselves a decent person:

Self-delusion is a powerful thing. Haruka doesn't - or didn't - see herself as a bad person. She has lived herself a normal life, and never paid much mind to any darker hungers she may have had until her husband's absence wore her psyche down to nothing. She knows how to be a good person though - and she knows how to be and sometimes genuinely is a caring person for those she cares about. She counsels and listens to Rin and Molly and is happy for her friends and employees when they're happy, and is glad to be able to do what she can to make them happy without it being transactional. She does have a "selfish" streak - she seems to have a habit of being bad at actively supporting her friends in times of need because she's too wrapped up in her own thoughts, or doesn't think to think about others. This, at least, is something I've been guilty of (so heck maybe I'm wrong about it and am just projecting).

It's notable that when she's going after Kirin, she says "I don't want to take advantage of you", and also makes rudimentary overtures at "checking in" with her, while also saying "you'll like this". I believe her when she says she doesn't want to take advantage, and also that she genuinely wants to check in and wants Kirin to like it. However, Haruka's hunger - the selfish parts of her nature that she always keeps in check as part of being a 'good everyday person' has overwhelmed her, and her usual amounts of consideration aren't nearly enough to let her stop and actually check in, nor to slap her in the face with the enormity of what she's doing. She says she'll stop calling Kirin pet names then continues doing it. She gets obsessed with Kirin's thighs and doesn't even hear her protestations. Meanwhile, her brain HAS technically been exercising the usual amount of consideration, even as its being completely washed out by her desires ... so the rest of her brain figures that as long as the checking force is in place, she isn't going over the line and is still being a good person - after all, that's what its supposed to be there for, to keep her from going over the line.

Meanwhile, taking advantage of someone is literally exactly what she's doing. It isn't until the heat of the moment has passed, and she's sitting there in front of Sara that her head is clear and she knows EXACTLY what she's done - her desires pull away and her 'normal' perceptions take the reins again and sees it all for what it is. She starts deflecting immediately then, and deflection only happens if you feel guilty. The same happened on a reduced scale with Chika earlier.

I guess what I'm trying to say is that Haruka is someone with no impulse control - and also no perspective. She knew what she wanted was bad, but thought she could mitigate it by technically receiving consent and also showing some sort of consideration while slaking her hunger. She also lacked the perspective to realize that that's impossible when consent is not being given enthusiastically and continually.

Again, none of this is to excuse her behavior. Several serial killers fall under the category of "a person with no impulse control". It does demonstrate that the drives and delusions that create this lack of impulse control are very human, however. Is that evil? I suppose its a question of whether she tries this again after failing so, so spectacularly at having her cake of being a good person and predatorially eating it at the same time.

There's another question to be asked, of is it worse if you do or don't know that the horrible thing you're doing is horrible? What if Haruka had Nodoka's mindset about her own actions, similar to when she aired out Futaba's life against her consent? What if Haruka had zero perception that what she did was wrong, couldn't be swayed from thinking that what she did was right, and actively thinks someone's upset reaction to what she did is only cause the other person didn't sufficiently know her motivations? Is it more horrible if the abuse and exploitation you see someone commit is somehow tangible and relatable, or if its alien and seemingly uncaring? Is that evil?

My own personal answer is that there's no such thing as evil: both possibilities are fucking horrible, for different reasons, and they don't need to be 'evil' to be so. But I can eminently understand other perspectives on this, too.

Edit: its also worth noting that I agree with what others in the thread have said, about how Haruka's hunger and lack of impulse control are as acute and uncontrollable as they are "only" because Sensei decided to go green path, and that without it, Haruka may have still had those desires but would still be able to exist in society not being a bother or abuser to anyone - which colors and textures this tapestry even more.
