posts.content_html_raw:
Okay, so, this is going to be a weird one… Assuming I didn’t miss anything similar among those 60000+ previous posts, I know that there have been that one meme of “femboy Sensei” (from a different game whose name I didn’t bother to write down nor remember) sometime in the past, as well as a few general “out there” theories proposing that Nozomu and/or Akira could have had some repressed gay inclinations as an explanation for some of their behavior, but did anyone ever try to take that line of thought even further?

First of all, just to ease everyone into whatever insanity this attempted “analysis” of mine is shaping up to be, I think it’s fair to point out one generally less relevant, but still particularly notable detail about Sensei’s behavior throughout the first three Chapters (as in, his pre-depression arc): the fact that one of the easiest ways to get a defensive reaction out of him, aside from anything related to Sekai, is to poke fun at his masculinity. This, as far as I’m aware, *never* fails: there are countless scenes of people calling Akira a creep, or a predator, and he just takes it in stride, not bothered in the slightest, which also goes for characters pointing out his other flaws (like his laziness, lack of willpower and dubious understanding of personal borders), but *the second* you bring up anything even remotely tangential to him “not being/acting like a man” he *immediately* claps back with a kindergarten-level retort of some kind, which are nowhere near on the level of his usual eloquence.

Some clearest examples of this can be relatively easily found during many of Akira’s pre-Chapter 4 interactions with Yuki (in her “Pride & Joy” especially, where there is a whole discussion between them about how Akira feels emasculated having to sit behind Yuki on her motorcycle, which in turn prompts a passionate rant about gender norms from her), Io’s “Two Of Us Are Thinking” as well as many of the things that the narrator (likely Pareidolia) says to Akira in “Not the Nightingale”, but even outside of those it is frequently noticeable when he is bantering with many other girls: when they make occasional half-jokes about him acting femininely, being physically weak or, god forbid, his sexual prowess and/or the size of his penis – although I am sadly unable to cite any specific scenes for those examples, because I always just passively paid attention to whenever it happened and never felt any necessity to properly take screenshots/notes.

As an aside to that, there is also a matter of Akira’s very visceral reactions to *any* insinuation of him being on the receiving end of penetrative sex. I can fully understand just not being into anal, sure – there is nothing wrong with that – but the way he almost instinctively recoils during those few scenes when Maki (and Ami in her “Rising to the Challenge”, though Akira is the one to mention it that time) even just voice the idea to fuck him with a strap-on, to me reads like it’s a matter of his ego/pride as a man rather than a simple physical turn-off. None of the girls ever react the same way to the things *they* aren’t into, that’s for sure: for them it’s “no, I’d rather not, thank you”, while Akira over here just immediately goes into full defense mode. And let’s just say, I’ve seen this reaction *a lot* in real life – from men who are very touchy about the subject of their own perceived masculinity.

(Finally, I believe that Sana, after meeting teenage Akira in her TSS, later mentions to someone that he looked very effeminate, but I don’t exactly remember when/if it happens and don’t have a quick way to look it up, so I leave this as just a small side note.)

But, fine. None of it is really all that damning and can technically be explained by some combination of Akira’s own personal hang-ups about stuff (which are always irrational and weird from an outside perspective) as well as him being a literal manchild (due to all of his past traumas), so Sensei reacting like an immature ten/eleven-year-old boy to anything that makes him to feel unmasculine is fairly expected and reasonable, as far as justifications go. However, here’s where we get to part two of my analysis, where things begin to quickly spiral into some truly wacky territory:

There are a few select scenes in the game that directly bring up the idea of Akira either wearing female clothes or otherwise expressing some desire to wear them. Specifically, this happens:

– In “Ode to a Marsh Warbler”, where Sensei looks at Sekai’s dress and comments how “this combination of clothes standing before me is the closest I’ve come to feeling whole since this life began” and that he wants to “wear this dress and look at myself in the mirror”, repeating that “I want to feel it again”.

– In Nodoka’s story that she tells in “Cicadian Rhythm (The Gardener)” that has multiple references to “the closet full of grandmother’s clothes” and how the protagonist of that story wishes to wear them. Now, this one is, admittedly, kinda weak, because I still only barely understand what is going on in that story and have a strong suspicion that it is just as much about Nodoka herself as it is about Akira, so the clothes stuff *could* be related to her instead, but… I dunno. Some parts of it are *absolutely* about Akira (the “vulture in reverse” part, being “back in the place you once were, where your story both begins and ends”, plus the “frozen flower” stuff is almost certainly speaking about Maya), so I put it here regardless.

– In “Every Day Birds (In Nothing But Blood)”, where Sensei makes a metaphor about there being “many doors” with “a new me” behind each of them and says, I quote: “Is there a new me behind this door? Is she [referring to Ami, I believe] playing patty-cake with him? Or dressing him up in women’s clothes as he scoffs and pretends he isn’t enjoying it?”

– In “SENSEI-QUEST”, where during the boss battle with Youdidit and Moyo Sensei randomly says, completely unprompted, that “the only thing I’m afraid of is you making me wear that dress”, which then in turn makes Youdidit question whether this is a reverse psychology thing and is thus a hint that Akira *would* like to wear it (something that he, obviously, vehemently denies).

– And finally, while this one is also kinda weak (and also not even the same thing), Akira’s childhood room that we see in events like “Am I Awake?”, “Lamb Legs” and most recently in “Beach(?) Babe Breakfast Barrage” has what appears to be a female beauty magazine related to makeup or some such (it is on the bottom right shelf, right next to the “cute puppy” one), which is, for all intents and purposes, a very unusual thing to find in a room of a “normal” teenage boy. Hell, to go even further, the room itself looks quite feminine, with no “typical” teenage boy things whatsoever, so unless this room isn’t actually his and rather belongs to Saki (which is technically possible, but this then raises its own questions), Akira’s childhood begins to raise even more questions.

Now, is any of this conclusive? Not at all. But speaking as someone who is *very* into this stuff when it comes up in fiction, it does make me wonder. Which brings me to:

What does it all mean? Well, from everything I listed above, I personally theorize that this is a combination of two things.

For one, there is a non-zero chance that during Akira’s pre-teen and early teen years, in addition to everything else that was happening with Saki, Nozomu and Sekai (or probably even related to all that), he *also* had some kind of gender… thing going on. Not necessarily anything major, but perhaps some occasional attempts at crossdressing, or maybe general feelings of inadequacy due to having a somewhat feminine look and not being “manly” enough – considering everything we know about both Saki and Nozomu and their treatment of Akira, this could very well track. This then significantly backfired somehow (his mother and brother are, once again, likely suspects), which in turn caused Sensei to develop a complex towards any and all potential displays of femininity and made him put all stocks into constantly maintaining the appearance of being a “real man”, explaining why he is so touchy about anything that threatens that facade.

As for the second thing, there is a certain anime (that I won’t name here, but will put under a separate spoiler at the end of the post) about a group of teenagers dealing with a loss of one of their friends, a girl, who died a few years before the beginning of the story. In one of the later episodes, it is revealed that one of these teenagers – a “normal”, fairly masculine boy – has been coping with this loss by secretly wearing one of the dead girl’s dresses late at night, when he is alone, in an attempt to figuratively “bring her back” and once again feel closer to her, at least for a little while. So, returning to Akira, I believe that he *also* may have tried to cope with Sekai’s death by sometimes wearing her dress (as told in “Ode to a Marsh Warbler”), which then only exacerbated the feelings of disgust and shame caused by the aforementioned complex regarding anything feminine and caused him to repress it all even harder.

So. How insane am I for coming up with all of that?

The anime I mentioned is
Anohana: The Flower We Saw That Day.

spoilers.html:
What does it all mean? Well, from everything I listed above, I personally theorize that this is a combination of two things.

For one, there is a non-zero chance that during Akira’s pre-teen and early teen years, in addition to everything else that was happening with Saki, Nozomu and Sekai (or probably even related to all that), he *also* had some kind of gender… thing going on. Not necessarily anything major, but perhaps some occasional attempts at crossdressing, or maybe general feelings of inadequacy due to having a somewhat feminine look and not being “manly” enough – considering everything we know about both Saki and Nozomu and their treatment of Akira, this could very well track. This then significantly backfired somehow (his mother and brother are, once again, likely suspects), which in turn caused Sensei to develop a complex towards any and all potential displays of femininity and made him put all stocks into constantly maintaining the appearance of being a “real man”, explaining why he is so touchy about anything that threatens that facade.

As for the second thing, there is a certain anime (that I won’t name here, but will put under a separate spoiler at the end of the post) about a group of teenagers dealing with a loss of one of their friends, a girl, who died a few years before the beginning of the story. In one of the later episodes, it is revealed that one of these teenagers – a “normal”, fairly masculine boy – has been coping with this loss by secretly wearing one of the dead girl’s dresses late at night, when he is alone, in an attempt to figuratively “bring her back” and once again feel closer to her, at least for a little while. So, returning to Akira, I believe that he *also* may have tried to cope with Sekai’s death by sometimes wearing her dress (as told in “Ode to a Marsh Warbler”), which then only exacerbated the feelings of disgust and shame caused by the aforementioned complex regarding anything feminine and caused him to repress it all even harder.

So. How insane am I for coming up with all of that?

I've definitely noticed some patterns of repressed trauma involving fear of emasculation, but deep down I kinda hope that it doesn't progress into a repressed sexuality. Not because I don't think I could like it per se, but rather I've seen it done countless times and it's rarely given any actual substance or effort. Nothing of value ever comes out of it and most of the time it just comes across as moral pandering for gay acceptance rather than an actual nuanced and pragmatic exploration of a closeted person's experience.

That being said, overcoming the insecurity of emasculation and learning to accept his feminine side could be a great character arc that I could definitely see myself appreciating

I can fully understand just not being into anal, sure – there is nothing wrong with that – but the way he almost instinctively recoils during those few scenes when Maki (and Ami in her “Rising to the Challenge”, though Akira is the one to mention it that time) even just voice the idea to fuck him with a strap-on, to me reads like it’s a matter of his ego/pride as a man rather than a simple physical turn-off. None of the girls ever react the same way to the things *they* aren’t into, that’s for sure: for them it’s “no, I’d rather not, thank you”, while Akira over here just immediately goes into full defense mode. And let’s just say, I’ve seen this reaction *a lot* in real life – from men who are very touchy about the subject of their own perceived masculinity.
(Finally, I believe that Sana, after meeting teenage Akira in her TSS, later mentions to someone that he looked very effeminate, but I don’t exactly remember when/if it happens and don’t have a quick way to look it up, so I leave this as just a small side note.)

spoilers.title: Crazy hour
spoilers.html:
There are a few select scenes in the game that directly bring up the idea of Akira either wearing female clothes or otherwise expressing some desire to wear them. Specifically, this happens:

– In “Ode to a Marsh Warbler”, where Sensei looks at Sekai’s dress and comments how “this combination of clothes standing before me is the closest I’ve come to feeling whole since this life began” and that he wants to “wear this dress and look at myself in the mirror”, repeating that “I want to feel it again”.

– In Nodoka’s story that she tells in “Cicadian Rhythm (The Gardener)” that has multiple references to “the closet full of grandmother’s clothes” and how the protagonist of that story wishes to wear them. Now, this one is, admittedly, kinda weak, because I still only barely understand what is going on in that story and have a strong suspicion that it is just as much about Nodoka herself as it is about Akira, so the clothes stuff *could* be related to her instead, but… I dunno. Some parts of it are *absolutely* about Akira (the “vulture in reverse” part, being “back in the place you once were, where your story both begins and ends”, plus the “frozen flower” stuff is almost certainly speaking about Maya), so I put it here regardless.

– In “Every Day Birds (In Nothing But Blood)”, where Sensei makes a metaphor about there being “many doors” with “a new me” behind each of them and says, I quote: “Is there a new me behind this door? Is she [referring to Ami, I believe] playing patty-cake with him? Or dressing him up in women’s clothes as he scoffs and pretends he isn’t enjoying it?”

– In “SENSEI-QUEST”, where during the boss battle with Youdidit and Moyo Sensei randomly says, completely unprompted, that “the only thing I’m afraid of is you making me wear that dress”, which then in turn makes Youdidit question whether this is a reverse psychology thing and is thus a hint that Akira *would* like to wear it (something that he, obviously, vehemently denies).

– And finally, while this one is also kinda weak (and also not even the same thing), Akira’s childhood room that we see in events like “Am I Awake?”, “Lamb Legs” and most recently in “Beach(?) Babe Breakfast Barrage” has what appears to be a female beauty magazine related to makeup or some such (it is on the bottom right shelf, right next to the “cute puppy” one), which is, for all intents and purposes, a very unusual thing to find in a room of a “normal” teenage boy. Hell, to go even further, the room itself looks quite feminine, with no “typical” teenage boy things whatsoever, so unless this room isn’t actually his and rather belongs to Saki (which is technically possible, but this then raises its own questions), Akira’s childhood begins to raise even more questions.

spoilers.title: Conclusion
spoilers.html:
What does it all mean? Well, from everything I listed above, I personally theorize that this is a combination of two things.

For one, there is a non-zero chance that during Akira’s pre-teen and early teen years, in addition to everything else that was happening with Saki, Nozomu and Sekai (or probably even related to all that), he *also* had some kind of gender… thing going on. Not necessarily anything major, but perhaps some occasional attempts at crossdressing, or maybe general feelings of inadequacy due to having a somewhat feminine look and not being “manly” enough – considering everything we know about both Saki and Nozomu and their treatment of Akira, this could very well track. This then significantly backfired somehow (his mother and brother are, once again, likely suspects), which in turn caused Sensei to develop a complex towards any and all potential displays of femininity and made him put all stocks into constantly maintaining the appearance of being a “real man”, explaining why he is so touchy about anything that threatens that facade.

As for the second thing, there is a certain anime (that I won’t name here, but will put under a separate spoiler at the end of the post) about a group of teenagers dealing with a loss of one of their friends, a girl, who died a few years before the beginning of the story. In one of the later episodes, it is revealed that one of these teenagers – a “normal”, fairly masculine boy – has been coping with this loss by secretly wearing one of the dead girl’s dresses late at night, when he is alone, in an attempt to figuratively “bring her back” and once again feel closer to her, at least for a little while. So, returning to Akira, I believe that he *also* may have tried to cope with Sekai’s death by sometimes wearing her dress (as told in “Ode to a Marsh Warbler”), which then only exacerbated the feelings of disgust and shame caused by the aforementioned complex regarding anything feminine and caused him to repress it all even harder.

I've definitely noticed some patterns of repressed trauma involving fear of emasculation, but deep down I kinda hope that it doesn't progress into a repressed sexuality. Not because I don't think I could like it per se, but rather I've seen it done countless times and it's rarely given any actual substance or effort. Nothing of value ever comes out of it and most of the time it just comes across as moral pandering for gay acceptance rather than an actual nuanced and pragmatic exploration of a closeted person's experience.

That being said, overcoming the insecurity of emasculation and learning to accept his feminine side could be a great character arc that I could definitely see myself appreciating
Click to expand...
I agree.

And, yeah, the way I see it, *if* my interpetation has any merit to it, Akira's situation is almost completely gender-related and has little to nothing to do with his sexuality. He is 100% straight, but simply has a lot of hang-ups related to his masculinity, likely due to the abundance of childhood trauma and forced repression.

From what we see of him in Sana's TSS and various Sekai flashbacks (except "Kyoto"), teenage Akira had a fairly meek, submissive personality, which lines up with a lot of things: one of his main triggers being called a "good boy", all three of his "true loves" having a "bossy" and assertive personality type, his general mother complex, not to mention the fact that Sensei directly states that he dislikes feeling "submissive" just as much as he hates feeling emasculated during the same discussion with Yuki in "Pride & Joy" - so it's likely that, if not for Saki, Nozomu and Sekai, Akira would have grew to become somewhat of a passive bottom. The overcorrection to being overly masculine and dominant is, if I were to venture a guess, just one of the aspects in which he tried to emulate his brother - someone who *was*, from what we know of him, a "true man" in a traditional sense.

Hell, Sekai would even compare her sex life with Nozomu to Akira's performance. His entire life was fucked up, no wonder he (likely) killed himself.

Back to the idea of his current masculinity being an emulation of Nozomu. Well, the little bit we do have about kid Akira was that he masturbated and then blamed it on god or something. This doesn't really point whichever way, but it does suggest he had high sexual energy. And masturbation for a boy is quite normal, so I'd point out that the event that Akira remembers is one very in line with what's expected of a "normal" boy, rather than women's clothes, or something like that.

This is repeated countless times, including when he finds himself close to the line of not taking someone's feelings into consideration (like the Molly incident during Halloween, or when he apologises and gives Karin a clear out). This is very clearly a rule that he set to himself to not be like his brother (or Sekai).

What I think is more likely is that Akira reacts strongly against any form of emasculation, or perceived emasculation, because he was beat to shit for years, locked up in a closet, peed on, and told multiple times he wasn't a man. For my closing thoughts, I'm not convinced Nozomu hasn't raped him. In fact, the narrative that Nozomu was the one that was secretly gay and hurt others because he had his sexuality denied makes much more sense to me. But we'll have to wait and see.

In relation to Akira's parents and their seemingly unknown fate (and also Sekai):

While this is LiL, and so there is always a good chance for a new insane piece of lore to be revealed and then promptly turn everything completely on its head, just from the information we have up to this point it is my belief that both of them have died due to an illness of some kind, possibly diabetes. To be more specific, the full list of relevant details we know about what happened to them is as follows:

– In “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus”, there is a line from Sensei’s POV that goes:

“And I remember many things about when I was young. They all flood back at once. The eyes of old family members who have since passed away due to undiscovered illnesses (or car accidents) leak into my mind.”

Now, the “family members who died due to car accidents” are, you guessed it, Sekai and Nozomu – that much is obvious – but then we have the “undiscovered illnesses” part. Furthermore:

– In “Second Sun”, Youdidit briefly brings up Akira’s parents, saying that “they died a long, long time ago”, the “simple” explanation for which is “diabetes”.

– Also, in “Clockless Watch” Pareidolia briefly mentions both of Akira’s parents, elaborating further after Sensei mentions that he doesn’t remember either of them: for Saki, the God states that “the mixture of childhood trauma and timeline fuckery will do that to you”, but in regards to Yuu he only says that “no one remembers him” and that “his vice was candy”.

– And finally, in “Haiku” Akira says that “[Nozomu] lorded it over me as if He was God himself, blaming me for what happened to my father, blaming me for what happened to my mother”.

So, to reiterate, we have repeated allusion to “an illness” of some kind that took away Sensei’s parents (or maybe there were multiple different illnesses that took them individually, I dunno), and then overlapping perspectives of three different characters: the first one openly mentions diabetes, the second one makes a note out that one of the aforementioned parents was apparently semi-addicted to candy (something that is a pretty bad thing in general, but is *especially* bad if you have diabetes), and then the third one is assured that Akira is to blame for what happened (which doesn’t mean that he’s right, but it’s still *a* perspective).

My guess would be that the timeline goes something like:

1) Akira is somehow involved in Yuu’s death due to diabetes (maybe they got together to eat sweet cake on Akira’s birthday, who knows);

2) Yuu’s death eventually causes Saki to break down, fall physically ill and later also die from an undiscovered/undiagnosed illness of some kind (she seemed pretty mental about Yuu, so that tracks, and this line of reasoning also accounts for Youdidit’s explanation, since diabetes *is* technically the thing that was the root cause for both of these deaths, figuratively speaking);

3) Both brothers are left completely alone, with no immediate family, which forces Nozomu into a caretaker position, similar to Chika/Chinami;

4) Unlike Chika/Chinami, however, Nozomu absolutely hates it and begins abusing his brother as a form of revenge (since, from his point of view, Akira *was* the one to trigger this chain reaction).

As for Sekai’s eventual involvement in all of this, we know that she strongly disliked her family (to the point of even refusing to respond to the family name) and that there was, at least initially, *a lot* of bad blood between Saki and Miu (due to Saki’s stalker-ish actions in regards to Yuu, as seen in “A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)”). So Sekai could have had a brilliant idea of “wow, wouldn’t it make my mom *really* mad if I started dating that one guy from a family she fucking hates ?” – her and Nozomu actually being blood-related could have very easily been just a “happy accident” that neither of them actually knew about, since their relationship clearly started long after Saki’s death (she only appeared in Akira’s life when the abuse was already in full swing), and Miu had a lot of reasons for never openly talking about it (or just also never knowing in the first place) . How does it account for the whole “you were born to someone who understood” line Yasu says to Akira in “Frankincense and Myrrh”? No clue. But we *do* kinda know a decent amount about all four of these characters (five, counting Miu), though a lot of it is, obviously, nothing more than pure speculation based on presented info.

In regards to the rest of your post, though, I fully agree.

“And I remember many things about when I was young. They all flood back at once. The eyes of old family members who have since passed away due to undiscovered illnesses (or car accidents) leak into my mind.”
Now, the “family members who died due to car accidents” are, you guessed it, Sekai and Nozomu – that much is obvious – but then we have the “undiscovered illnesses” part. Furthermore:
– In “Second Sun”, Youdidit briefly brings up Akira’s parents, saying that “they died a long, long time ago”, the “simple” explanation for which is “diabetes”.
– Also, in “Clockless Watch” Pareidolia briefly mentions both of Akira’s parents, elaborating further after Sensei mentions that he doesn’t remember either of them: for Saki, the God states that “the mixture of childhood trauma and timeline fuckery will do that to you”, but in regards to Yuu he only says that “no one remembers him” and that “his vice was candy”.
– And finally, in “Haiku” Akira says that “[Nozomu] lorded it over me as if He was God himself, blaming me for what happened to my father, blaming me for what happened to my mother”.
So, to reiterate, we have repeated allusion to “an illness” of some kind that took away Sensei’s parents (or maybe there were multiple different illnesses that took them individually, I dunno), and then overlapping perspectives of three different characters: the first one openly mentions diabetes, the second one makes a note out that one of the aforementioned parents was apparently semi-addicted to candy (something that is a pretty bad thing in general, but is *especially* bad if you have diabetes), and then the third one is assured that Akira is to blame for what happened (which doesn’t mean that he’s right, but it’s still *a* perspective).

spoilers.title: Theorycrafting
spoilers.html:
1) Akira is somehow involved in Yuu’s death due to diabetes (maybe they got together to eat sweet cake on Akira’s birthday, who knows);

2) Yuu’s death eventually causes Saki to break down, fall physically ill and later also die from an undiscovered/undiagnosed illness of some kind (she seemed pretty mental about Yuu, so that tracks, and this line of reasoning also accounts for Youdidit’s explanation, since diabetes *is* technically the thing that was the root cause for both of these deaths, figuratively speaking);

3) Both brothers are left completely alone, with no immediate family, which forces Nozomu into a caretaker position, similar to Chika/Chinami;

4) Unlike Chika/Chinami, however, Nozomu absolutely hates it and begins abusing his brother as a form of revenge (since, from his point of view, Akira *was* the one to trigger this chain reaction).

As for Sekai’s eventual involvement in all of this, we know that she strongly disliked her family (to the point of even refusing to respond to the family name) and that there was, at least initially, *a lot* of bad blood between Saki and Miu (due to Saki’s stalker-ish actions in regards to Yuu, as seen in “A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)”). So Sekai could have had a brilliant idea of “wow, wouldn’t it make my mom *really* mad if I started dating that one guy from a family she fucking hates ?” – her and Nozomu actually being blood-related could have very easily been just a “happy accident” that neither of them actually knew about, since their relationship clearly started long after Saki’s death (she only appeared in Akira’s life when the abuse was already in full swing), and Miu had a lot of reasons for never openly talking about it (or just also never knowing in the first place) . How does it account for the whole “you were born to someone who understood” line Yasu says to Akira in “Frankincense and Myrrh”? No clue. But we *do* kinda know a decent amount about all four of these characters (five, counting Miu), though a lot of it is, obviously, nothing more than pure speculation based on presented info.

Okay, so, I effectively went through an entire mini-arc while trying to gather my thoughts on how to respond to your comment.

My first reaction was an excited "holy shit, this makes so much sense, I can't believe I never thought of that myself, seems very obvious in retrospect", and I had an entire rant prepared on how me being ETL (English third language, basically self-taught) lead me to mistakenly believe that the line "born to someone who understood" could *only* refer to the mother, Saki, and never even consider that it could have been referring to Yuu instead. I felt like quite an idiot for a moment there.

But then I actually went into my notes to re-check the specifics of what Yasu says in "Frankincense & Myrrh", and the *full* quote actually goes like this:

“[…] you are the product of something wonderful. You learned to crawl in the light of someone who understood the importance of that light. If you listen closely, you’ll hear her voice. She whispers your name. Reminds you of a time when things were better. Before that light began to dim and you were forced to crawl in the dark instead.”

With that added context, Yuu being the one she is talking about seems very, *very* unlikely. Even ignoring the repeated mentions of “she” and “her”, which by itself is already a huge dealbreaker, the text specifically implies that Akira was not only “born to” that person, but also raised by them – and the only one who fits that role is Saki, considering that pretty much all of the current evidence suggests she was a single mother who never got over her first love (refer to Pareidolia’s monologue in “Goodnight Moon” for the clearest indication of that).

To go even further, the scene that follows directly *after* Yasu says all of this stuff about "being born to someone who understood" is her transporting Akira back to his old childhood room – something that she then clarifies is explicitly done with HOPE’s blessing, because he wants Sensei to “fill his lungs with nostalgic air he’d wake up to every single day before he lost touch with the meaning of this world” and make Akira “feel as if he belongs”. None of this makes any particular sense if we suppose Yuu is the one they were talking about this entire time, because the guy was seemingly never a part of their actual family, but it makes *perfect* sense if we read this scene as an older brother (Nozomu) taking his younger brother (Akira) to their old family home, trying to invoke nostalgic memories of the time before their beloved mother (Saki) tragically passed away.

Now, there are two potential counterpoints to this interpretation that I can already envision, and I’ll try to preempt them here:

The first one is the idea that the “she” Yasu is referring to is not actually Saki, but rather Sekai. Almost all of the things Yasu says *do* technically fit both of them, like the stuff about effectively raising Akira or reminding him of “better times”, and the part about “losing touch with the meaning of this world” is generally *only* used for Sekai if we look at the rest of the text. However – from my understanding, anyway – the game strongly implies that HOPE/Yasu and Sekai are actually *enemies*, not allies (the way Yasu reacts to touching Sekai’s heart within Kaori in “Fruits of Torment” says it all, in my opinion), and so it would be strange for her to speak about Sekai so highly if “someone who understood” *was* supposed to be her. I also just can’t see HOPE being all like “yeah, dude, let’s return to the nostalgic time when you were fucking my wife”, especially with the context from “Second Sun”, but this might just be me mistakenly equating HOPE and Nozomu – which is a whole separate can of worms. Finally, Yasu also says something about “revealing the voice of the one who follows you”, which, as I interpret it, *does* refer to Sekai, as Sensei only started feeling that “something is following me” after her return in “Inai inai… baa!” (“Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)” also substantiates this theory, if we look at it as Sensei’s desperate attempt to escape from Sekai backfiring spectacularly, because he somehow chose *the one person* who was *also* part-Sekai, resulting in Sekaori kissing him at the end of that event.)

The second counterpoint is the fact that this interpretation of both Saki and HOPE being these semi-benevolent figures who cared/care for Akira and only wish the best for him doesn’t exactly align with what we know of them from the rest of the story, even more so considering Yasu’s own words about how Saki “didn’t like [Akira] very much”. This one, however, is much easier to explain, because Yasu has *also* been on the record of repeatedly denying the “callous” aspect of HOPE, insisting that it’s just a misunderstanding made by those who “don’t see the true light” and that HOPE is actually very fair, and just, and yada-yada-yada – hell, she even does it during that very same scene in "Frankincense & Myrrh", asking Sensei whether HOPE taking him to his childhood room “truly seem like a callous gesture to you”. So I can 100% believe that Yasu could have easily justified Saki’s abuse/neglect towards Akira as a form of “harsh love” that was all “for the greater good” because she “understood the importance of the light”, thus portraying her as mostly caring and benevolent despite her earlier words and what the rest of the narrative seems to be implying.

To go even further, the scene that follows directly *after* Yasu says all of this stuff about "being born to someone who understood" is her transporting Akira back to his old childhood room – something that she then clarifies is explicitly done with HOPE’s blessing, because he wants Sensei to “fill his lungs with nostalgic air he’d wake up to every single day before he lost touch with the meaning of this world” and make Akira “feel as if he belongs”. None of this makes any particular sense if we suppose Yuu is the one they were talking about this entire time, because the guy was seemingly never a part of their actual family, but it makes *perfect* sense if we read this scene as an older brother (Nozomu) taking his younger brother (Akira) to their old family home, trying to invoke nostalgic memories of the time before their beloved mother (Saki) tragically passed away.

spoilers.title: Further reasoning
spoilers.html:
The first one is the idea that the “she” Yasu is referring to is not actually Saki, but rather Sekai. Almost all of the things Yasu says *do* technically fit both of them, like the stuff about effectively raising Akira or reminding him of “better times”, and the part about “losing touch with the meaning of this world” is generally *only* used for Sekai if we look at the rest of the text. However – from my understanding, anyway – the game strongly implies that HOPE/Yasu and Sekai are actually *enemies*, not allies (the way Yasu reacts to touching Sekai’s heart within Kaori in “Fruits of Torment” says it all, in my opinion), and so it would be strange for her to speak about Sekai so highly if “someone who understood” *was* supposed to be her. I also just can’t see HOPE being all like “yeah, dude, let’s return to the nostalgic time when you were fucking my wife”, especially with the context from “Second Sun”, but this might just be me mistakenly equating HOPE and Nozomu – which is a whole separate can of worms. Finally, Yasu also says something about “revealing the voice of the one who follows you”, which, as I interpret it, *does* refer to Sekai, as Sensei only started feeling that “something is following me” after her return in “Inai inai… baa!” (“Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)” also substantiates this theory, if we look at it as Sensei’s desperate attempt to escape from Sekai backfiring spectacularly, because he somehow chose *the one person* who was *also* part-Sekai, resulting in Sekaori kissing him at the end of that event.)

The second counterpoint is the fact that this interpretation of both Saki and HOPE being these semi-benevolent figures who cared/care for Akira and only wish the best for him doesn’t exactly align with what we know of them from the rest of the story, even more so considering Yasu’s own words about how Saki “didn’t like [Akira] very much”. This one, however, is much easier to explain, because Yasu has *also* been on the record of repeatedly denying the “callous” aspect of HOPE, insisting that it’s just a misunderstanding made by those who “don’t see the true light” and that HOPE is actually very fair, and just, and yada-yada-yada – hell, she even does it during that very same scene in "Frankincense & Myrrh", asking Sensei whether HOPE taking him to his childhood room “truly seem like a callous gesture to you”. So I can 100% believe that Yasu could have easily justified Saki’s abuse/neglect towards Akira as a form of “harsh love” that was all “for the greater good” because she “understood the importance of the light”, thus portraying her as mostly caring and benevolent despite her earlier words and what the rest of the narrative seems to be implying.

Plenty of reasons I can imagine for wanting to break things!

Ami caused Maya Primes death in the lead up to that reset, and her body was also found ritualistically sacrificed(Twice now, interestingly!).

Sekai is influencing Koko(Or whatever Nodoka's moms name was), who is Influencing Nodoka. Nodoka, through her attempts to use sex to break the world, opens the way for Ami to slip in. Ami slips in, and then immediately sets into motion the events needed to kill off the only 'real' rival she has, which is Maya Prime. Maya dies, and she immediately inserts herself as the only way to fix Sensei.

In regards to "why Ami decides to show her true and highly vicious colors now rather than just keep feigning ignorance, playing along, blocking out, or whatever plot-convenient shit she does to remain incognito" – I think the reason for that is pretty simple, actually. It only *seems* strange and complicated because people are looking at it from the perspective of meta/narrative significance rather than just normal psychology and character writing, seeking some hidden ploy or a 5D-chess move made by Selebus where there is none. Now, the usual disclaimers of “it’s just my interpretation” and “I am not insisting that everyone who thinks otherwise is wrong” aside, here’s the long and short of it:

Basically – discounting the whole stuff about Ami’s partial retaining of memories with eventual recollection that was mentioned by Himawari in 0.53, which *is* relevant to what I’m about to say, but only tangentially – what happens to Ami throughout the first three Chapters of the story is the exact same thing that happens to Maya Prime: every “new” thing that occurs within the loops as a consequence of *this* Sensei being the “true” one starts to very gradually chip away at their masks, making it progressively more and more difficult to hide who both of them truly are.

Maya is someone who got pretty much broken by the world itself, forced into an eternal Hell of having to perpetually maintain this distant and uncaring façade in order to protect both herself and Sensei. She effectively resigned herself to the life of misery, preferring this suffocating status quo to even *the slightest* chance of possible annihilation. But then this Akira comes along, achieving things she thought were no longer possible: remembering things without his mind exploding, making progress with the Resets, roping other people into retaining their memories – and so it gets harder and harder for her to pretend that she hates him and finds him disgusting, when what she *truly* wants (and has always wanted) is to jump his bones right then and there. For her, the cracking of the mask is a good thing: she never wanted to wear it in the first place and is thus more than happy to see more and more fractures appearing on its surface. But for Ami, it’s the exact opposite.

Ami’s perfect world *relies* on her pretending to be a ditzy, air-headed niece who is hopelessly in love and posing zero threat to anyone, because that’s who she *wants* to be, but no longer *is*: living through billions upon billions of Resets fundamentally changed who she is as a person (because it is literally impossible to experience something like that and still remain exactly the same), and so she has no option *but* to wear a mask if she wants to truly be happy with Sensei – except, to her great dismay, the entire story thus far has been about everything progressively moving farther and farther away from the status quo she so desperately desires, which makes Ami very, very unhappy.

So while Maya openly celebrates the inevitable destruction of her façade, Ami both dreads it and yet is unable to actually do anything to prevent it from happening, as any attempt to counter it on her part ends up only accelerating this destruction – this effectively explains Ami showing more and more unhinged moments as we go from Chapter 1 to Chapter 2 and then from Chapter 2 to Chapter 3, as it becomes increasingly harder for her to still pretend to be pure and innocent when reality itself conspires to test this poor girl’s composure at pretty much every opportunity.

So, no, Ami isn’t really planning anything; she isn’t preparing some grand master plan, and there is no hidden endgame for her outside of the things that have already been revealed – she simply stopped giving a shit, plain and simple.

I don't think that's the issue that's being raised. It's very easy to cherry-pick evidence of Ami being aware and go "it was there all along!".
The issue that people have raised plenty of times throughout the replays of the end of 2024, when we started examining the Ami reveal, is that it is inconsistent. At times events do showcase that Ami knew everything all along, and at times they really don't. Which led to the theory of Ami remembering things at some point, or her having split personality.

This was later explained in 0.53 by Himawari saying that her mindwipe never takes for long, but it does take for some time. Does this erase every inconsistency, since we do know when the resets happen and could examine if the inconsistency of her not knowing follows this pattern? I don't know. I'll take a look at it in a future playthrough.
But without this explanation from Himawari in 0.53, just going "there were clues and I noticed it a long time ago!" would be ignoring the clues that she did not know, which are also there - because Ami doesn't seem to know all the time.

In relation to Akira's parents and their seemingly unknown fate (and also Sekai):

While this is LiL, and so there is always a good chance for a new insane piece of lore to be revealed and then promptly turn everything completely on its head, just from the information we have up to this point it is my belief that both of them have died due to an illness of some kind, possibly diabetes. To be more specific, the full list of relevant details we know about what happened to them is as follows:

– In “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus”, there is a line from Sensei’s POV that goes:

“And I remember many things about when I was young. They all flood back at once. The eyes of old family members who have since passed away due to undiscovered illnesses (or car accidents) leak into my mind.”

Now, the “family members who died due to car accidents” are, you guessed it, Sekai and Nozomu – that much is obvious – but then we have the “undiscovered illnesses” part. Furthermore:

– In “Second Sun”, Youdidit briefly brings up Akira’s parents, saying that “they died a long, long time ago”, the “simple” explanation for which is “diabetes”.

– Also, in “Clockless Watch” Pareidolia briefly mentions both of Akira’s parents, elaborating further after Sensei mentions that he doesn’t remember either of them: for Saki, the God states that “the mixture of childhood trauma and timeline fuckery will do that to you”, but in regards to Yuu he only says that “no one remembers him” and that “his vice was candy”.

– And finally, in “Haiku” Akira says that “[Nozomu] lorded it over me as if He was God himself, blaming me for what happened to my father, blaming me for what happened to my mother”.

So, to reiterate, we have repeated allusion to “an illness” of some kind that took away Sensei’s parents (or maybe there were multiple different illnesses that took them individually, I dunno), and then overlapping perspectives of three different characters: the first one openly mentions diabetes, the second one makes a note out that one of the aforementioned parents was apparently semi-addicted to candy (something that is a pretty bad thing in general, but is *especially* bad if you have diabetes), and then the third one is assured that Akira is to blame for what happened (which doesn’t mean that he’s right, but it’s still *a* perspective).

My guess would be that the timeline goes something like:

1) Akira is somehow involved in Yuu’s death due to diabetes (maybe they got together to eat sweet cake on Akira’s birthday, who knows);

2) Yuu’s death eventually causes Saki to break down, fall physically ill and later also die from an undiscovered/undiagnosed illness of some kind (she seemed pretty mental about Yuu, so that tracks, and this line of reasoning also accounts for Youdidit’s explanation, since diabetes *is* technically the thing that was the root cause for both of these deaths, figuratively speaking);

3) Both brothers are left completely alone, with no immediate family, which forces Nozomu into a caretaker position, similar to Chika/Chinami;

4) Unlike Chika/Chinami, however, Nozomu absolutely hates it and begins abusing his brother as a form of revenge (since, from his point of view, Akira *was* the one to trigger this chain reaction).

As for Sekai’s eventual involvement in all of this, we know that she strongly disliked her family (to the point of even refusing to respond to the family name) and that there was, at least initially, *a lot* of bad blood between Saki and Miu (due to Saki’s stalker-ish actions in regards to Yuu, as seen in “A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)”). So Sekai could have had a brilliant idea of “wow, wouldn’t it make my mom *really* mad if I started dating that one guy from a family she fucking hates ?” – her and Nozomu actually being blood-related could have very easily been just a “happy accident” that neither of them actually knew about, since their relationship clearly started long after Saki’s death (she only appeared in Akira’s life when the abuse was already in full swing), and Miu had a lot of reasons for never openly talking about it (or just also never knowing in the first place) . How does it account for the whole “you were born to someone who understood” line Yasu says to Akira in “Frankincense and Myrrh”? No clue. But we *do* kinda know a decent amount about all four of these characters (five, counting Miu), though a lot of it is, obviously, nothing more than pure speculation based on presented info.

In regards to the rest of your post, though, I fully agree.

I actually find it completely believable, but not for any obvious reasons. I have two Ami theories that I've been kicking around as things have progressed

1. The Ami from Chapter 1, and Ami from Chapter 3 are completely different people:

What if Ami is an 'Incursion' of sorts, from one of the many other Universes? Someone who learned how to slip from her home Universe to whichever Universe the "Real" Akira is currently in. She kills or replaces current Ami, and just continues her life. One thing that caught me as really odd was when Sensei was in the alternate timeline with Sekai alive, and Ami as their daughter. They mention being worried that he had broken again, and needed to get the "Jars", which IYKYK. It seems either this is something that frequently happens to all versions of Akira, OR, it only happens to Akira Prime, and this Ami and Sekai have had experience with him before. Ami definitely makes it clear in the Broken Akira events that she thinks the only way to heal him is with this bizarre, horrid ritual jar milking. That's not something Ami would have been doing the FIRST time Akira was broken. IE when Sekai died, as Ami was like 7 or whatever. So where did that knowledge come from, if not from either another timeline, OR:

2. Ami from Chapter 1 is the same Ami all along, just pretending because she needs events to play out VERY specifically for some goal:

If this is the case, then she has even more knowledge than Maya does, who has been the focal point of the loop since the start. Ami from Chapter 3 on never seems fully surprised, while Maya's future knowledge seemed to stop around the end of Chapter 1. So maybe Ami, when aware that the Akira she is dealing with is Akira Prime, knows she needs to let things play out in a specific way to push the Universe towards some specific goal? What that goal is, I dunno. Maybe the resurrection of Sekai permanently? To break the Universe hard enough that she can steal Akira back to her own timeline where Sekai isn't dead? She certainly acts like someone that has gone through these various events multiple times.

Plenty of reasons I can imagine for wanting to break things!

I lean towards Option 1 for one reason:

Ami caused Maya Primes death in the lead up to that reset, and her body was also found ritualistically sacrificed(Twice now, interestingly!).

If I had to guess HOW it happens?

Sekai is influencing Koko(Or whatever Nodoka's moms name was), who is Influencing Nodoka. Nodoka, through her attempts to use sex to break the world, opens the way for Ami to slip in. She was obviously expecting something to happen from the multi hour long sexual romp she had with Sensei in the build up to the Karaoke scene, but the only thing we see is Futaba teleporting through her Symposium event. But what if that's because the REAL fallout was happening elsewhere:

Ami slips in, and then immediately sets into motion the events needed to kill off the only 'real' rival she has, which is Maya Prime. Maya dies, and she immediately inserts herself as the only way to fix Sensei.

I tend toward the two Ami theory but I don't think Psycho Ami killed and replaced the other Ami, at least not permanently. I think she can slip into this universe's Ami when she needs to, but otherwise let's her counterpart run things, and that's why she can switch between traumatized teenager and collected supervillain so easily.
I don't have definitive evidence for this but I'd point to the end of .53. There's no way the Ami that casually threatened to kill Akira is the same one that went into a nervous breakdown over accidently nicking his hand with scissors.

In regards to Sekai, Sensei said that she first entered his life because his brother "met a girl", and she didn't even know Akira existed before she found him in the closet. I think this establishes that Akira and Nozomu didn't know that Sekai was their sister. On the other hand, I suspect that Sekai did know - her obsession with incest and "keeping the bloodline strong" would explain her initial interest in Nozomu.

There's an old idea worth mentioning here that Yuu's children come from different timelines. I don't know if I really believe it, but it has become a lot more plausible after what we've learned about people moving between worlds, both voluntarily and not. (Brief version: Sekai comes from a timeline where Yuu completed the "Miu route", Akira and Nozomu from one where he completed the "Saki route". They first met when Sekai and Nozomu were adults because she somehow managed to travel to a different world which had brothers she could fuck without anyone knowing they're related.)
Click to expand...
Huh. Thank you for pointing out the Niki line from “Beauty in What's Broken” – I must have somehow completely blacked out on the fact that she said this, as it doesn’t show anywhere in my notes.

Saki still being in the picture at that point in time does indeed contradict my earlier proposed timeline, and while I wasn't particularly gung-ho about its validity or anything, I’m… not really sure how to mentally reconcile all of my assumptions about things relating to Sekai and Nozomu with the idea that both the abuse and the illicit relationship between Akira and Sekai were apparently going on *while* Saki was still alive. Maybe she was like Kyoko: technically present, but not *truly* there, even if not necessarily to the same extent? That could potentially work, and still line up with the majority of my previous guesses. I will have to think on it some more at a later date.

As for the Yuu stuff, on a slightly unrelated note, it does kinda make me wonder how this supposed remake of Nothing is Beautiful that Selebus plans to make after LiL would even look like. Because I would assume that, with how many direct connections to NiB characters there currently are in the game (and their number is only going to grow as the narrative develops further), by the time Lessons in Love finishes we are going to have a fairly decent idea of who most of the Terminal 22 inhabitants were and how they ultimately ended up – like, I can’t imagine that Saki’s eventual fate doesn’t *directly* relate to the childhood development of both Akira and Nozomu, or that who Miu grew up to be as an adult and a mother didn’t at least partially influence the person Sekai ended up becoming.

And so going from LiL, where learning *anything* about *anyone* is a huge struggle, to the point where we’re 150+ hours in and people are still speculating about most of the stuff, to this new story where it’s like “yep, I know who you are; yep, I know what happens to you” is… weird to think about. I’m sure Selebus will find a way to somehow make it work, perhaps with alternate timelines/routes that branch into a brand new future where some wacky things happen, but what I *am* 100% certain of is that reading Nothing is Beautiful (*if* it ever actually gets remade, that is) will be a completely different experience from reading Lessons in Love.

Yes, and we have an answer for that in the way of trigger guides that are posted a few hours after the release. There's a link to it on the first page. So, for people that are up to date with the update, they follow the trigger guides. For people that are late to the update by two weeks, or doing a replay - it's the trigger guide all the way.
In your case, the current runtime of this game is about a month and a half of reading time (without skipping anything), so the two weeks will not be an issue at all for a long while. I do recommend you downloading it because 1. it's not intrusive at all, the only way to use it is to bring up the menu and check what the requirements for the next events are. It won't show up in your game otherwise. And 2. is that there will be many times where the requirements and triggers will very much not be logical. Like having to phone someone at a specific time of day, of a specific day.

Another point of consideration is that you can miss events on this game. This is taken to be called "the red path", because when you miss an event it turns red. If you care about seeing every single event of the game in a single playthrough, the guide will also help with that. Again, if you care to check it between events.

Lastly, this game has puzzles from time to time, and the guide doesn't cover that. So you'll have to come here for that as well (there's a simplified document linked on the first page, and an in-depth guide to each one on their respective trigger guides - at least for the newer ones).

Though, obviously that was the start. It doesn't mean it kept being just that over the years. After all, NAO does state that the both of them perceived it as actual love. Inai inai baa has Sekai saying she played with Akira, which is quite weird for her to play with a child his age when she meets him, but I guess he would have been completely broken mentally.
Then "Kyoto" states that Nozomu became physically abusive of Sekai, that Akira witnessed many of her episodes, and that she got pregnant. Intepretation could go either way about her shock, it being either that she was shocked that Akira would reject her for having Nozomu's child, or that she really was out of her mind trying to get a teenager to flee with his groomer to have their child.

Akira then starts to have a life again, meets up with Niki, and has an ongoing relationship with Sekai for years. Sekai starts getting physically abused by Nozomu for some reason, and presents (likely) the same blackouts Akira has.

Sekai gets pregnant with Ami and tries to get Akira to flee with her to Kyoto. He refuses and this likely changes their relationship, if nothing else because Ami is born and she has to be a mother. One year prior to her death, Sekai's episodes deteriorate to such an extent that Ami is quite aware of it, and yet Akira is unable to/refuses to help her.

Sekai dies in a car accident alongside Nozomu. Akira breaks up with Niki, adopts Ami and begins tutoring. After a time he starts tutoring Noriko (that is sent as an attempt to keep an eye on him). He then makes the wish for Maya, "adopts" Maya and stops tutoring Noriko (likely at Maya's behest). He is then fatherly towards Ami's friend Ayane, and Maya covertly makes friends with them. Moving to Maya cucking Ami her entire life, while Ayane is clueless to the situation. Fast-forward to teaching at their school, and Akira starts going after Yumi. Akira's possible suicide and Maya makes a wish.

We don't know at which point Saki and Yuu die. But i'd assume that it was before Sekai's death, for the simple fact that they don't offer to adopt Ami. No mention of Miu either, but that's not surprising given that Sekai likely hated her.

By the way, while we’re still on the subject of Saki and Yuu, there is a certain glaring detail that (as far as I’m aware) hasn’t really been brought up in discussion yet, and it’s a detail that deepens the mystery of whatever the fuck was going on in Terminal 22 even further:
the fact that Saki had *two* children, not *one*.

Like, how did that even happen? If it was just one child – which, timeline-wise, would logically have to be Nozomu – I could easily see it just being the case of Yuu double-timing Saki and Miu due to his inability to choose between them, accidentally getting both of the girls pregnant and then deciding (or perhaps being forced) to ultimately stay with Miu and start a proper family with her, thus abandoning Saki to deal with pregnancy on her own. Or perhaps it happened some other way, but the result of “two different women, two different children” ultimately doesn’t change much regardless of the specifics – the situation isn’t that far-fetched either way.

Yet Saki got pregnant *twice*. We know that Nozomu and Akira aren’t twins, as there was a fairly significant age difference between them: Nozomu was old enough to marry Sekai while Akira was still just barely a teenager. And since there is zero evidence that Saki ever got together with anyone else, with all clues pointing to her being a single mother who never married and was raising the boys alone, does this imply that Yuu was also the father the second time, meaning that he somehow got together with Saki *again* after at least half a decade of being married to another woman and also having a daughter?

I mean, Pareidolia’s comment in “Goodnight Moon” about how Saki used to come to Akira’s room at night and “cry into your shoulder, screaming at the top of her lungs at how you smelled like him” pretty much confirms it, but then this just opens a whole separate can of worms. What exactly was the relationship between Yuu, Saki and Miu in their adult years? Did Miu know that Yuu was secretly cheating on her? Did *Sekai* know? Was *that* the reason why she got together with Nozomu in the first place? Or if Miu and Yuu had already got divorced by that point, why didn’t he just officially marry Saki?

I don’t really have answers to any of these questions – nor even any particularly good guesses, to be completely honest – but I was just going through some of my notes I made upon seeing “A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)” for the first time, trying to further connect the dots between the characters from Terminal 22, and this specific detail immediately stuck out to me.

If it was just one child – which, timeline-wise, would logically have to be Nozomu – I could easily see it just being the case of Yuu double-timing Saki and Miu due to his inability to choose between them, accidentally getting both of the girls pregnant and then deciding (or perhaps being forced) to ultimately stay with Miu and start a proper family with her, thus abandoning Saki to deal with pregnancy on her own. Or perhaps it happened some other way, but the result of “two different women, two different children” ultimately doesn’t change much regardless of the specifics – the situation isn’t that far-fetched either way.
Yet Saki got pregnant *twice*. We know that Nozomu and Akira aren’t twins, as there was a fairly significant age difference between them: Nozomu was old enough to marry Sekai while Akira was still just barely a teenager. And since there is zero evidence that Saki ever got together with anyone else, with all clues pointing to her being a single mother who never married and was raising the boys alone, does this imply that Yuu was also the father the second time, meaning that he somehow got together with Saki *again* after at least half a decade of being married to another woman and also having a daughter?
I mean, Pareidolia’s comment in “Goodnight Moon” about how Saki used to come to Akira’s room at night and “cry into your shoulder, screaming at the top of her lungs at how you smelled like him” pretty much confirms it, but then this just opens a whole separate can of worms. What exactly was the relationship between Yuu, Saki and Miu in their adult years? Did Miu know that Yuu was secretly cheating on her? Did *Sekai* know? Was *that* the reason why she got together with Nozomu in the first place? Or if Miu and Yuu had already got divorced by that point, why didn’t he just officially marry Saki?
I don’t really have answers to any of these questions – nor even any particularly good guesses, to be completely honest – but I was just going through some of my notes I made upon seeing “A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)” for the first time, trying to further connect the dots between the characters from Terminal 22, and this specific detail immediately stuck out to me.

You will basically be busy for 100 or so hours before you catch up with the current update, so it would take weeks anyway.

"Everything is Connected" has to be triggered during the reset. You can miss it either by not visiting the soccer field, or not having enough progression with Miku. The error there is that it should not be present in your guide anymore.

To make sure, go over the happy event tab, and there should be a red crossed line event in the place where "Everything is Connected" should be.

Ouch. This, coming from a girl who previously would break into his room to sleep? From someone with HER background? That this poor girl later decides that she still loves Akira, and wants to be around him, and thinks the only way she can be is by being "available" to him isn't progress...it's trauma response.

Saying no, proving that SHE can have a choice in how her body is used, is the fundamentally correct option. We WANT to see Akira grow as a person, especially considering the events of 0.53. We need to take him from the version of him that is fine with Wizard Path, fine with breaking Io, to the version of him that finds a way to Aomori.

If we take the Aomori future as the "Best" ending, then at some point Akira stops wanting to fuck everything that moves, becomes a better person, and settles down with Ayane.

Consider Himawari's words: "You think you can just take a shortcut to happiness?! That my mistake is enough to carry you from WHO you are now to WHO you'll be for me?! That's something you have to do on your own! No amount of meddling is going to fix that, no matter how much I want it to!"

Ultimately, Akira becomes a better person eventually, without the knowledge that he has to be. He has to make that choice...and seeing as we're the ones that control him...ultimately we need to make that choice for him.

In fiction there is a trope called Subversion of Expectations that pops up fairly often. Selebus makes use of it often.

Subverting expectations means the author deliberately leads the reader to predict Outcome A, then delivers Outcome B, but in a way that still makes sense, but only in retrospect.

-Key traits:

-The reader’s prediction is reasonable

-The author knew the ending all along

-The reversal is intentional, not a mistake

-On reread, the behavior feels inevitable

Considering the type of game that LIL is; Horror, Parody, with a huge dose of mind fuckery...I think Selebus is leading us on when he says that Green Path is the intended path.

From a "Content" perspective, then yes, to see it all, green path is the path to take.

From a "Character" perspective, if you expect Akira to grow as a person, some level of red path is to be expected. Chapter 3/4 is all about Akira trying to grow as a person, figure out why he's so fucked up, and how he can be a better person for the people he cares about. Last time I played through the beginning of the game, I came away with the impression that Ami knew what was going on from the start. Here's four clues to that effect (with the benefit of hindsight):


Maya Prime created the journal as a way to introduce fake Senseis to the world. It didn't exist before the resets, so Ami shouldn't know about it after a factory reset. She also claims not to know what's in it but clearly does, and pushes Sensei to study it for the exact reason that Maya had in mind: learn enough so that he can maintain the pretense that he's the same guy.

The book is conspicuously sitting out on Sensei's table because someone placed it there during the reset. That could have been Maya, but I have to suspect Ami at least knows it's there with the way she's pushing him to read it.



If this was a freshly rebooted Ami, she should have only been calling him Sensei for a few months. Before high school, he was never her teacher or her tutor.

The "role-playing" comment hints at her belief that he's another fake Akira.


Obviously this has a purpose outside the story: Selebus wants to introduce the game to the readers. But I think what Ami does goes far beyond what's necessary. For example, she introduces all of the places where Sensei can find girls to groom, even when there's no in-universe reason for her to send him there; it would have been more natural to introduce the shrine (to pick an example) by having Sensei walk around and stumble on it the first time you choose to go there.


There's no way that Ami really wants Sensei to get actual medical help. If he was having a real mental episode, we know now what Ami would do: shift into caretaker mode and try to isolate him from the rest of the world. In her mind, he doesn't need to be cured because he's already perfect.

She also acts like Sensei's brain malfunctioning is a completely new thing, but that's not true at all. He went into a catatonic state after Sekai's accident, and has been experiencing hallucinations and other weird brain stuff for at least that long.


Ami of course would be fully aware of this, even an Ami who has just been reset.

For her to draw no connection between his "amnesia" and his preexisting brain issues is extremely suspicious.

Bonus clue from much later in the game, but also pertaining to the first scenes:
During her breakdown, Ami quotes verbatim from the O. Henry story "The Gift of the Magi". This is both topical (she cut her hair off) and thematic (the two of them are supposed to be partners who sacrifice to support each other, but Sensei hasn't held up his part of the bargain).

Abruptly, she switches to quoting the things she said at the beginning of the game. I think she goes from one memorized work to another - her beginning speech is something she's prepared and practiced over and over for different Senseis.

And she reinforces that by explaining how Sensei was supposed to respond to her tutorial.
My belief continues to be:
  • Ami has known about the resets from the start.
  • She remained stagnant and was afraid to grow as a person or risk change in the world, but she wasn't murdering anyone or trying to advance some master plan. She was content to play her role for an unending stream of fake Senseis.
  • She has a mental infection that has caused her to go increasingly mad and do things she otherwise wouldn't, culminating in "Della".
I think the last point especially is being ignored by everyone taking the "Evil Ami has always been here" claim at face value. Her infection was growing for multiple chapters before Evil Ami's sudden reveal, and it's in the narration as well so it's not just an act.

Bingoogus said:
How do you reconcile that with Sekai playing peekaboo with what pretty much has to be a baby Akira? That game stops working by the first birthday for just about all kids as they gain object permanence by that point...
Click to expand...
I agree that it doesn't make much sense. Moonflare covered the relevant info, but I'll give my own perspective. Ghost Sekai says that Akira played peekaboo with her as well as with his mother.
On the other hand, Sensei is unambiguous when he describes his trauma to Noriko: unless he's lying or incorrect, before Sekai found him in the closet he had never met her and she didn't even know he existed.
  • Possibility #1: Sekai was around him as a baby, but left before he was old enough to remember her, then returned later on. But if that were the case, surely Nozomu and Saki would know who she is.
  • Possibility #2: Sekai played peekaboo with a five-year-old (or whatever). Could it have helped a traumatized kid come out of his shell? It doesn't seem likely to me, but I don't know much about child psychology.
  • Possibility #3: One of them is lying. Of the two, I'm more inclined to trust a seemingly sane Sensei than a Ghost Sekai appearing directly in his malfunctioning mind. I can't come up with any reason for Sensei to lie to Noriko about it.
  • Possibility #4: Some weird timeline thing, like Sekai met Akira as a baby in this world's timeline, but Sensei didn't meet her until later in his original world. I'm throwing this in for completeness, but I'm not giving it any credence unless we get concrete evidence that there were multiple versions of Akira's childhood.

Yummyjuice22 said:
Loving the game so far, I just want to make sure I get everything without possibly having to replay since the game is so long.
Click to expand...
1. Download the guide mod, it will provide an additional tab on the menu that will notify you of both the triggers for the next events, and will provide a notice (most of the time) about the requirements and order of events you need to select to not miss anything. Make sure to check it between every event, and don't advance the main plot before clearing the character events.

2. There absolutely is a path that sees every event in the game in a single playthrough, we've taken to calling it the green path. The obvious stuff is choosing to do everything you possibly can (having sex with everyone, for instance). A few (very few) choices are not that obvious. Like you having to choose a specific person for something, but those are minor (and should be in the guide mod as well).

3. Make sure to keep a separate save from time to time, so that you can reload and fast-forward if you ever miss something. This shouldn't happen, but better safe than sorry. Keep one at the very least for every 5/10 hours of gameplay or so.

4. We call the path of missing stuff the "red path". Apart from one specific choice, its content isn't noteworthy. There is some variation in dialogue and the story makes less sense. Save it for a second playthrough is my advice.

So, since the previous main topic of discussion seems to have pretty much run its course (for now), and since I (sadly) wasn’t here back in early November to participate in the original wave of debates regarding the hot new release of 0.53, I would like to briefly (?) return to that event chain and echo a sentiment I’ve only seen having been brought up by exactly two people: givemeabeer and DeSkel15 (sorry in advance if I accidentally misspelled anyone’s names). Because for me personally, the idea I struggled the most with after reading 0.53 was “why even bother creating this insanely well-written harem story where the protagonist has amazing (and different) chemistry with literally every single girl if you’re just going to blatantly come out and point at one of them as being ‘the objectively canon choice’ halfway through” (which was before I ever learned about the planned existence of Purity Routes, mind you) – and, after sitting on it for a couple of days, I believe that I *did* eventually come up with a decently satisfying answer for that question.

[Trigger warning: slight Himawari “hate” incoming.]

If you are someone who wholeheartedly believed that Akira will end up with Ayane by the end of the narrative even prior to 0.53 – good for you, genuinely.
