Likewise, if you *never* believed in it and still don’t, despite 0.53 obviously pushing for it, that’s fine too – you’re fully entitled to your opinions, and all that. And if you’re completely ambivalent to Ayane’s entire existence and just want to see Sensei finally go on an amusement park date with Io or something – cool, you’re also perfectly valid.

However, with all that being said, I strongly suspect that the very specific subset of people who *weren’t* originally on board with Akira x Ayane being the OTP of Lessons in Love but then readily jumped on the bandwagon *after* experiencing 0.53 were successfully manipulated by both Himawari (in-universe) and Selebus (IRL) into thinking exactly what you are *supposed to* think at this present moment in the story, because this is very likely a set-up for a huge narrative twist/conflict later down the line.

It is important to understand that Himawari is neither impartial nor objective when it comes to her involvement in the whole clusterfuck of conflicting agendas that is Terminal 23. She is exactly like all of the other God-affiliated parties in that she has a personal objective in mind (that directly requires Sensei) and is deliberately working towards realizing said objective through whatever means are available to her. The sole virtue of being a much more “wholesome” and trustworthy entity compared to the likes of HOPE or Pareidolia doesn’t exactly change the fact that the “happy ending” Himawari wants for Akira isn’t inherently any different from similar “happy endings” that each of the members of the Trinity has in store for him: all of these outcomes have, presumably, the exact the same end result of “making Sensei happy” – even if the specifics of what would it mean for him to “be happy” obviously greatly differ in each case – and the proponent of each “happy ending” is obviously going to insist that “my way is the best way” while severely downplaying all of the others.

The point I’m trying to make here is that it’s prudent to take all of Himawari’s claims about “how things should be” and “what is best for everyone” with a huge grain of salt, because she absolutely isn’t above selectively revealing information and lying by omission in order to stack the deck in her favor, regardless of how noble her intentions are. Remember: this is LiL, and so the truth is always much more complex than it initially appears; nothing is ever black or white – not to mention the fact that what’s on the line here is not just Himawari’s ability to finally reunite with her parents, but the girl’s own continuous existence, as well. This is why she so quickly and decisively shuts down Sensei when he starts to wonder whether it would be possible to bring Maya back to his original world together with him and Ayane in “Behind the Scenes”: even if it *could* be done and would thus arguably lead to a happier outcome overall (for Sensei – probably, for Maya – definitely), Himawari is strongly opposed to even entertaining the idea, because doing so would go directly against her personal interests (like being born).

And just to be perfectly clear, I m not calling her “evil”, or “selfish”, or anything of the sort: the poor girl just wants to exist in peace together with her mom and dad, which is a 100% understandable desire to have, and her willingness to effectively “sacrifice” Maya for the sake of achieving her own perfect world is a very human thing, and I don’t really hold it against her. It’s just that, from what I’ve seen, a lot of people seemed to have taken most of Himawari’s exposition from 0.53 at face value, while I was a lot more critical of it: not necessarily of the Wishing Well stuff (since that *does* line up with a lot of cryptic bullshit that was said by both Pareidolia and Yasu all the way back in Chapter 3), but rather the idea that Akira settling down with Ayane is *the* happy future that awaits him at the end of the road. *A* happy future, one of possible many? Sure. But *the* one and only, like Himawari tries to paint it as? I don’t believe it.

Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.

Either way, while I’m *not* insisting that Lessons in Love will necessarily end on a miserable or tragic note, I would absolutely advise people who think that it’s going to look something like 0.53 to greatly temper their expectations, or otherwise prepare to cry, cry, cry.

The sole virtue of being a much more “wholesome” and trustworthy entity compared to the likes of HOPE or Pareidolia doesn’t exactly change the fact that the “happy ending” Himawari wants for Akira isn’t inherently any different from similar “happy endings” that each of the members of the Trinity has in store for him: all of these outcomes have, presumably, the exact the same end result of “making Sensei happy” – even if the specifics of what would it mean for him to “be happy” obviously greatly differ in each case – and the proponent of each “happy ending” is obviously going to insist that “my way is the best way” while severely downplaying all of the others.
The point I’m trying to make here is that it’s prudent to take all of Himawari’s claims about “how things should be” and “what is best for everyone” with a huge grain of salt, because she absolutely isn’t above selectively revealing information and lying by omission in order to stack the deck in her favor, regardless of how noble her intentions are. Remember: this is LiL, and so the truth is always much more complex than it initially appears; nothing is ever black or white – not to mention the fact that what’s on the line here is not just Himawari’s ability to finally reunite with her parents, but the girl’s own continuous existence, as well. This is why she so quickly and decisively shuts down Sensei when he starts to wonder whether it would be possible to bring Maya back to his original world together with him and Ayane in “Behind the Scenes”: even if it *could* be done and would thus arguably lead to a happier outcome overall (for Sensei – probably, for Maya – definitely), Himawari is strongly opposed to even entertaining the idea, because doing so would go directly against her personal interests (like being born).
And just to be perfectly clear, I m not calling her “evil”, or “selfish”, or anything of the sort: the poor girl just wants to exist in peace together with her mom and dad, which is a 100% understandable desire to have, and her willingness to effectively “sacrifice” Maya for the sake of achieving her own perfect world is a very human thing, and I don’t really hold it against her. It’s just that, from what I’ve seen, a lot of people seemed to have taken most of Himawari’s exposition from 0.53 at face value, while I was a lot more critical of it: not necessarily of the Wishing Well stuff (since that *does* line up with a lot of cryptic bullshit that was said by both Pareidolia and Yasu all the way back in Chapter 3), but rather the idea that Akira settling down with Ayane is *the* happy future that awaits him at the end of the road. *A* happy future, one of possible many? Sure. But *the* one and only, like Himawari tries to paint it as? I don’t believe it.

Conclusion
Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.
Either way, while I’m *not* insisting that Lessons in Love will necessarily end on a miserable or tragic note, I would absolutely advise people who think that it’s going to look something like 0.53 to greatly temper their expectations, or otherwise prepare to cry, cry, cry.

spoilers.title: Conclusion
spoilers.html:
Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.

Either way, while I’m *not* insisting that Lessons in Love will necessarily end on a miserable or tragic note, I would absolutely advise people who think that it’s going to look something like 0.53 to greatly temper their expectations, or otherwise prepare to cry, cry, cry.

So, since the previous main topic of discussion seems to have pretty much run its course (for now), and since I (sadly) wasn’t here back in early November to participate in the original wave of debates regarding the hot new release of 0.53, I would like to briefly (?) return to that event chain and echo a sentiment I’ve only seen having been brought up by exactly two people: givemeabeer and DeSkel15 (sorry in advance if I accidentally misspelled anyone’s names). Because for me personally, the idea I struggled the most with after reading 0.53 was “why even bother creating this insanely well-written harem story where the protagonist has amazing (and different) chemistry with literally every single girl if you’re just going to blatantly come out and point at one of them as being ‘the objectively canon choice’ halfway through” (which was before I ever learned about the planned existence of Purity Routes, mind you) – and, after sitting on it for a couple of days, I believe that I *did* eventually come up with a decently satisfying answer for that question.

[Trigger warning: slight Himawari “hate” incoming.]

If you are someone who wholeheartedly believed that Akira will end up with Ayane by the end of the narrative even prior to 0.53 – good for you, genuinely. My personal bets were (and still kinda are) on either Ami or Maya, but I could certainly see Ayane being “the one” for him, as well – there are a lot of scenes and lines of dialogue (in Chapter 4 especially) that clearly support this reading. Likewise, if you *never* believed in it and still don’t, despite 0.53 obviously pushing for it, that’s fine too – you’re fully entitled to your opinions, and all that. The sole virtue of being a much more “wholesome” and trustworthy entity compared to the likes of HOPE or Pareidolia doesn’t exactly change the fact that the “happy ending” Himawari wants for Akira isn’t inherently any different from similar “happy endings” that each of the members of the Trinity has in store for him: all of these outcomes have, presumably, the exact the same end result of “making Sensei happy” – even if the specifics of what would it mean for him to “be happy” obviously greatly differ in each case – and the proponent of each “happy ending” is obviously going to insist that “my way is the best way” while severely downplaying all of the others.

The point I’m trying to make here is that it’s prudent to take all of Himawari’s claims about “how things should be” and “what is best for everyone” with a huge grain of salt, because she absolutely isn’t above selectively revealing information and lying by omission in order to stack the deck in her favor, regardless of how noble her intentions are. Remember: this is LiL, and so the truth is always much more complex than it initially appears; nothing is ever black or white – not to mention the fact that what’s on the line here is not just Himawari’s ability to finally reunite with her parents, but the girl’s own continuous existence, as well. This is why she so quickly and decisively shuts down Sensei when he starts to wonder whether it would be possible to bring Maya back to his original world together with him and Ayane in “Behind the Scenes”: even if it *could* be done and would thus arguably lead to a happier outcome overall (for Sensei – probably, for Maya – definitely), Himawari is strongly opposed to even entertaining the idea, because doing so would go directly against her personal interests (like being born).

And just to be perfectly clear, I m not calling her “evil”, or “selfish”, or anything of the sort: the poor girl just wants to exist in peace together with her mom and dad, which is a 100% understandable desire to have, and her willingness to effectively “sacrifice” Maya for the sake of achieving her own perfect world is a very human thing, and I don’t really hold it against her. It’s just that, from what I’ve seen, a lot of people seemed to have taken most of Himawari’s exposition from 0.53 at face value, while I was a lot more critical of it: not necessarily of the Wishing Well stuff (since that *does* line up with a lot of cryptic bullshit that was said by both Pareidolia and Yasu all the way back in Chapter 3), but rather the idea that Akira settling down with Ayane is *the* happy future that awaits him at the end of the road. *A* happy future, one of possible many? Sure. But *the* one and only, like Himawari tries to paint it as? I don’t believe it.

Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.

Either way, while I’m *not* insisting that Lessons in Love will necessarily end on a miserable or tragic note, I would absolutely advise people who think that it’s going to look something like 0.53 to greatly temper their expectations, or otherwise prepare to cry, cry, cry.

DeanNoriko said:
Personally I'm not convinced yet that everything is as it seems to be, the game is full of unreliable narrators, gods have been proven to misinform and misguide just for the fun of it or to escalate situations. Is everything that Himawari is saying actually true?
Click to expand...
As you already mentioned, Himawari, just like every other character, has her own intentions. Obviously, it's in her own interest to highlight the importance of Akira & Ayane being her parents and her origins. The events of 0.53 really did feel like a sort of sneak peak at the ending, but yeah, it's hard to argue with something that is being presented to you by an omniscient being that is also your daughter, so you double trust her.

Think about it this way though: If an unknown character started appearing and telling you she is Akira's and Yumi's daughter and that in her timeline, the two got together and had their own happy ending and lived a wonderful life, yadda yadda, would that somehow override Himawari's and their parents experiences? Would this now be the new true ending?
No, logically, there would be a million timelines in which any number of times Akira could have been a happy father and have a loving family and everything went on to be well. The one scenario presented by Himawari (again, only from her telling it and from a different, artificially created wish world that is not based on our Akira and Ayane) would just be one possible example.

In my opinion, the take away from 0.53 should be one thing: That Akira now has a goal. And that is not "I have to be with Ayane and create Himawari and 1:1 recreate what I experienced in this wish world", but much simpler: Fatherhood.
Deep down the essence of what truly made him happy and gave him purpose is that he had a child that he loved, a human being he could form and cherish and that would love him back. A working, loving family without chaos and pain. Something he always felt he missed. Something he thought he found with Ami, but what he may realize only to have been a substitute at best, a compromise.

Therefore, I think that there would be still many viable "true" endings to this.
Right now, I would even tend towards none of the girls to be the girl for him. I would expect something more grand, a last reveal by Sel maybe.
Otherwise, if you think about it, if there was only one girl from the main cast that Akira would experience the true ending with, all the other purity routes would kind of feel like sloppy seconds, no?
It would feel like a consolation prize, something to give out of pity for not being selected as the one.


I mean it's entirely possible that that's how it ends, that Maya is the one, or whoever else, and all the rest will have to make do with that.
But I suppose the more elegant way to resolve this whole story would be to make the ultimate ending more...neutral? Objective? Equal? Essentially to wrap it up nicely and not make a lot of the story almost feel pointless when it'll inevitably feel like "Oh it was always about this girl in the end", especially if you were to replay the game.

Also if there will be the pivotal girl in the story, it's gonna turn out to be Yumi, mark my words

spoilers.title: The Great Pretender(s) of 0.53
spoilers.html:
If you are someone who wholeheartedly believed that Akira will end up with Ayane by the end of the narrative even prior to 0.53 – good for you, genuinely. My personal bets were (and still kinda are) on either Ami or Maya, but I could certainly see Ayane being “the one” for him, as well – there are a lot of scenes and lines of dialogue (in Chapter 4 especially) that clearly support this reading. Likewise, if you *never* believed in it and still don’t, despite 0.53 obviously pushing for it, that’s fine too – you’re fully entitled to your opinions, and all that. And if you’re completely ambivalent to Ayane’s entire existence and just want to see Sensei finally go on an amusement park date with Io or something – cool, you’re also perfectly valid.

However, with all that being said, I strongly suspect that the very specific subset of people who *weren’t* originally on board with Akira x Ayane being the OTP of Lessons in Love but then readily jumped on the bandwagon *after* experiencing 0.53 were successfully manipulated by both Himawari (in-universe) and Selebus (IRL) into thinking exactly what you are *supposed to* think at this present moment in the story, because this is very likely a set-up for a huge narrative twist/conflict later down the line.

It is important to understand that Himawari is neither impartial nor objective when it comes to her involvement in the whole clusterfuck of conflicting agendas that is Terminal 23. She is exactly like all of the other God-affiliated parties in that she has a personal objective in mind (that directly requires Sensei) and is deliberately working towards realizing said objective through whatever means are available to her. The sole virtue of being a much more “wholesome” and trustworthy entity compared to the likes of HOPE or Pareidolia doesn’t exactly change the fact that the “happy ending” Himawari wants for Akira isn’t inherently any different from similar “happy endings” that each of the members of the Trinity has in store for him: all of these outcomes have, presumably, the exact the same end result of “making Sensei happy” – even if the specifics of what would it mean for him to “be happy” obviously greatly differ in each case – and the proponent of each “happy ending” is obviously going to insist that “my way is the best way” while severely downplaying all of the others.

The point I’m trying to make here is that it’s prudent to take all of Himawari’s claims about “how things should be” and “what is best for everyone” with a huge grain of salt, because she absolutely isn’t above selectively revealing information and lying by omission in order to stack the deck in her favor, regardless of how noble her intentions are. Remember: this is LiL, and so the truth is always much more complex than it initially appears; nothing is ever black or white – not to mention the fact that what’s on the line here is not just Himawari’s ability to finally reunite with her parents, but the girl’s own continuous existence, as well. This is why she so quickly and decisively shuts down Sensei when he starts to wonder whether it would be possible to bring Maya back to his original world together with him and Ayane in “Behind the Scenes”: even if it *could* be done and would thus arguably lead to a happier outcome overall (for Sensei – probably, for Maya – definitely), Himawari is strongly opposed to even entertaining the idea, because doing so would go directly against her personal interests (like being born).

And just to be perfectly clear, I m not calling her “evil”, or “selfish”, or anything of the sort: the poor girl just wants to exist in peace together with her mom and dad, which is a 100% understandable desire to have, and her willingness to effectively “sacrifice” Maya for the sake of achieving her own perfect world is a very human thing, and I don’t really hold it against her. It’s just that, from what I’ve seen, a lot of people seemed to have taken most of Himawari’s exposition from 0.53 at face value, while I was a lot more critical of it: not necessarily of the Wishing Well stuff (since that *does* line up with a lot of cryptic bullshit that was said by both Pareidolia and Yasu all the way back in Chapter 3), but rather the idea that Akira settling down with Ayane is *the* happy future that awaits him at the end of the road. *A* happy future, one of possible many? Sure. But *the* one and only, like Himawari tries to paint it as? I don’t believe it.

spoilers.title: Conclusion
spoilers.html:
Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.

Either way, while I’m *not* insisting that Lessons in Love will necessarily end on a miserable or tragic note, I would absolutely advise people who think that it’s going to look something like 0.53 to greatly temper their expectations, or otherwise prepare to cry, cry, cry.

And if so, wouldn't it make her change her behaviour from previous iterations? Curiously, when I thought of this, my mind went in the opposite direction than yours, ara: Maya had revealed that psycho Ami was a thing, there were lots of talk about resets in front of her, and yet there were no killings. I could only rationalized it as if there were more at stakes in this cycle, Ami had something to lose (Akira) as well.

Also, Maya said that whenever Ami was triggered, she would not stop at anybody, even Sensei. But in "Della" she's very remorseful after injuring Sensei's hand, and that's because he is Sensei. As you pointed out, Ami is reverting to the beggining of the game, she is treating him like another fake Sensei for a minute and goes as far as harming him. That's where she knows she lost it, when she realizes she is out of control and needs to stop and come out with a new plan. At least, that was my interpretation.

So you see, while you are looking for reasons that explain her becoming deranged I'm actually wondering why she is still not as bad as the way Maya painted her. And you can call me crazy, but let's see what she's really done so far: Nodoka's killing doesn't count, it was another universe. The bloodbath in Tsukioka's mansion seemed to happen after they were unconscious and more of an annoyance for the janitors than murderous purposes.

"All" (emphasis on the quotes, please) we have is the continuous torture towards Maya. A fake Maya. I mean, this is another thing I wondered at the time Maya revealed the nature of Ami. Why would Ami attack every girl with the only exception of prime Maya. And the moment there is a fake one, she can't stop toying with her, as if she's been waiting million of years for the opportunity.

Of course, by then I thought being killed would get you factory reset by default, and now I can't really rule out the posibbility of prime Maya getting killed and or tortured by Ami at some time. But I still lean to that not happening. Now, I'm sure there's more to this than Ami seeing people either as dolls or "real" and it's not like I don't double guess myself all the time. All my little brain can do is ask questions instead of coming up with a well rounded theory.

DeanNoriko said:
Think about it this way though: If an unknown character started appearing and telling you she is Akira's and Yumi's daughter and that in her timeline, the two got together and had their own happy ending and lived a wonderful life, yadda yadda, would that somehow override Himawari's and their parents experiences? Would this now be the new true ending?
No, logically, there would be a million timelines in which any number of times Akira could have been a happy father and have a loving family and everything went on to be well. The one scenario presented by Himawari (again, only from her telling it and from a different, artificially created wish world that is not based on our Akira and Ayane) would just be one possible example.
Click to expand...
I'd have to say no considering part of the rub with Himawari here is that our Akira and Ayane are her actual parents though, right? Like, she's not just a random child of theirs from a different timeline, she literally won't exist if they don't get together. A random child of alternate versions of Akira and one of the other girls coming in wouldn't really override that for me, personally, there's no stakes there. I would really like to see what Yumi and Akira's kid would look like now though lol

DeanNoriko said:
Otherwise, if you think about it, if there was only one girl from the main cast that Akira would experience the true ending with, all the other purity routes would kind of feel like sloppy seconds, no?
It would feel like a consolation prize, something to give out of pity for not being selected as the one.

I mean it's entirely possible that that's how it ends, that Maya is the one, or whoever else, and all the rest will have to make do with that.
But I suppose the more elegant way to resolve this whole story would be to make the ultimate ending more...neutral? Objective? Equal? Essentially to wrap it up nicely and not make a lot of the story almost feel pointless when it'll inevitably feel like "Oh it was always about this girl in the end", especially if you were to replay the game.
Click to expand...
I get what you're saying about sloppy seconds but I don't think the rest of the girls not being end-game would make them feel pointless, all of the pieces are a vital part of our Akira's growth, that's a big part of the point. I'm also not sure I'd find it particularly elegant if he wound up with everyone or had a more neutral true ending, that could just as easily wind up feeling like a cop out instead. I'm sure I could get behind something more neutral depending on how it's done but I'd much rather Sel have the balls to just pick someone and go for it if that's what he wants to do for the true ending.

Even if it's somehow not Ayane I want the true ending to have him with someone personally, and I think it would make more sense thematically considering his inability to settle on one person is pegged as being the result of his trauma. It's hard for me to see how it could feel like he's really grown if the end result is that he's still completely incapable of not being romantically involved with literally everyone who cares about him. I would hope everyone is still an important part of his life, mind you, instead of a scenario like what we saw in Himawari's little dimension.

As far as the purity routes go it's pretty on brand for a VN to have optional routes for all the girls and a canon one so it's not out of place on the face of it either.

I have a lot to say about the Himawari slander (how dare you), but I'll just drop this here in the meantime:

Himawari explains the purity routes as her idea, but what no one managed to notice was the possible link between that and the fate of her parents.

What if her idea is only to *link* the purity routes, her "travel agency" as she puts it? Meaning that her Akira created the purity routes on his own, and that's why he's gone? That could be what Sana is referencing in Ayane's epilogue, and the flash of adult Maya.

All the purity routes are already true, Himawari is canon, but so is everyone else. Himawari is just trying to link all of them, rather than everyone have Akira be gone to another reality after each epilogue.

Give me back my theory cap.

The point I’m trying to make here is that it’s prudent to take all of Himawari’s claims about “how things should be” and “what is best for everyone” with a huge grain of salt, because she absolutely isn’t above selectively revealing information and lying by omission in order to stack the deck in her favor, regardless of how noble her intentions are. Remember: this is LiL, and so the truth is always much more complex than it initially appears; nothing is ever black or white – not to mention the fact that what’s on the line here is not just Himawari’s ability to finally reunite with her parents, but the girl’s own continuous existence, as well. This is why she so quickly and decisively shuts down Sensei when he starts to wonder whether it would be possible to bring Maya back to his original world together with him and Ayane in “Behind the Scenes”: even if it *could* be done and would thus arguably lead to a happier outcome overall (for Sensei – probably, for Maya – definitely), Himawari is strongly opposed to even entertaining the idea, because doing so would go directly against her personal interests (like being born).

And just to be perfectly clear, I m not calling her “evil”, or “selfish”, or anything of the sort: the poor girl just wants to exist in peace together with her mom and dad, which is a 100% understandable desire to have, and her willingness to effectively “sacrifice” Maya for the sake of achieving her own perfect world is a very human thing, and I don’t really hold it against her. It’s just that, from what I’ve seen, a lot of people seemed to have taken most of Himawari’s exposition from 0.53 at face value, while I was a lot more critical of it: not necessarily of the Wishing Well stuff (since that *does* line up with a lot of cryptic bullshit that was said by both Pareidolia and Yasu all the way back in Chapter 3), but rather the idea that Akira settling down with Ayane is *the* happy future that awaits him at the end of the road. *A* happy future, one of possible many? Sure. But *the* one and only, like Himawari tries to paint it as? I don’t believe it.

Due to all of this, I am fairly confident in my suspicion that Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised. Maybe we’ll learn that the price for achieving that future is unreasonably high, and so the characters will be unable to fully go through with it, or perhaps it will be revealed that the union between two lovers that gave birth to Himawari is no Certainty, but a fragile, fleeting Miracle that would take billions upon billions of years to try and find amidst the boundless Sea of Fragments.

spoilers.title: Expanding on that topic a bit
spoilers.html:
Maybe this is wishful thinking and naive optimism, but I feel like everything we've seen from her points to her really just being a good-natured girl who truly wants to help everyone regardless of her biases. There is still a chance she is deceiving us of course but I'm going to roll with the assumption that she's not for this hypothetical:

I think at some point in the story she is going to figure out how the world created by Maya works and repurpose it for "good."

As in, she will use it to unlock the possibility of her own dream to allow everyone to have their own "happy ending" that actually exists.






To me this comes across as a innocent and naive but genuine desire of hers. Narratively this feels a lot like foreshadowing. I think it's very possible that she will be able to turn the tide against the gods' meddling and effectively even rewrite how the world works, succeeding in creating a new company that supersedes the one she is in now and offers people the chance to have more control and reap the direct benefits of their wishes.

I still think Maya Prime is still the more likely candidate to be the OTP if the concept exists in this story, but I'm heavily leaning towards the point being that there IS no OTP. All endings can exists at once as possible worlds/futures and still have meaning, especially if Himawari achieves her goals.

I just want to remind, as part of our current Himawari discussion, that Ayane has already been pregnant. She was 100% pregnant as part of the reset that she kept her memories in; Post reset she mentions that she felt like she had just lost something important, and forgets that she was pregnant, which mirrors what Akira and Ayane say as part of 0.53's reset. IE, when Himawari resets them and takes their memories.

Seeing as time runs differently in resets, it's entirely possible that as part of that reset, Ayane has already given birth to Himawari. Either through Himawari waiting, and letting her give birth to ensure that she continues to exist, OR, due to how the Timeloop functions.

The thing about timeloops is that there are two different kinds:

Actual loops, in which everything resets into the same universe. IE, time is a circle.

Fractal Loops, in which everyone is shifted into a universe that is kinda the same, just backwards in time. IE, time is a Loop De Loop. It reverses upon itself, but to be adjacent to itself, not on top of itself.

Seeing as how progress is actually made, new people, new buildings, new events, it's obvious they are in the second kind of timeloop.

The special part of Fractal Loops is that the Universe they leave continues on per usual, it's only the POVs that shift into a new universe.

So it's possible that the Ayane that was pregnant continued on in that Universe, a Universe that DOESN'T loop, and gives birth to Himawari in Aomori. Does anyone know if we see any hint of Himawari prior to Sensei and Ayane having sex, and Ayane started to act weird(After she realizes she is pregnant)?

Time travel is weird, and with Himawari being outside of time, technically she has always existed, but only AFTER she begins to exist, if that makes sense?

IE, the universe is deterministic. If someone travels back in time to do something, than from someone else's POV that new event will have always have happened as part of their recollection.

OR

As part of the reset, Ayane gives birth to Himawari, and once she exists(And so has now always existed), she erases Ayane's memory of being pregnant, sends herself off to be raised by loving parents, and then the reset continues on as expected.

I lean towards Theory 1, if only because in order for their to be an ultimate timeline, everything will need to converge in the end. Collapsing all the timelines into a single one, which is the version that leads to Aiomori, makes sense from a certain POV.

DeanNoriko said:

I absolutely agree with your post, a very good take once again.

And not to toot my own horn oh well who am I kidding, also to toot my own horn, I did question Himawari's reliability in a post after 0.53 as well:

As you already mentioned, Himawari, just like every other character, has her own intentions. Obviously, it's in her own interest to highlight the importance of Akira & Ayane being her parents and her origins. The events of 0.53 really did feel like a sort of sneak peak at the ending, but yeah, it's hard to argue with something that is being presented to you by an omniscient being that is also your daughter, so you double trust her.

Think about it this way though: If an unknown character started appearing and telling you she is Akira's and Yumi's daughter and that in her timeline, the two got together and had their own happy ending and lived a wonderful life, yadda yadda, would that somehow override Himawari's and their parents experiences? Would this now be the new true ending?
No, logically, there would be a million timelines in which any number of times Akira could have been a happy father and have a loving family and everything went on to be well. The one scenario presented by Himawari (again, only from her telling it and from a different, artificially created wish world that is not based on our Akira and Ayane) would just be one possible example.

In my opinion, the take away from 0.53 should be one thing: That Akira now has a goal. And that is not "I have to be with Ayane and create Himawari and 1:1 recreate what I experienced in this wish world", but much simpler: Fatherhood.
Deep down the essence of what truly made him happy and gave him purpose is that he had a child that he loved, a human being he could form and cherish and that would love him back. A working, loving family without chaos and pain. Something he always felt he missed. Something he thought he found with Ami, but what he may realize only to have been a substitute at best, a compromise.

Therefore, I think that there would be still many viable "true" endings to this.
Right now, I would even tend towards none of the girls to be the girl for him. I would expect something more grand, a last reveal by Sel maybe.
Otherwise, if you think about it, if there was only one girl from the main cast that Akira would experience the true ending with, all the other purity routes would kind of feel like sloppy seconds, no?
It would feel like a consolation prize, something to give out of pity for not being selected as the one. View attachment 5531175

I mean it's entirely possible that that's how it ends, that Maya is the one, or whoever else, and all the rest will have to make do with that.
But I suppose the more elegant way to resolve this whole story would be to make the ultimate ending more...neutral? Objective? Equal? Essentially to wrap it up nicely and not make a lot of the story almost feel pointless when it'll inevitably feel like "Oh it was always about this girl in the end", especially if you were to replay the game.

Also if there will be the pivotal girl in the story, it's gonna turn out to be Yumi, mark my words
Click to expand...
I fully agree with your thoughts on the theme of "fatherhood" being very important to Akira's current development as a character *and* a human being (especially considering that he never had one himself), though I *disagree* with the notion that his relationship with Ami is somehow fundamentally inferior to what he had/will have with Himawari for you to call it "a substitute at best, a compromise". Yes, the thing they have going on right now is GIGA scuffed on every conceivable level, and it will require a fuckton of personal growth on both of their ends in order to reach a point they both *have to be at* for this relationship to properly work out... but if it *does* happen? If the stars align and Ami *truly* opens up to Akira, and he'll have both the mental maturity and the physical means to fully take care of the broken mess that is his niece/daughter and be there for her when she really needs him? Man, shit's going to be GLORIOUS. (…What? You have your Yumi cope, let me have mine.)

As for the rest of it, I honestly have no idea how to even *begin* to envision what this eventual “true” ending of LiL is going to look like. I had my fair share of educated guesses in the past, sure, but they were all made before I learned how the game is *actually* going to be structured, and that knowledge retroactively turned all of my theories into complete impossibilities. For example, I had originally expected LiL to end on a fairly dark and depressing note, but considering that we’ll have an entire Route for that and that the True Ending is going to require you experiencing all of the Purity Routes first, there is basically no chance of that happening – too big of a tonal whiplash.

I *would* like for the True Ending to be something narratively different and unique, though – not just a partial rehash of one of the thirty-five Purity Endings (or anything that came before, for that matter).

I both agree and disagree with this. I don't think Ami has ever been a good person, though that's more due to fucked up priorities than a lack of capacity for goodness. She's capable of empathy for her friends, but she'll also completely set that aside if it conflicts with her codependent relationship with Sensei.

I think her Chapter 3 character arc is the perfect encapsulation of this. She spent the whole chapter acting like a murderous psychopath who could snap at any moment. Then Ayane confronts her on the beach and it's revealed Ami's behavior was all a bluff, a calculated attempt to scare other people away from Sensei. What she was doing was cruel and selfish, but she wasn't capable of actually hurting anyone (physically). It doesn't sit right with me to turn around and claim this was all a double bluff, and she's actually been murdering people all along (but conveniently stopped when the game started).

Evil Ami has to have always been lurking in some sense, given all the murdering that Maya Prime witnessed (though it's also worth noting that Maya Prime never suspected any continuity between Evil Ami and Normal Ami). Is she a separate entity that sometimes slips into this world? Something that's always in the back of Ami's mind, threatening to take over? If it's the latter, is Evil Ami herself Ami's infection? I don't know the answer.

I do, however, think that there is a clear dividing line between two different Amis: the seventh reset. As I've written about before, I think the Ami who raped Maya and stuck around after the reset is a fundamentally different person than the one who walked into that infinity house. This showed up again in the most recent update: I have a hard time believing the Ami who toyed with Uta this time is the same one who tried to seduce her earlier in the chapter. Her demeanor is completely different.




The first time, she initiates things but lets Uta control what actually happens. It's two people being vulnerable together. After Uta leaves, she's flustered and disappointed - it seems like a genuine seduction attempt.



The second time, she's assertive and aggressive, taking away Uta's physical space. Ami isn't connecting with Uta here, she's exploiting Uta's vulnerability. Her acting is over the top and it's clearly all a game to her.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Selebus intentionally wrote 0.53 in such a way to make the readers completely believe Himawari’s words, no questions asked, just through the sheer emotional weight of those scenes and nothing else – while also fully aware that everyone who sincerely bought into her idyllic vision of the future is going to eventually be mercilessly blindsided by the crushing realization that the future that *actually* comes to pass is nowhere near the heartwarming “Akira x Ayane happy end” that they were promised.
Click to expand...
Okay, so, I have a couple of problems with this.
First one is a matter of logistics. We're past half of the game, and Himawari has been present from the very start, to having been a constant part of the flow of events in general (when she's not directly involved). To shift from Himawari to another character with similar role is unlikely. Her role as the daughter, as the savior, and eventual owner of Himawarico (and the purity routes tour guide) is just too important for the plot. For it all to be misdirection, when it's all over 5 years of game is just unlikely imo. I truly believe she is what was presented, evidenced from the fact that we do have access to her internal dialogue multiple times, and even after Ayane and Akira are gone.

Second is a comparison you make between Himawari and the makeshift gods - I really disagree with that one. We have in no shape or form have been given conclusive evidence that either HOPE, Wires or Pareidolia actually want anything good for Akira. Furthermore, our Akira isn't even the Akira from TERMINAL 23. There is a huge difference from the very start in that our Akira is Himawari's Akira, whereas these gods watch over Maya's world, not his (either 22 or wherever else). So, in essence, any "plan" Himawari has for Akira is incompatible with any plan these gods have because, fundamentally, one involves getting out of 23 (and being free), while the others have to have him stay there (or at least still bound).

For further proof of this, you can rewatch "Mother's Milk", as NAO straight up says that while she has no use for him anymore, those other gods do. Word of reference being "use". Himawari doesn't want to use Akira, she wants to be with him and that the road up until that point is less painful than it would otherwise.

I don't think anyone's being manipulated by Himawari either because she's not that powerful. A lot of her plans just go nowhere, if you'll recall. She really is in a desperate situation, have been breaking the rules whenever's possible, but has to bend for the freelancers (quiz situation), Pareidolia (when she tried to save Nodoka), and even erasing her parents memories while the three gods watch over her, and she's basically banished from working on 23 from then on (and Shiori takes over).

The little bit I do agree with you on is that there is obviously more to this situation. Why is Himawari getting involved with the company after she already had her parents with her? What happened to Akira and Ayane that was so bad that their 15 year old daughter had to do all this? What did she mean in previous appearances by "having skipped her growing up", and all the weird flashes we have of Akira with a baby (presumed to be her)? At some point, Ami's role has to be justified by the existence of a greater evil, or at least a circumstance that we're unaware of. I just don't know that it has to do with Himawari.

One final point is that Himawari has never said "how things should be", just that she wanted to make things better for everyone, and that everyone could get their happy ending. In fact, she very much wants to have no influence on Akira and Ayane because they have to get there by themselves, much less telling them what they have to do.

The information she does give them is all correct. She says that Ami knows things, explains what she does between resets, and also what they do to her. She explains that the world is Maya's wish, and that she herself is a wish, and that's the reason for all the fucked up things that happen in 23. All of these, I'd argue, should be taken at face value - because, well, they fit with everything presented prior and after. She's not saying to have either Maya or Ami as enemies (even the opposite in Ami's case), she's just providing information and letting them do whatever they want with it. Hell, she doesn't even say to prioritize Ayane or drop everything to go after her ending.

As to what you say about Himawari establishing the Ayane epilogue as the canon end, that's just not true. They experience her dream world, that's not the canon ending. In fact, the reason she's in TERMINAL 23 at all is that something goes wrong with the Himawari ending. So it's actually the opposite. That dream world is one of the many purity routes she's trying to establish for everyone.

Because for me personally, the idea I struggled the most with after reading 0.53 was “why even bother creating this insanely well-written harem story where the protagonist has amazing (and different) chemistry with literally every single girl if you’re just going to blatantly come out and point at one of them as being ‘the objectively canon choice’ halfway through”
Click to expand...
Assuming that the game where there's literally a harem part where he fucks all the girls and then has a section where every girl gets a perfect 1 on 1 ending epilogue, before we go back to a true ending, to then have that ending be a 1 on 1 monogamous relationship is the trap I think. There won't be a OTP at the end. This could mean a harem-ish ending where they share to some degree, but it could also end with him dying, among other options.

For all the supposed hints that Ayane and Sensei are the canon couple Sensei doesn't seem to agree with it. Even in his perfect wife life of 0.53 was he ever happy about it? No I don't think so. When it started he was the one who always had his guard up. When he was introduced to Hima chan and then got to speak to Ayane afterwards, Ayane was willing to commit to this reality immediately while Sensei always said don't get attached. Before he flashes forward to the arcade he's having an inner monologue where he's worried about the future, and manages to compare it to what Maya did. When they're sitting for their first anniversary dinner he thinks about how happy he's ended up despite all the pain and trauma he's been in...


and tries (and fails) to convince himself he's happy and has no regrets.

When the curtain falls and they're sent back to the rooftop, he just feels vindicated for not settling for the ending. When he sees his 'wife' break down, he still picks Himawari without hesitation because she's what's important. He loves Himawari and wants her to be happy at most costs, Ayane is quite secondary here. Sensei's goal motivating him past 0.53 is to reach Himawari again, but that does not specify that he's going to be exclusive with Ayane.
And I'm pretty sure Himawari knows this. She outright tells him that him and Ayane are her priorities, but we've also seen Himawari trying to make Maya x Akira happen since chapter 2 so she's not blind to what Sensei wants. She's also had other things to keep an eye on like appearing in front of Tsubasa as her daughter.

If there is an ending where they all make it out into some place they can live, Himawari should end up with some sort of life where Sensei is there as a father figure. Ayane's just gonna be sharing him a bit.

Okay, I've been absolutely dead wrong about all my theorycrafting I've done so far (though there is still a possibility that Nodoka's not supposed to be here), but this update has had the most transparent language in a while that's so intriguing that I'm ready to be dead wrong again:
There was one moment in particular that caught my interest, that felt just out of place enough that I decided that I needed to play this update over again (three more times) to try to read into it all. During Himawari's tearful parting, when she's wiping Akira and Ayane's memories of her, she blurts this out as a throwaway line, not really expecting anyone to know what she's talking about but more for herself:
View attachment 5412006
She...misses them.
She...misses them? Why? Why would she miss them? As far as we knew up until this point, she was just a time-traveler messing with the past. If she ever wanted to see her beloved parents again, why not go back to the future? Why does she miss them so much? Where are they that she can't get back to them just by going back to the future? You might already know where I'm going with this, but hold on to this moment; we'll come back to it as we break down more moments from the update.
For starters, the fact that Himawari's pocket dimension (and by extension Himawari) exists at all means that Akira and Ayane are going to break free from Terminal23 and have Himawari, and she says so herself:
View attachment 5412031
During Playthrough #3 of this update, I fully realized that the "fake" nature of Himawari's pocket dimension serves as hints of what the True Timeline is like, kinda like how when you know for a fact that someone is lying to you, you can invert some of their statements to find out what's actually going on. Akira also figured that out himself, and this moment is some of the most transparent and least ambiguous writing we've seen in a while.
View attachment 5412045
So, in Himawari's fantasy of what a perfect life looks like, the family moved as far away as they could possibly get from Kumon-Mi and left everything and everyone behind, except for some long-distance contact with Sana for some reason (I'll be honest I haven't figured out why) and some very low contact with Ami under controlled circumstances. She then lives every day carefree with just her Mama and Papa making casual good-faith jabs at each other and making precious memories with each other.

So what's the reflection of this?

In the true timeline, Akira still hasn't reconciled his relationships with the greater harem or his relationship with himself, and it's made for a very unstable upbringing for Himawari, regardless of how much he clearly loves her and how much she clearly loves him. Akira's attention was constantly being pulled away from his family to all the other women in his life, and no one was ever satisfied with having only a portion of his attention (evidenced by how Himawari's dream, which is clearly the purity routes, is for each person to get the opportunity to "vacation" in their own happy ending, no strings attached, as well as a quick quip about "dad's harem" in the breakfast scene), and Himawari briefly touches on her broken home when she's getting chastised by Shiori.
View attachment 5412082
"I want my family to be a family", bless her.
Akira also hasn't made peace with himself and has not corrected his corrupted understanding of love. He spends years and years feeling empty and searching for something to fill that emptiness, and the closest thing he every found was his daughter Himawari, though he never truly knew how to show his love for her (thankfully, clearly it was not sexually). He still spends every moment paranoid that the good things in life are about to be stolen from him, and that's even still the first thing he's thinking when He and Ayane get whisked away to Himawari's pocket dimension.
View attachment 5412109
Granted, that's a logical conclusion to come to given all they've seen, but the fact that our Akira, the same one who will eventually break out of Terminal23 without any outside guidance immediately thought about how they could lose it all really tells us how even after he's emotionally grown, he's not prepared for his freedom from Terminal 23 and by extension created the broken household Himawari was raised in.

This was so bad, that something happened that meant that Himawari can't see her parents anymore. Something so permanent that plucking them out of their timeline into a manufactured future wasn't goo enough, that the only possible way she could see them again was joining the Megacorp of the gods (I think it's called the Shiawase Group) and subtlety messing with the timeline in the hope that Akira will come out of it a fully emotionally realized person who can be the father that Himawari wants back.
View attachment 5412124
You've probably pieced together what I'm implying here, so let's piece this all together along with other theories from the thread and come up with The Greater Timeline of LiL
Akira spends most of his life getting physically or sexually abused by Nozomu and Sekai. After years and years of the most fucked up game of Good Cop/Bad Cop, Nozomu and Sekai suddenly die in an unexpected car crash. Sekai is desperately experimented on, both scientifically and pseudoscientifically with the full resources of House Tsukioka under the direction of her friend Tsubasa in a desperate attempt to keep her alive to no avail, but it does result in Sekai's soul being bound to the world and the beginning of her ascendancy to godhood. As Akira is reeling and directionless in his newfound freedom, he makes a wish of uknown wording that result in Maya coming into his life. The wording of his wish could be anything from "Keeping Sekai's memory alive" or "I wish someone could love me like Her." Maya falls in love with him, but it doesn't help him at all, as Akira sinks further and further into depression. In desperation, Maya somehow makes a wish that defies the expected metaphysics of the multiverse, phrased something along the lines of "I wish everyone loves him as much as he loves me". She makes this wish/pact with a god, and curiously, it seems to be the only god she knows of. Maya only ever talks about God (singular) and never the gods (plural), so what kind of god could make a wish that so fundamentally changes the nature of the world, unless it's the god of the world itself: Sekai, god of Terminal23. Sekai fulfills Maya's wish, but not in the way she wanted and even swapped her place with Ami as Akira's main partner. What follows is eons of a predatory orgy that the gods just can't figure out how to stop until one cycle the true Akira re-emerged. Akira eventually unravels the mystery of Terminal23 and breaks the timeloop, setting everyone free...who still all want his dick. He has Himawari with Ayane, and Himawari grows up in the middle of a chaotic harem as everyone constantly fights and bickers over Akira while he tries and fails to keep the peace while being spread thin over so many people. After 15 years of this, he's mentally and emotionally exhausted with all of his relationships broken, just as lost and directionless as when his abusers first died. Something with some degree of finality happens. Perhaps it's a relapse into his taste for younger girls, or perhaps it's a particularly brutal argument with Ayane or Himawari, but one day, mirroring the start of Himawari's pocket dimension, she returned home from school, immediately launching into a prepared speech about dropping out of school to keep an eye on her father, when she found his stone-cold corpse hanging in the living room. In grief, she searched for any possible way she could time travel until she contacted the Shiawase Group (or whatever the Megacorp of the gods is called) and joined as a custodian with the express intention of meddling with the timeline in hopes of producing a different result, leading right to where we are now in the story.
In any rate, 10/10 update. Absolutely loved every part of it, and I'm really bummed that it's gonna be a long while before we see Himawari again. The single cutest thing she did was when she thought Geoffrey was ringing the doorbell, she went:

Akira spends most of his life getting physically or sexually abused by Nozomu and Sekai. After years and years of the most fucked up game of Good Cop/Bad Cop, Nozomu and Sekai suddenly die in an unexpected car crash. Sekai is desperately experimented on, both scientifically and pseudoscientifically with the full resources of House Tsukioka under the direction of her friend Tsubasa in a desperate attempt to keep her alive to no avail, but it does result in Sekai's soul being bound to the world and the beginning of her ascendancy to godhood. As Akira is reeling and directionless in his newfound freedom, he makes a wish of uknown wording that result in Maya coming into his life. The wording of his wish could be anything from "Keeping Sekai's memory alive" or "I wish someone could love me like Her." Maya falls in love with him, but it doesn't help him at all, as Akira sinks further and further into depression. In desperation, Maya somehow makes a wish that defies the expected metaphysics of the multiverse, phrased something along the lines of "I wish everyone loves him as much as he loves me". She makes this wish/pact with a god, and curiously, it seems to be the only god she knows of. Maya only ever talks about God (singular) and never the gods (plural), so what kind of god could make a wish that so fundamentally changes the nature of the world, unless it's the god of the world itself: Sekai, god of Terminal23. Sekai fulfills Maya's wish, but not in the way she wanted and even swapped her place with Ami as Akira's main partner. Akira eventually unravels the mystery of Terminal23 and breaks the timeloop, setting everyone free...who still all want his dick. He has Himawari with Ayane, and Himawari grows up in the middle of a chaotic harem as everyone constantly fights and bickers over Akira while he tries and fails to keep the peace while being spread thin over so many people. After 15 years of this, he's mentally and emotionally exhausted with all of his relationships broken, just as lost and directionless as when his abusers first died. Something with some degree of finality happens. Perhaps it's a relapse into his taste for younger girls, or perhaps it's a particularly brutal argument with Ayane or Himawari, but one day, mirroring the start of Himawari's pocket dimension, she returned home from school, immediately launching into a prepared speech about dropping out of school to keep an eye on her father, when she found his stone-cold corpse hanging in the living room. In grief, she searched for any possible way she could time travel until she contacted the Shiawase Group (or whatever the Megacorp of the gods is called) and joined as a custodian with the express intention of meddling with the timeline in hopes of producing a different result, leading right to where we are now in the story.

spoilers.html:
Considering Shiori advises her to let things be and play out the way they're supposed I think it's safe to assume her interference is not a natural part of how they got together originally. It wouldn't really make sense for Shiori to discourage her meddling by bringing up the potential consequences of being caught if her meddling is a prerequisite to her existence - ergo, the fact that she's meddling at all implies something bad happened.

Putting that aside she says she's helping things along in order to get a better outcome than the one she/their family had, which I would say also implies something pretty significant happened if she feels the need to risk both divine retribution and her existence in order to change things for the better. I mean, it would be pretty weird if she were doing all this over trivial problems in an otherwise happy life with her otherwise happy parents, especially considering her idea of a perfect life is literally just hanging out with her parents every day.

Speaking of her parents at home, in the handful of times in her various presumed narrations and 0.53 where she refers specifically to the future versions of our Akira and Ayane there's a couple times in which she refers to her mother in the present tense but she only ever refers to her father/Akira in the past tense. There's also instances like this in her narrations;

View attachment 5532248 View attachment 5532250

which make me think that not only did something significant happen but that whatever happened caused Akira to be absent from Hima's life in some way or another.

So what's the reflection of this?
In the true timeline, Akira still hasn't reconciled his relationships with the greater harem or his relationship with himself, and it's made for a very unstable upbringing for Himawari, regardless of how much he clearly loves her and how much she clearly loves him. Akira's attention was constantly being pulled away from his family to all the other women in his life, and no one was ever satisfied with having only a portion of his attention (evidenced by how Himawari's dream, which is clearly the purity routes, is for each person to get the opportunity to "vacation" in their own happy ending, no strings attached, as well as a quick quip about "dad's harem" in the breakfast scene), and Himawari briefly touches on her broken home when she's getting chastised by Shiori.

spoilers.title: Tying it All Together
spoilers.html: Akira spends most of his life getting physically or sexually abused by Nozomu and Sekai. After years and years of the most fucked up game of Good Cop/Bad Cop, Nozomu and Sekai suddenly die in an unexpected car crash. Sekai is desperately experimented on, both scientifically and pseudoscientifically with the full resources of House Tsukioka under the direction of her friend Tsubasa in a desperate attempt to keep her alive to no avail, but it does result in Sekai's soul being bound to the world and the beginning of her ascendancy to godhood. As Akira is reeling and directionless in his newfound freedom, he makes a wish of uknown wording that result in Maya coming into his life. The wording of his wish could be anything from "Keeping Sekai's memory alive" or "I wish someone could love me like Her." Maya falls in love with him, but it doesn't help him at all, as Akira sinks further and further into depression. In desperation, Maya somehow makes a wish that defies the expected metaphysics of the multiverse, phrased something along the lines of "I wish everyone loves him as much as he loves me". She makes this wish/pact with a god, and curiously, it seems to be the only god she knows of. Maya only ever talks about God (singular) and never the gods (plural), so what kind of god could make a wish that so fundamentally changes the nature of the world, unless it's the god of the world itself: Sekai, god of Terminal23. Sekai fulfills Maya's wish, but not in the way she wanted and even swapped her place with Ami as Akira's main partner. What follows is eons of a predatory orgy that the gods just can't figure out how to stop until one cycle the true Akira re-emerged. Akira eventually unravels the mystery of Terminal23 and breaks the timeloop, setting everyone free...who still all want his dick. He has Himawari with Ayane, and Himawari grows up in the middle of a chaotic harem as everyone constantly fights and bickers over Akira while he tries and fails to keep the peace while being spread thin over so many people. After 15 years of this, he's mentally and emotionally exhausted with all of his relationships broken, just as lost and directionless as when his abusers first died. Something with some degree of finality happens. Perhaps it's a relapse into his taste for younger girls, or perhaps it's a particularly brutal argument with Ayane or Himawari, but one day, mirroring the start of Himawari's pocket dimension, she returned home from school, immediately launching into a prepared speech about dropping out of school to keep an eye on her father, when she found his stone-cold corpse hanging in the living room. In grief, she searched for any possible way she could time travel until she contacted the Shiawase Group (or whatever the Megacorp of the gods is called) and joined as a custodian with the express intention of meddling with the timeline in hopes of producing a different result, leading right to where we are now in the story.

Why would Ami attack every girl with the only exception of prime Maya. And the moment there is a fake one, she can't stop toying with her, as if she's been waiting million of years for the opportunity.
Click to expand...
There's a lot to say here.
For one, Maya "Prime" is quite questionable. The Alt Maya Prime that Ayane meets during the "alternate realities/timetravel reset" has difficulty placing herself in Maya Prime's timeline - is she in the future or the past? It's unclear if they're even the same person. My point with this is that Ami could have tortured countless Mayas up until what we see of Maya Prime.

I do agree that it's weird that Maya Prime says that she has seen Ami do all kinds of fucked up shit, and yet fails to mention anything happening to her. But then, what does she see in "Scary Room"? Is it the obvious torture Ami puts New Maya through (in the same room)? Is it something else? That's still unclear (although I think aramaug has written about it).

There's a lot of weird stuff overall in their relationship. Ami's supposed to know a lot of stuff, and yet she treats New Maya as if she was a doll - when we know that TERMINAL 23 is her world (she's everything but a doll). Is Ami saying that out of spite (because it's Maya's world)? Does she know something we don't? Is she simply lacking information?

There's also a secondary aspect about Ami that we have to consider, and that has to do with memories. We know for sure that Maya (whichever) does not hold all her memories. Be that by design by the company (as Tsuneyo suggests), or simply a result of living for thousands of years is unclear. But what about Ami? Because they cannot tamper with her memory for good, it always comes back. Well, ponder that for a bit. What does it mean for her memory to always come back? How much memory?

Imagine an Ami that was just mind-wiped. She lives with her uncle and then, all of a sudden, boom! 5 years of memories? 50? 5 thousand? I have no idea what that'd do to a person. And this could be relevant because, for an Ami that has lived for that long and has done all sorts of shit to everyone, and recognizes the pointlessness of it all, does torturing Maya or not really make a difference? It could be that the Ami change has more to do with what she remembered, rather than a New Maya - as she does change a lot in her treatment of everyone during chapter 4.

There are too many Ami theories to mention here. This was all to showcase how I don't think we really know enough to conclusively interpret what Ami's doing to Maya (or other people) yet.
The points you raise are definitely worth talking about though, good going.
