Moonflare said:
Okay, so, I have a couple of problems with this.
First one is a matter of logistics. We're past half of the game, and Himawari has been present from the very start, to having been a constant part of the flow of events in general (when she's not directly involved). To shift from Himawari to another character with similar role is unlikely. Her role as the daughter, as the savior, and eventual owner of Himawarico (and the purity routes tour guide) is just too important for the plot. For it all to be misdirection, when it's all over 5 years of game is just unlikely imo. I truly believe she is what was presented, evidenced from the fact that we do have access to her internal dialogue multiple times, and even after Ayane and Akira are gone.

Second is a comparison you make between Himawari and the makeshift gods - I really disagree with that one. We have in no shape or form have been given conclusive evidence that either HOPE, Wires or Pareidolia actually want anything good for Akira. Furthermore, our Akira isn't even the Akira from TERMINAL 23. There is a huge difference from the very start in that our Akira is Himawari's Akira, whereas these gods watch over Maya's world, not his (either 22 or wherever else). So, in essence, any "plan" Himawari has for Akira is incompatible with any plan these gods have because, fundamentally, one involves getting out of 23 (and being free), while the others have to have him stay there (or at least still bound).

For further proof of this, you can rewatch "Mother's Milk", as NAO straight up says that while she has no use for him anymore, those other gods do. Word of reference being "use". Himawari doesn't want to use Akira, she wants to be with him and that the road up until that point is less painful than it would otherwise.

I don't think anyone's being manipulated by Himawari either because she's not that powerful. A lot of her plans just go nowhere, if you'll recall. She really is in a desperate situation, have been breaking the rules whenever's possible, but has to bend for the freelancers (quiz situation), Pareidolia (when she tried to save Nodoka), and even erasing her parents memories while the three gods watch over her, and she's basically banished from working on 23 from then on (and Shiori takes over).

The little bit I do agree with you on is that there is obviously more to this situation. Why is Himawari getting involved with the company after she already had her parents with her? What happened to Akira and Ayane that was so bad that their 15 year old daughter had to do all this? What did she mean in previous appearances by "having skipped her growing up", and all the weird flashes we have of Akira with a baby (presumed to be her)? At some point, Ami's role has to be justified by the existence of a greater evil, or at least a circumstance that we're unaware of. I just don't know that it has to do with Himawari.

One final point is that Himawari has never said "how things should be", just that she wanted to make things better for everyone, and that everyone could get their happy ending. In fact, she very much wants to have no influence on Akira and Ayane because they have to get there by themselves, much less telling them what they have to do.

The information she does give them is all correct. She says that Ami knows things, explains what she does between resets, and also what they do to her. She explains that the world is Maya's wish, and that she herself is a wish, and that's the reason for all the fucked up things that happen in 23. All of these, I'd argue, should be taken at face value - because, well, they fit with everything presented prior and after. She's not saying to have either Maya or Ami as enemies (even the opposite in Ami's case), she's just providing information and letting them do whatever they want with it. Hell, she doesn't even say to prioritize Ayane or drop everything to go after her ending.

As to what you say about Himawari establishing the Ayane epilogue as the canon end, that's just not true. They experience her dream world, that's not the canon ending. In fact, the reason she's in TERMINAL 23 at all is that something goes wrong with the Himawari ending. So it's actually the opposite. That dream world is one of the many purity routes she's trying to establish for everyone.
Click to expand...
Wow, there is *a lot* to go over with this response. And, judging by some of your counterpoints, many of my actual thoughts on Himawari’s situation seems to have once again gotten “lost in translation” – I’ll chalk it up to me being half-sick and partially sleep-deprived when I was writing my “Himawari exposé” and try to be a lot more direct this time, in order to not leave even the slightest bit of room for any potential misunderstandings:

First of all – no offense to you, or anyone else who also got a similar impression from my words – but I am genuinely not sure where this idea of me insisting that Himawari herself is “fake” or a “misdirection” is even coming from. I *never* implied anything like this, nor have I ever personally doubted her being Akira’s and Ayane’s biological daughter. She is 100% who she says she is – that’s not even up to debate. My only goal was to try to highlight the simple fact that Himawari is a lot more nuanced and morally complex than she pretends to be, not to bring the entire nature of her existence into question, so to see multiple people somehow misconstrue my point as “Himawari is going to get shafted by another character with a similar role later down the line” is… mind-boggling, to say the least.

Also, since we are already on this topic, there are multiple reasons for why the “Himawari 2.0” plot point won’t ever happen. For one, we have Selebus’ own in-universe statement that “you’ve already met everyone” – which, yes, does *technically* include Shiori, as she was mentioned very early on in the story, despite only properly showing up in 0.53. But even more important proof is the fact that Ayane is *the only* character in the entire game who had a very obvious pregnancy foreshadowing/arc, and there is no chance in Hell that Selebus will ever compromise the quality of his narrative by pulling something like that *again* without properly setting it up first. The only exception to what I just said is *Ami* with her “As Light as Air”: an event that, very curiously, happens right after Ayane’s “Before the Sun Comes Up” (where she becomes un-pregnant) and features Ami in a state of what can only be described as bestial heat, half-delirious with arousal and constantly begging Sensei to come inside her and whatnot (potentially implying that she *was* potentially extremely fertile in this scene and that a creampie *would* have resulted in a successful pregnancy) – except that Akira *mysteriously* pulls out of her at the very last second, accompanied by a flash that usually signifies either a blackout or divine intervention, which I personally took to signify that there is an actual “divine failsafe” of some kind that literally prevents Sensei from impregnating anyone *but* Ayane (or perhaps it targets Ami specifically because she is also an anomaly within Terminal 23, I dunno).

Second of all, in regards to “we have in no shape or form have been given conclusive evidence that either HOPE, Wires or Pareidolia actually want anything good for Akira”: I guess that’s where our personal differences in perspectives once again shine through, because while you *are* correct in that there hasn’t been any *definitive* proof of them ultimately having Akira’s best interests in mind (only a bunch of cryptic one-sided interactions that can be realistically read either way), the thing that brings all of that together and convinces me personally is the sentiment that keeps getting echoed again and again by multiple characters – from Maya, to Ami, to Tsubasa, to Akira himself – throughout the entire game: “sometimes, forcing people to do things they’re not comfortable with is the best way to move them forward”.

Now, I am not a particularly religious person and do generally respect free will and individual choice, but I *also* believe that there 100% are certain choices and outcomes in life that could make you truly happy, and yet you would *never* actually make those choices and reach those outcomes on your own, without some outside intervention – either because what lies beyond those doors meshes with your preconceptions of “what’s right”, forcing you to strongly reject them as an emotional knee-jerk reaction, or because you simply don’t see those possibilities as actually being available to you at all. So the idea of a higher-level entity – a “god” (or “gods”, in this case) – looking over you from high above, seeing the “golden path” you *could* take and then subtly pushing you onto it for your own benefit doesn’t sound that far-fetched or inherently malicious to me. Thus, the way I see it, going back to the Trinity, whether you describe their actions as “using” Akira or “helping” him is just semantics – after all, what’s wrong with HOPE or Pareidolia also getting what they want when all is said and done, if Akira is going to be happy either way?

I understand that your perspective is likely some combination of “Sensei can only be happy if he becomes a better person” and “Sensei can only be happy if he escapes the loops and begins living a quiet life together with Ayane and Himawari”, but I just don’t see it that way. From where I’m standing, “Collector Akira” and “God-King Akira” (plus whatever Tenchou is planning for him) are all equally valid paths for him to take, in the sense that he’ll be able to look back on his life and conclude that “I have no regrets” at the end of it all – which is honestly the only thing that matters, in my opinion.

Thirdly, all of Himawari’s “manipulation” I mentioned is mostly limited to just 0.53 – I wasn’t implying that she has been cleverly plotting in the background since the very beginning of the story (like Pareidolia did), setting up various misdirections and intentionally lying to everyone left and right, or anything of the sort. In fact, I would go as far as to say that *all* of her appearances prior to the 0.53 event chain have been almost entirely genuine, with every single half-truth and lie by omission Himawari ever told being the result of her just trying to survive and not bring too much attention to what she is actually doing, not intentional manipulation. Throughout 0.53, however, there are multiple scenes (that I and the others have pointed out) where she is clearly presenting herself as “the objectively superior option”, despite this not actually being the case, and tries to talk Akira into believing that what he experienced within her wish-world is *the* future that is effectively set in stone, and so the only thing he has to care about is figuring how to get there – both of which *are* clear examples of manipulation.

This also directly ties into my final point, which is that I unfortunately got lazy and tired and decided to not change anything about how I worded my “Conclusion” part, despite *fully knowing* that some people would misinterpret what I said there. For the record, I fully agree with your “as to what you say about Himawari establishing the Ayane epilogue as the canon end, that's just not true: they experience her dream world, that's not the canon ending” – because, yes, that is exactly what happens: 0.53 was just a dream world that was intentionally created to be as sweet and wholesome as possible, and it is *not* a one-to-one copy of the “real” true ending.

What I was trying to bring everyone’s attention to, however, is the fact that the implication of what Himawari is saying to Akira isn’t “I exist, so you and mom must have gotten together in *at least one* timeline” – it’s “I exist, therefore you and mom getting together is *something that always happens*”. We don’t actually know if the latter is true, but Hima is clearly pushing for it, because it is directly beneficial for her if Sensei *believes* it is true. *That’s* my point of contention: the idea that Akira and Ayane are effectively bound to end up together in some way, shape or form, which ultimately results in Himawari’s birth – not that LiL is destined to end exactly the same way we saw in 0.53.

As for everyone else: sorry, I’ll reply to your posts a bit later.

So the idea of a higher-level entity – a “god” (or “gods”, in this case) – looking over you from high above, seeing the “golden path” you *could* take and then subtly pushing you onto it for your own benefit doesn’t sound that far-fetched or inherently malicious to me. Thus, the way I see it, going back to the Trinity, whether you describe their actions as “using” Akira or “helping” him is just semantics – after all, what’s wrong with HOPE or Pareidolia also getting what they want when all is said and done, if Akira is going to be happy either way?
I understand that your perspective is likely some combination of “Sensei can only be happy if he becomes a better person” and “Sensei can only be happy if he escapes the loops and begins living a quiet life together with Ayane and Himawari”, but I just don’t see it that way. From where I’m standing, “Collector Akira” and “God-King Akira” (plus whatever Tenchou is planning for him) are all equally valid paths for him to take, in the sense that he’ll be able to look back on his life and conclude that “I have no regrets” at the end of it all – which is honestly the only thing that matters, in my opinion.
Spoiler:
Point three: Manipulation
Thirdly, all of Himawari’s “manipulation” I mentioned is mostly limited to just 0.53 – I wasn’t implying that she has been cleverly plotting in the background since the very beginning of the story (like Pareidolia did), setting up various misdirections and intentionally lying to everyone left and right, or anything of the sort. In fact, I would go as far as to say that *all* of her appearances prior to the 0.53 event chain have been almost entirely genuine, with every single half-truth and lie by omission Himawari ever told being the result of her just trying to survive and not bring too much attention to what she is actually doing, not intentional manipulation. Throughout 0.53, however, there are multiple scenes (that I and the others have pointed out) where she is clearly presenting herself as “the objectively superior option”, despite this not actually being the case, and tries to talk Akira into believing that what he experienced within her wish-world is *the* future that is effectively set in stone, and so the only thing he has to care about is figuring how to get there – both of which *are* clear examples of manipulation.
Spoiler:
Point four: the True Ending
This also directly ties into my final point, which is that I unfortunately got lazy and tired and decided to not change anything about how I worded my “Conclusion” part, despite *fully knowing* that some people would misinterpret what I said there. For the record, I fully agree with your “as to what you say about Himawari establishing the Ayane epilogue as the canon end, that's just not true: they experience her dream world, that's not the canon ending” – because, yes, that is exactly what happens: 0.53 was just a dream world that was intentionally created to be as sweet and wholesome as possible, and it is *not* a one-to-one copy of the “real” true ending.
What I was trying to bring everyone’s attention to, however, is the fact that the implication of what Himawari is saying to Akira isn’t “I exist, so you and mom must have gotten together in *at least one* timeline” – it’s “I exist, therefore you and mom getting together is *something that always happens*”. We don’t actually know if the latter is true, but Hima is clearly pushing for it, because it is directly beneficial for her if Sensei *believes* it is true. *That’s* my point of contention: the idea that Akira and Ayane are effectively bound to end up together in some way, shape or form, which ultimately results in Himawari’s birth – not that LiL is destined to end exactly the same way we saw in 0.53.
As for everyone else: sorry, I’ll reply to your posts a bit later.

spoilers.title: many disagreements
spoilers.html:
First one is a matter of logistics. We're past half of the game, and Himawari has been present from the very start, to having been a constant part of the flow of events in general (when she's not directly involved). To shift from Himawari to another character with similar role is unlikely. Her role as the daughter, as the savior, and eventual owner of Himawarico (and the purity routes tour guide) is just too important for the plot. For it all to be misdirection, when it's all over 5 years of game is just unlikely imo. I truly believe she is what was presented, evidenced from the fact that we do have access to her internal dialogue multiple times, and even after Ayane and Akira are gone.

Second is a comparison you make between Himawari and the makeshift gods - I really disagree with that one. We have in no shape or form have been given conclusive evidence that either HOPE, Wires or Pareidolia actually want anything good for Akira. Furthermore, our Akira isn't even the Akira from TERMINAL 23. There is a huge difference from the very start in that our Akira is Himawari's Akira, whereas these gods watch over Maya's world, not his (either 22 or wherever else). So, in essence, any "plan" Himawari has for Akira is incompatible with any plan these gods have because, fundamentally, one involves getting out of 23 (and being free), while the others have to have him stay there (or at least still bound).

For further proof of this, you can rewatch "Mother's Milk", as NAO straight up says that while she has no use for him anymore, those other gods do. Word of reference being "use". Himawari doesn't want to use Akira, she wants to be with him and that the road up until that point is less painful than it would otherwise.

I don't think anyone's being manipulated by Himawari either because she's not that powerful. A lot of her plans just go nowhere, if you'll recall. She really is in a desperate situation, have been breaking the rules whenever's possible, but has to bend for the freelancers (quiz situation), Pareidolia (when she tried to save Nodoka), and even erasing her parents memories while the three gods watch over her, and she's basically banished from working on 23 from then on (and Shiori takes over).

The little bit I do agree with you on is that there is obviously more to this situation. Why is Himawari getting involved with the company after she already had her parents with her? What happened to Akira and Ayane that was so bad that their 15 year old daughter had to do all this? What did she mean in previous appearances by "having skipped her growing up", and all the weird flashes we have of Akira with a baby (presumed to be her)? At some point, Ami's role has to be justified by the existence of a greater evil, or at least a circumstance that we're unaware of. I just don't know that it has to do with Himawari.

One final point is that Himawari has never said "how things should be", just that she wanted to make things better for everyone, and that everyone could get their happy ending. In fact, she very much wants to have no influence on Akira and Ayane because they have to get there by themselves, much less telling them what they have to do.

The information she does give them is all correct. She says that Ami knows things, explains what she does between resets, and also what they do to her. She explains that the world is Maya's wish, and that she herself is a wish, and that's the reason for all the fucked up things that happen in 23. All of these, I'd argue, should be taken at face value - because, well, they fit with everything presented prior and after. She's not saying to have either Maya or Ami as enemies (even the opposite in Ami's case), she's just providing information and letting them do whatever they want with it. Hell, she doesn't even say to prioritize Ayane or drop everything to go after her ending.

As to what you say about Himawari establishing the Ayane epilogue as the canon end, that's just not true. They experience her dream world, that's not the canon ending. In fact, the reason she's in TERMINAL 23 at all is that something goes wrong with the Himawari ending. So it's actually the opposite. That dream world is one of the many purity routes she's trying to establish for everyone.

spoilers.title: Point one: Himawari
spoilers.html:
First of all – no offense to you, or anyone else who also got a similar impression from my words – but I am genuinely not sure where this idea of me insisting that Himawari herself is “fake” or a “misdirection” is even coming from. I *never* implied anything like this, nor have I ever personally doubted her being Akira’s and Ayane’s biological daughter. She is 100% who she says she is – that’s not even up to debate. My only goal was to try to highlight the simple fact that Himawari is a lot more nuanced and morally complex than she pretends to be, not to bring the entire nature of her existence into question, so to see multiple people somehow misconstrue my point as “Himawari is going to get shafted by another character with a similar role later down the line” is… mind-boggling, to say the least.

Also, since we are already on this topic, there are multiple reasons for why the “Himawari 2.0” plot point won’t ever happen. For one, we have Selebus’ own in-universe statement that “you’ve already met everyone” – which, yes, does *technically* include Shiori, as she was mentioned very early on in the story, despite only properly showing up in 0.53. But even more important proof is the fact that Ayane is *the only* character in the entire game who had a very obvious pregnancy foreshadowing/arc, and there is no chance in Hell that Selebus will ever compromise the quality of his narrative by pulling something like that *again* without properly setting it up first. The only exception to what I just said is *Ami* with her “As Light as Air”: an event that, very curiously, happens right after Ayane’s “Before the Sun Comes Up” (where she becomes un-pregnant) and features Ami in a state of what can only be described as bestial heat, half-delirious with arousal and constantly begging Sensei to come inside her and whatnot (potentially implying that she *was* potentially extremely fertile in this scene and that a creampie *would* have resulted in a successful pregnancy) – except that Akira *mysteriously* pulls out of her at the very last second, accompanied by a flash that usually signifies either a blackout or divine intervention, which I personally took to signify that there is an actual “divine failsafe” of some kind that literally prevents Sensei from impregnating anyone *but* Ayane (or perhaps it targets Ami specifically because she is also an anomaly within Terminal 23, I dunno).

From where I’m standing, “Collector Akira” and “God-King Akira” are all equally valid paths for him to take, in the sense that he’ll be able to look back on his life and conclude that “I have no regrets” at the end of it all.

That's fine as a game interpretation, and obviously fine as a personal one. But it is also ignoring what has been presented in the game. The gods in LiL are not our own personal interpretations of what a god is. They have been described as beings that need mortals to believe in them, so that they can exist. It's a give and take. The way they give is by "answering prayers", which are called "wishes", by fullfiling them to a counterpart of the devotee in another reality, through the wishing well.

The company came in as a way of facilitating the transaction, keeping an eye on these wish worlds, and assuring the security for both the devotee and the gods, in general. TERMINAL 23, or Maya's world, is not a world created to help Akira become a better person. The original Akira that was put there was a doll created from Maya's wish, and our Akira is not even from that world. They'd have zero responsability towards either Akira, but even less towards ours. Mind you, the three make numerous references to have been going back and forth on this for a long time (like having lost spring and fall along the way) - and all those cycles were without our Akira.

I think it makes no sense, from what we've been shown, to assume that said entities would go "oh, another Akira, I guess we should guide this one towards a satisfying life". In fact, this even ignores the chain of events in the game, as HOPE has very clearly given up on Akira and left him to be reset. Ami has made numerous references of trying to prevent Akira from being lost to gods as well. And I'll throw in another example: Does it seem like either Sekai or Sara were guided towards a satisfying end? Cause it sure doesn't to me.

Equating gods designs to Himawari's plans (in a potentially positive life to Akira or anyone else) is an incorrect evaluation of things imo. Maybe they can lead to an acceptable conclusion, but they're definitely not the same in intention or design.

Thirdly, all of Himawari’s “manipulation” I mentioned is mostly limited to just 0.53 –
I wasn’t implying that she has been cleverly plotting in the background since the very beginning of the story (like Pareidolia did), setting up various misdirections and intentionally lying to everyone left and right, or anything of the sort. In fact, I would go as far as to say that *all* of her appearances prior to the 0.53 event chain have been almost entirely genuine, with every single half-truth and lie by omission Himawari ever told being the result of her just trying to survive and not bring too much attention to what she is actually doing, not intentional manipulation. Throughout 0.53, however, there are multiple scenes (that I and the others have pointed out) where she is clearly presenting herself as “the objectively superior option”, despite this not actually being the case, and tries to talk Akira into believing that what he experienced within her wish-world is *the* future that is effectively set in stone, and so the only thing he has to care about is figuring how to get there – both of which *are* clear examples of manipulation.

We don’t actually know if the latter is true, but Hima is clearly pushing for it, because it is directly beneficial for her if Sensei *believes* it is true.
Click to expand...
Again, it is not beneficial to Himawari in the least, because she herself erases it from Akira's mind. Her assumption is that it is erased, it's no devious plan. Just look back at her conversation with Shiori.

throughout the entire game: “sometimes, forcing people to do things they’re not comfortable with is the best way to move them forward”.

I *also* believe that there 100% are certain choices and outcomes in life that could make you truly happy, and yet you would *never* actually make those choices and reach those outcomes on your own, without some outside intervention – So the idea of a higher-level entity – a “god” (or “gods”, in this case) – looking over you from high above, seeing the “golden path” you *could* take and then subtly pushing you onto it for your own benefit doesn’t sound that far-fetched or inherently malicious to me. going back to the Trinity, whether you describe their actions as “using” Akira or “helping” him is just semantics – after all, what’s wrong with HOPE or Pareidolia also getting what they want when all is said and done, if Akira is going to be happy either way?

From where I’m standing, “Collector Akira” and “God-King Akira” are all equally valid paths for him to take, in the sense that he’ll be able to look back on his life and conclude that “I have no regrets” at the end of it all.

I see no big misunderstanding (on my part) with what you said.
It comes from this:
"the very specific subset of people who *weren’t* originally on board with Akira x Ayane being the OTP of Lessons in Love but then readily jumped on the bandwagon *after* experiencing 0.53 were successfully manipulated by both Himawari (in-universe) and Selebus (IRL) into thinking exactly what you are *supposed to* think at this present moment in the story, because this is very likely a set-up for a huge narrative twist/conflict later down the line.

It is important to understand that Himawari is neither impartial nor objective when it comes to her involvement in the whole clusterfuck of conflicting agendas that is Terminal 23. She is exactly like all of the other God-affiliated parties in that she has a personal objective in mind (that directly requires Sensei) and is deliberately working towards realizing said objective through whatever means are available to her."
while you do put this inside a tag that says "0.53", what you're talking about here is her actions throughout the whole game, and even linking it to an eventual twist/conflict. This is what I wrote in response to it:
"We're past half of the game, and Himawari has been present from the very start, to having been a constant part of the flow of events in general (when she's not directly involved). To shift from Himawari to another character with similar role is unlikely. Her role as the daughter, as the savior, and eventual owner of Himawarico (and the purity routes tour guide) is just too important for the plot. For it all to be misdirection, when it's all over 5 years of game is just unlikely imo. I truly believe she is what was presented, evidenced from the fact that we do have access to her internal dialogue multiple times, and even after Ayane and Akira are gone."
What I said was that Himawari has been presented as a daughter/savior/owner of himawarico as genuinely positive things, and that should be taken at face value. The similar role isn't that of another daughter, but of a savior figure (the one on Akira's corner), which is the joining of all those aspects. The misdirection isn't that she is/isn't his daughter, or that another character would show up to fill the daughter's role - but the misdirection that you suggest, that Himawari's objectives were more devious than they appear.

While, yes, most of said misdirection would be during 0.53, you suggest that she has been doing so in the past, by choosing what to reveal and what not to reveal to further her interests, while I can't agree with it. The original Akira that was put there was a doll created from Maya's wish, and our Akira is not even from that world. They'd have zero responsability towards either Akira, but even less towards ours. Mind you, the three make numerous references to have been going back and forth on this for a long time (like having lost spring and fall along the way) - and all those cycles were without our Akira.

Holy hell, this one took a LONG time to write. People who aren’t particularly interested in Himawari and/or my speculations about the Trinity (in Part 2), be warned: the following is not for the faint of heart.

Ah, I see. The only thing I’d truly disagree with here is your statement that “the misdirection that you suggest, that Himawari's objectives were more devious than they appear”, because what I was *actually* suggesting is that her objectives were more *selfish*, not devious, which are not the same thing: she can still be Akira’s savior and liberator who genuinely fights for his happiness, just with slightly less “noble” and slightly more self-motivated intentions than she pretends to have – there is no inherent contradiction in this. Aside from that, though – sure, I understand where you’re coming from and how people could interpret my words that way. That one’s on me.

See, I think people are making a mistake by prematurely dismissing the Trinity as just “makeshift Gods” who are nothing more than just a few more cogs in the grand machine that is the Wishing Well, because a lot of the recent revelations about how all of this stuff supposedly works (according to Himawari) *really* bring into question just how exactly do HOPE, Tenchou and Pareidolia fit into this whole picture.

For one, we still have an entire “Nozomu creates the world” origin story – and the Tenchou one, as well – neither of which have been properly addressed as of yet. You could potentially say that this is just a very metaphorical way of describing them creating Terminal 23 or something, but I believe there is a whole lot more to it than just that baseline interpretation: after all, it’s pretty clear that each member of the Trinity directly corresponds to one of the USERs, of which there are four in total, and none of the other “outer” Gods (or other “divine” entities) that keep repeatedly showing up in Chapter 4 ever reference them or even give any indication that the USER stuff is something perfectly normal to how the Wishing Well generally operates. They repeatedly bring up Branches and Offices, for example, so we can clearly take that this is just a publicly known detail of how this company is internally structured, but USERs? Not a peep. Curious…

There is also an interesting “coincidence” that HOPE – who, as shown in “God of Light”, proudly bears the title of being a “Peerless One” – just so happens to share the name of Akira’s biological brother (with “HOPE – HOPE” even being written on the Arakawa family grave), or the fact that, as we learn from a very significant conversation between Himawari and Shiori in “F4972-B”, Ami is apparently under completely undocumented protection of someone so high up on their internal hierarchy, that not even other Peerless Ones are willing to touch her. Also, speaking of Himawari, how come that throughout the entirety of 0.53 she *not once* mentions HOPE, or Wires, or Pareidolia when talking to Akira – or, hell, when talking to Shiori, if there is some undisclosed reason why she can’t say it directly to Sensei? Is she even aware that the Trinity exists? Perhaps about Pareidolia, if the cyber sleuths’ deduction that she is the one narrating the “Pareidolia will have my head for this” line in “Miserably Ever After” is correct, but what about the other two?

On another note, while we *do* know that the HOPE/Wires cycle of summer and winter has been a fundamental staple of the Resets since, presumably, their very inception, there is little to no evidence to suggest that the Gods were actually actively involved in any of the Terminal 23 business *before* “our” Akira arrived there. Maya didn’t know shit about Yasu and only seemed to originally regard Tsuneyo as a regular classmate who occasionally transferred in during some cycles, so there is a fair chance that, with the sole exception of Pareidolia (who has been constantly scheming in the background, seeking a way overthrow the other two), both of the main members of the Trinity have just kind of passively been biding their time, completely uninterested in getting involved exactly *because* “true” Akria wasn’t there.

And finally, in regards to “Ami has made numerous references of trying to prevent Akira from being lost to gods as well. And I'll throw in another example: Does it seem like either Sekai or Sara were guided towards a satisfying end? Cause it sure doesn't to me.” – well, Ami *also* has multiple instances of openly speaking *in favor* of the Gods (or “God”, singular, most likely HOPE), like in her “Somnambula”; Sara’s only confirmed divine contacts in “Worthless Me” are Pegasus and Gossamer, not anyone from the Trinity; and who the fuck even knows what was going on with Sekai during the last few years of her life. It’s also equally possible that both Sara and Sekai ended up like they did specifically *because* they resisted their “divine purpose” too much (like Akira does throughout Chapter 3 and early Chapter 4), and that it’s not in any way indicative of the intended end state of “true ascension” – either way, none of these examples are particularly conclusive to your point *or* mine.

To finally conclude this part of the post, all of the things I just listed make me strongly suspect that Himawari’s own understanding of the full picture is *far* from complete, and that the role these Gods play in the grand scheme of things is likely much greater than we currently assume. And if my theory about Akira being USER4 is correct (the “autumn” connection certainly checks out), then that could also potentially imply that he, together with the rest of Trinity (who would then all represent some fragment or aspect of him), was the one who created the Wishing Well in the first place… in some weird, time/reality-looping way, shape or form. This would explain why Terminal 23 and Maya are both such extreme anomalies that deny all known logic (one houses the capital ‘G” GOD, the other was directly manifested by him), how HOPE’s and Tenchou’s origin stories can both be true at the same time, who is the one that protects Ami (it’s HOPE, or, hell, just a single stamp on some document somewhere, from the dude who created the universe, saying “don’t touch her”), as well as why Himawari wasn’t able to locate Akira’s original world (because he actually comes from the “true” reality, and normal people, including custodians, aren’t allowed to go there – not that Himawari would even think of that as being a possibility in the first place).

So…that went slightly off-track by the end – my apologies – but, yeah, don’t discount the Trinity as either being “too evil to care about Akira” or “too insignificant to actually matter”. And I already said my piece about how Himawari’s “happy ending” is, in my eyes, not really any different from theirs, so if none of my arguments convince you, then I guess we’ll have to agree to disagree.

My personal take on the apparent contradiction of “why did Himawari only try to manipulate Akira in 0.53, but not at any prior point?” is that it was her simply grasping at any potential straws she could, in an otherwise all-around dogshit situation. It wasn’t planned – *none* of 0.53 was planned, as the narrative makes it *abundantly* clear just how much of a fucking trainwreck that entire event chain was for everyone involved – and so while she was running high on emotions, stuck somewhere in-between desperate damage control mode and mentally screaming at herself for accidentally causing this whole mess, Himawari’s pragmatic side still sees this rare opportunity that could potentially lead to her directly furthering her goals, and then she takes it. That’s it: no master plan, no evil Himawari – just the spur of the moment thing, trying to make the best play with an abysmally shitty hand (so exactly what she always did in the past). If this all sounds too “headcanon-y” to you, though – fair enough, I understand this myself.

As for you point about how “this is quite literally the opposite of what she says” – damn, I *want to* disagree with you here, really-really want to, but genuinely don’t know how. Like, I could certainly point to a bunch of lines from “Behind the Scenes”, “The Web This World Has Spun”, “Engagement Farming”, “Last Supper” and “All That’s Left Are Stars” and read them all in such a way that *kind of* validates my interpretation of Himawari saying “yeah, what you saw in my wish-world wasn’t real, but *I’m* real, which means that the two of you *must* eventually get together, so don’t give up, keep fighting the good fight and we’ll reach our mutual happy ending yet!”, but that would be *really* pushing it, so I’ll just take the L on this one. Not taking back anything else I said about Himawari, but, yes, you are completely correct in that she never quite went *that* far.

My counterpoint to that is also a little bit headcanon-y, but, to my credit, it *does* at least partially tie in with something Himawari says in “Behind the Scenes”, and also helps explain some stuff regarding Sensei, Ayane and potentially even Ami: specifically, the fact that even when *memories* of people or events are removed, the *feelings* that were associated with those people and events still seem to persist, at least to some degree.

Think back on one of earliest things Sensei narrates to himself in the entire game, right when he follows Ami out of his classroom at the very end of “Every Day I Grow Some More”: he states that it all seems familiar to him somehow, “like it’s something I’ve done time and time before”. The logical question is: how would he even know, and why would he even feel that? I mean, the dude doesn’t remember literally anything about anything, including his name or age, and appears to be fully convinced that this isn’t his body and isn’t life. And yet this strange and unexplainable feeling of familiarity still haunts him – because it *is* his body, it *is* his life, and it *is* something that he repeatedly felt in the past during his time as a teacher: the memories are gone, but *emotions* remain. Holy hell, this one took a LONG time to write. People who aren’t particularly interested in Himawari and/or my speculations about the Trinity (in Part 2), be warned: the following is not for the faint of heart.
Spoiler:
Point 1
Ah, I see. The only thing I’d truly disagree with here is your statement that “the misdirection that you suggest, that Himawari's objectives were more devious than they appear”, because what I was *actually* suggesting is that her objectives were more *selfish*, not devious, which are not the same thing: she can still be Akira’s savior and liberator who genuinely fights for his happiness, just with slightly less “noble” and slightly more self-motivated intentions than she pretends to have – there is no inherent contradiction in this. Aside from that, though – sure, I understand where you’re coming from and how people could interpret my words that way. That one’s on me.
Spoiler:
Point 2
See, I think people are making a mistake by prematurely dismissing the Trinity as just “makeshift Gods” who are nothing more than just a few more cogs in the grand machine that is the Wishing Well, because a lot of the recent revelations about how all of this stuff supposedly works (according to Himawari) *really* bring into question just how exactly do HOPE, Tenchou and Pareidolia fit into this whole picture.
For one, we still have an entire “Nozomu creates the world” origin story – and the Tenchou one, as well – neither of which have been properly addressed as of yet. You could potentially say that this is just a very metaphorical way of describing them creating Terminal 23 or something, but I believe there is a whole lot more to it than just that baseline interpretation: after all, it’s pretty clear that each member of the Trinity directly corresponds to one of the USERs, of which there are four in total, and none of the other “outer” Gods (or other “divine” entities) that keep repeatedly showing up in Chapter 4 ever reference them or even give any indication that the USER stuff is something perfectly normal to how the Wishing Well generally operates. They repeatedly bring up Branches and Offices, for example, so we can clearly take that this is just a publicly known detail of how this company is internally structured, but USERs? Not a peep. Curious…
There is also an interesting “coincidence” that HOPE – who, as shown in “God of Light”, proudly bears the title of being a “Peerless One” – just so happens to share the name of Akira’s biological brother (with “HOPE – HOPE” even being written on the Arakawa family grave), or the fact that, as we learn from a very significant conversation between Himawari and Shiori in “F4972-B”, Ami is apparently under completely undocumented protection of someone so high up on their internal hierarchy, that not even other Peerless Ones are willing to touch her. Also, speaking of Himawari, how come that throughout the entirety of 0.53 she *not once* mentions HOPE, or Wires, or Pareidolia when talking to Akira – or, hell, when talking to Shiori, if there is some undisclosed reason why she can’t say it directly to Sensei? Is she even aware that the Trinity exists? Perhaps about Pareidolia, if the cyber sleuths’ deduction that she is the one narrating the “Pareidolia will have my head for this” line in “Miserably Ever After” is correct, but what about the other two?
On another note, while we *do* know that the HOPE/Wires cycle of summer and winter has been a fundamental staple of the Resets since, presumably, their very inception, there is little to no evidence to suggest that the Gods were actually actively involved in any of the Terminal 23 business *before* “our” Akira arrived there. Maya didn’t know shit about Yasu and only seemed to originally regard Tsuneyo as a regular classmate who occasionally transferred in during some cycles, so there is a fair chance that, with the sole exception of Pareidolia (who has been constantly scheming in the background, seeking a way overthrow the other two), both of the main members of the Trinity have just kind of passively been biding their time, completely uninterested in getting involved exactly *because* “true” Akria wasn’t there.
And finally, in regards to “Ami has made numerous references of trying to prevent Akira from being lost to gods as well. And I'll throw in another example: Does it seem like either Sekai or Sara were guided towards a satisfying end? Cause it sure doesn't to me.” – well, Ami *also* has multiple instances of openly speaking *in favor* of the Gods (or “God”, singular, most likely HOPE), like in her “Somnambula”; Sara’s only confirmed divine contacts in “Worthless Me” are Pegasus and Gossamer, not anyone from the Trinity; and who the fuck even knows what was going on with Sekai during the last few years of her life. It’s also equally possible that both Sara and Sekai ended up like they did specifically *because* they resisted their “divine purpose” too much (like Akira does throughout Chapter 3 and early Chapter 4), and that it’s not in any way indicative of the intended end state of “true ascension” – either way, none of these examples are particularly conclusive to your point *or* mine.
To finally conclude this part of the post, all of the things I just listed make me strongly suspect that Himawari’s own understanding of the full picture is *far* from complete, and that the role these Gods play in the grand scheme of things is likely much greater than we currently assume. And if my theory about Akira being USER4 is correct (the “autumn” connection certainly checks out), then that could also potentially imply that he, together with the rest of Trinity (who would then all represent some fragment or aspect of him), was the one who created the Wishing Well in the first place… in some weird, time/reality-looping way, shape or form. This would explain why Terminal 23 and Maya are both such extreme anomalies that deny all known logic (one houses the capital ‘G” GOD, the other was directly manifested by him), how HOPE’s and Tenchou’s origin stories can both be true at the same time, who is the one that protects Ami (it’s HOPE, or, hell, just a single stamp on some document somewhere, from the dude who created the universe, saying “don’t touch her”), as well as why Himawari wasn’t able to locate Akira’s original world (because he actually comes from the “true” reality, and normal people, including custodians, aren’t allowed to go there – not that Himawari would even think of that as being a possibility in the first place).
So…that went slightly off-track by the end – my apologies – but, yeah, don’t discount the Trinity as either being “too evil to care about Akira” or “too insignificant to actually matter”. And I already said my piece about how Himawari’s “happy ending” is, in my eyes, not really any different from theirs, so if none of my arguments convince you, then I guess we’ll have to agree to disagree.

It wasn’t planned – *none* of 0.53 was planned, as the narrative makes it *abundantly* clear just how much of a fucking trainwreck that entire event chain was for everyone involved – and so while she was running high on emotions, stuck somewhere in-between desperate damage control mode and mentally screaming at herself for accidentally causing this whole mess, Himawari’s pragmatic side still sees this rare opportunity that could potentially lead to her directly furthering her goals, and then she takes it. That’s it: no master plan, no evil Himawari – just the spur of the moment thing, trying to make the best play with an abysmally shitty hand (so exactly what she always did in the past). If this all sounds too “headcanon-y” to you, though – fair enough, I understand this myself.
As for you point about how “this is quite literally the opposite of what she says” – damn, I *want to* disagree with you here, really-really want to, but genuinely don’t know how. Like, I could certainly point to a bunch of lines from “Behind the Scenes”, “The Web This World Has Spun”, “Engagement Farming”, “Last Supper” and “All That’s Left Are Stars” and read them all in such a way that *kind of* validates my interpretation of Himawari saying “yeah, what you saw in my wish-world wasn’t real, but *I’m* real, which means that the two of you *must* eventually get together, so don’t give up, keep fighting the good fight and we’ll reach our mutual happy ending yet!”, but that would be *really* pushing it, so I’ll just take the L on this one. Think back on one of earliest things Sensei narrates to himself in the entire game, right when he follows Ami out of his classroom at the very end of “Every Day I Grow Some More”: he states that it all seems familiar to him somehow, “like it’s something I’ve done time and time before”. So if you’re asking what reason did Himawari have to still try to manipulate her mom and dad despite knowing full well that she’ll have to erase their memories anyway – *that’s* why. To emotionally “supercharge” them into loving her and wanting to be with her, so that those residual feelings will be the main motivation and driving force – something that both of them previously lacked – for Akira and Ayane to actually get together for real and eventually escape the cycle, even if neither of them has any idea *who* those feelings are for. spoilers.title: Point 2
spoilers.html:
See, I think people are making a mistake by prematurely dismissing the Trinity as just “makeshift Gods” who are nothing more than just a few more cogs in the grand machine that is the Wishing Well, because a lot of the recent revelations about how all of this stuff supposedly works (according to Himawari) *really* bring into question just how exactly do HOPE, Tenchou and Pareidolia fit into this whole picture.

For one, we still have an entire “Nozomu creates the world” origin story – and the Tenchou one, as well – neither of which have been properly addressed as of yet. You could potentially say that this is just a very metaphorical way of describing them creating Terminal 23 or something, but I believe there is a whole lot more to it than just that baseline interpretation: after all, it’s pretty clear that each member of the Trinity directly corresponds to one of the USERs, of which there are four in total, and none of the other “outer” Gods (or other “divine” entities) that keep repeatedly showing up in Chapter 4 ever reference them or even give any indication that the USER stuff is something perfectly normal to how the Wishing Well generally operates. They repeatedly bring up Branches and Offices, for example, so we can clearly take that this is just a publicly known detail of how this company is internally structured, but USERs? Not a peep. Curious…

There is also an interesting “coincidence” that HOPE – who, as shown in “God of Light”, proudly bears the title of being a “Peerless One” – just so happens to share the name of Akira’s biological brother (with “HOPE – HOPE” even being written on the Arakawa family grave), or the fact that, as we learn from a very significant conversation between Himawari and Shiori in “F4972-B”, Ami is apparently under completely undocumented protection of someone so high up on their internal hierarchy, that not even other Peerless Ones are willing to touch her. Also, speaking of Himawari, how come that throughout the entirety of 0.53 she *not once* mentions HOPE, or Wires, or Pareidolia when talking to Akira – or, hell, when talking to Shiori, if there is some undisclosed reason why she can’t say it directly to Sensei? Is she even aware that the Trinity exists? Perhaps about Pareidolia, if the cyber sleuths’ deduction that she is the one narrating the “Pareidolia will have my head for this” line in “Miserably Ever After” is correct, but what about the other two?

On another note, while we *do* know that the HOPE/Wires cycle of summer and winter has been a fundamental staple of the Resets since, presumably, their very inception, there is little to no evidence to suggest that the Gods were actually actively involved in any of the Terminal 23 business *before* “our” Akira arrived there. Maya didn’t know shit about Yasu and only seemed to originally regard Tsuneyo as a regular classmate who occasionally transferred in during some cycles, so there is a fair chance that, with the sole exception of Pareidolia (who has been constantly scheming in the background, seeking a way overthrow the other two), both of the main members of the Trinity have just kind of passively been biding their time, completely uninterested in getting involved exactly *because* “true” Akria wasn’t there.

And finally, in regards to “Ami has made numerous references of trying to prevent Akira from being lost to gods as well. And I'll throw in another example: Does it seem like either Sekai or Sara were guided towards a satisfying end? Cause it sure doesn't to me.” – well, Ami *also* has multiple instances of openly speaking *in favor* of the Gods (or “God”, singular, most likely HOPE), like in her “Somnambula”; Sara’s only confirmed divine contacts in “Worthless Me” are Pegasus and Gossamer, not anyone from the Trinity; and who the fuck even knows what was going on with Sekai during the last few years of her life. It’s also equally possible that both Sara and Sekai ended up like they did specifically *because* they resisted their “divine purpose” too much (like Akira does throughout Chapter 3 and early Chapter 4), and that it’s not in any way indicative of the intended end state of “true ascension” – either way, none of these examples are particularly conclusive to your point *or* mine.

To finally conclude this part of the post, all of the things I just listed make me strongly suspect that Himawari’s own understanding of the full picture is *far* from complete, and that the role these Gods play in the grand scheme of things is likely much greater than we currently assume. And if my theory about Akira being USER4 is correct (the “autumn” connection certainly checks out), then that could also potentially imply that he, together with the rest of Trinity (who would then all represent some fragment or aspect of him), was the one who created the Wishing Well in the first place… in some weird, time/reality-looping way, shape or form. This would explain why Terminal 23 and Maya are both such extreme anomalies that deny all known logic (one houses the capital ‘G” GOD, the other was directly manifested by him), how HOPE’s and Tenchou’s origin stories can both be true at the same time, who is the one that protects Ami (it’s HOPE, or, hell, just a single stamp on some document somewhere, from the dude who created the universe, saying “don’t touch her”), as well as why Himawari wasn’t able to locate Akira’s original world (because he actually comes from the “true” reality, and normal people, including custodians, aren’t allowed to go there – not that Himawari would even think of that as being a possibility in the first place).

So…that went slightly off-track by the end – my apologies – but, yeah, don’t discount the Trinity as either being “too evil to care about Akira” or “too insignificant to actually matter”. And I already said my piece about how Himawari’s “happy ending” is, in my eyes, not really any different from theirs, so if none of my arguments convince you, then I guess we’ll have to agree to disagree.

spoilers.title: Point 3
spoilers.html:
My personal take on the apparent contradiction of “why did Himawari only try to manipulate Akira in 0.53, but not at any prior point?” is that it was her simply grasping at any potential straws she could, in an otherwise all-around dogshit situation. It wasn’t planned – *none* of 0.53 was planned, as the narrative makes it *abundantly* clear just how much of a fucking trainwreck that entire event chain was for everyone involved – and so while she was running high on emotions, stuck somewhere in-between desperate damage control mode and mentally screaming at herself for accidentally causing this whole mess, Himawari’s pragmatic side still sees this rare opportunity that could potentially lead to her directly furthering her goals, and then she takes it. That’s it: no master plan, no evil Himawari – just the spur of the moment thing, trying to make the best play with an abysmally shitty hand (so exactly what she always did in the past). If this all sounds too “headcanon-y” to you, though – fair enough, I understand this myself.

As for you point about how “this is quite literally the opposite of what she says” – damn, I *want to* disagree with you here, really-really want to, but genuinely don’t know how. Like, I could certainly point to a bunch of lines from “Behind the Scenes”, “The Web This World Has Spun”, “Engagement Farming”, “Last Supper” and “All That’s Left Are Stars” and read them all in such a way that *kind of* validates my interpretation of Himawari saying “yeah, what you saw in my wish-world wasn’t real, but *I’m* real, which means that the two of you *must* eventually get together, so don’t give up, keep fighting the good fight and we’ll reach our mutual happy ending yet!”, but that would be *really* pushing it, so I’ll just take the L on this one. Not taking back anything else I said about Himawari, but, yes, you are completely correct in that she never quite went *that* far.

spoilers.title: Point 4
spoilers.html:
My counterpoint to that is also a little bit headcanon-y, but, to my credit, it *does* at least partially tie in with something Himawari says in “Behind the Scenes”, and also helps explain some stuff regarding Sensei, Ayane and potentially even Ami: specifically, the fact that even when *memories* of people or events are removed, the *feelings* that were associated with those people and events still seem to persist, at least to some degree.

Think back on one of earliest things Sensei narrates to himself in the entire game, right when he follows Ami out of his classroom at the very end of “Every Day I Grow Some More”: he states that it all seems familiar to him somehow, “like it’s something I’ve done time and time before”. The logical question is: how would he even know, and why would he even feel that? I mean, the dude doesn’t remember literally anything about anything, including his name or age, and appears to be fully convinced that this isn’t his body and isn’t life. And yet this strange and unexplainable feeling of familiarity still haunts him – because it *is* his body, it *is* his life, and it *is* something that he repeatedly felt in the past during his time as a teacher: the memories are gone, but *emotions* remain. Likewise, Ayane still retained the conflicting feelings of fear and adoration she felt towards her unborn baby even after everything related to it was scrubbed clean both from mind and her body (as confirmed in “Untitled”), and early 0.53 is *full* of moments of Ayane and Akira being directly influenced by lingering memories of the versions of themselves they replaced – memories that neither of them actually experienced or remembers, but still make them *feel* things.

So if you’re asking what reason did Himawari have to still try to manipulate her mom and dad despite knowing full well that she’ll have to erase their memories anyway – *that’s* why. To emotionally “supercharge” them into loving her and wanting to be with her, so that those residual feelings will be the main motivation and driving force – something that both of them previously lacked – for Akira and Ayane to actually get together for real and eventually escape the cycle, even if neither of them has any idea *who* those feelings are for. And it fucking worked – “The First Christmalloween” is all the proof that you need to see how effective the first stage of Himawari’s strategy ended up being, and then the effect in had on 0.54.

A standard logic would be that "Himawari didn't manipulate her parents, because she knew the memories wouldn't hold, and she herself erased them. We have seen her telling them that, as well as Shiori once they're gone, and it is also reflected in her own internal dialogue when she's alone".

Your logic is "despite every indication that she didn't plan for this and didn't intend for it to happen, that Yasu made them somewhat remember that they lost something important is a heavy indication that we should disconsider all that was shown regarding what Himawari did and said, and conclude that it was a ploy from Himawari that she's, for some reason, hiding from an unseen viewer, aka the player".

Surely you can also see the likelihood of one option being much higher than the other?

Okay, now that the Himawari-posting has passed, I want to do some Yasu-posting, and quite topically named too, since this theory I've been thinking about is a lot more schizo than anything else I've come up with so far
This idea came to me in passing before the 0.54 update, and I'm gonna stick with it since the Yasu events started to lean into a more clinical look at Yasu as Akira and Ayane started to ask her about her religion. I'm just gonna say it, I'm not actually convinced Yasu's god actually exists. To be clear, "I'm not convinced that Yasu's god exists" is NOT the same statement as "Yasu's god definitely does not exist." I'll be honest, thinking over it some more, at the time Yasu was introduced into the story, I'm pretty sure that Sel intended for Yasu's god to be real (and probably HOPE/Nozomu), and at the time of writing this post it's very possible (and quite frankly most likely) that Yasu's god still exists as a concrete plot point, but enough has changed with Sel's depiction of divinity and the metaphysics of this multiverse that has made me doubt if he's actually going to stick with that for future writings.

Okay, we're getting ahead of ourselves. First thing's first: if Yasu's god doesn't exist, then how the hell does she know so much about what's going on both in this world and about the greater narrative (for example, like knowing that Nozomu fucked the world into existence). Simple: she's schizophrenic. To expand upon that, nearly all of the girls who entered into their TSS's have done so at a time of great emotional distress or otherwise altered state of mind, and in each of these events they received strange revelations about the multiverse, with Kirin's in particular being a rather stark example of such (referring to Himawari's offhand comments about how Terminal23 has turned into a show of sorts to the gods and their employees, and Kirin momentarily being plucked out of Terminal23 and placed directly in front of said audience). Where all the other characters have had temporary moments of altered perception, that's just Yasu's natural resting point, just more mild. What I'm claiming is that because Yasu's a schizophrenic, her altered perception is constantly revealing to her bits and pieces of information about the world and greater multiverse. She says as much several times (no screenshot at the moment, and I'm too lazy, sorry) that she "constantly hears the noise of the world." If I remember correctly she made a comment like this immediately before predicting that Makoto would be called to the office to be informed that her dad was dead, a seemingly unnatural alteration to the timeline.

And okay, that's a neat little theory and all, but that's just too shaky to out and speculate that Yasu's god doesn't exist, and when Yasu was first introduced into the story, I'd agree with that. At that time, the only three gods we were aware of were HOPE/Nozomu, Wires, and Paredolia. At the time, there was also a lot of Trinitarian verbage written into a lot of Akira's Happy Events, so the theology of Yasu's religion, a culty corrupted form of Christian theology, made perfect sense and had no reason for question. That has changed, and only just a few updates ago the pantheon of gods exploded from just the 3 into thousands and thousands of gods for every little human concept, and update 0.53 confirmed once and for all that they run a megacorporation of all things. The theology and relationship between gods and man have departed so far away from the corrupted Christian theology that Sel started with to the point that Yasu's religion sticks out like a sore thumb from how we know for a fact the rest of the gods behave. I mean, Akira hasn't mentioned her again, but he distinctly remembers meeting and talking with Amber, the god of reconstruction, who behaves absolutely nothing like what you would expect from any version of Christian theology, even the real-world offshoot cults, so what gives?

To piece this together here, what I'm claiming is that because Yasu's schizophrenia is constantly altering her perception, she's constantly glimpsing the nature of the greater metaphysics of the setting, but she's also constantly misinterpreting it and has formed a cult of misinterpreted Christian theology based on what she's seen. A large portion of what she's seen is related in some way to HOPE/Nozomu, which is where she gets the patriarchal focus-worship-on-one elements that she incorportated into Christian theology, to the point of outright ignoring Akira's and Ayane's comments about gods (plural) at McDonald's and going straight back to rambling about god (singular). This could be reason alone to say that Yasu's god exists and is HOPE, but what I'm claiming is that the voices commanding Yasu to do things is not HOPE but her own schizophrenia, and her rituals are not a codified sacred rite but rather the right-answer-with-a-wrong-formula kind of deal. This would also fit in with the theme that if HOPE is Nozomu, the same Nozomu that was an abuser to Akira, that he really wouldn't give a damn about Yasu or if she's practicing her veneration of him correctly, just that he has her attention in some fucky-wucky roundabout way. Yasu also had an important moment when she was temporarily strongly medicated and no longer experiencing psychosis where she had a brief talk with nu-Maya, speaking eloquently (by Yasu's standards) about how she knows about her nature, but also speaking as if these revelations had previously come to her, that is to say when she was unmedicated/partially medicated, implying that her schizophrenic psychosis is directly linked to her ability to receive revelations about the world.

I'll end this rant by stating that my interpretation of Yasu is strongly colored by my own personal biases. I personally consider myself a Christian, and I was raised by a mother who had some form of religious psychosis (never properly diagnosed, even when a therapist directly told her she needed one, naturally). She spent her time openly ignoring the unambiguous direct statements in scripture in favor of the weirder esoteric ones that most religious scholars are still locked in debate on or otherwise admit they do not know the meaning of. As I've come to learn about various cults that have formed as offshoots of Christianity, I've found they often begin by hyper-focusing on these weird details trying to explain them to the point of ignoring or even over-writing the unambiguous parts of scripture about even basic morality. Often these weird offhand comments in scripture forming the basis of these heretical cults is referencing the end of the world, much like my mother's religous psychosis and, back to our topic at hand, much like Yasu's. Her story grips me in a way that none of the other characters can and has the potential to be the most interesting character in the game to me.

I may be absolutely dead wrong in my suspicion that Yasu's god doesn't exist (and quite frankly for the simplicity of the story I would hope so). I may be misinterpreting Sel's writing of divinity as a result of my own religous biases, or maybe Sel is also as lost as I am, the both of us driving ourselves mad trying to connect the red twine between the tacks on the tackboard. If nothing else, I'd like to get a conversationg going on Yasu, because at the moment, the simple fact that she knows as much as she does about the nature of the world means that she is going to be a pivotal character in revealing information on how to break the cycle, in one form or another.

I really want to see how Akira's relationship with Rin and Chika develops from now on.
With Chika trying to get back to her "old self," it will be interesting to see if she tries to rebuild her relationship with him or if, like with Rin, she asks him to take some time apart. I can even imagine a situation where she asks him not to try to seduce Rin until she can sort out her feelings, similar to how Rin asked him not to pursue things with Chika until she confessed her feelings.

And regarding Rin, from what I see in the previews, it seems she took their "breakup" better than I expected. There could be three reasons for this. The first would be that Rin has matured and accepts her situation with Chika. The second option is that she has matured but doesn't accept her situation with Chika and decides to form some kind of plan to win her back so she can be with both of them, which might or might not involve Akira as her accomplice. The third one is the most interesting to me because it could lead to an event like "insert name of that Io event" where all that maturity is just a facade that cracks in front of Akira.

Where do Chika and Rin go for now?
Click to expand...
I think, based on both 0.54 and previous evidence, that we won't see much change in them, other than them stopping to "hang out" together.
On Rin's side of the situation, she's horny for Chika, sure. But she romantically loves Akira. Selebus has confirmed this both in-game (through Otoha's talk with Futaba and Rin's silence), and outside on the discord. The times when she would waver towards Chika's side are gone. She has deep feelings for her, yes - but those are not romantic anymore.

And on Chika's side of the situation, I really don't think she'd get in the way of Akira and Rin cause that'd be an insanely dick move to Rin. When Rin asked Akira not to hit on Chika, it wasn't until either one could sort out their feelings, but that he'd wait until she made her move. After she does and breaks in his arms, she's fine with him hitting on Chika. By comparison, Chika not only made her move, but has already had sex with Rin and declared her feelings. The time to stall is long gone.

If I have to make a prediction, 0.55 is likely to be the very last barrier between Akira and Rin (if it finally happens in this update I don't know). But we'll have Rika having some sort of sexual interaction with Akira (and her plan was to have sex with him so that he doesn't fuck Rin), and we'll have Rin dealing with a "previous" Chika, the one that most resembles the one she was in love with, and they'll be in the reversed positions they were back then. This will end up with Rin rejecting her for good (since Chika didn't allow her to answer back in 0.54).
I do hope Chika breaks up with Akira though. I think we can all agree we've had enough of her insanity by now. Focusing on a secondary romance isn't the answer at all, and doesn't solve the problem. Plus, it opens up the scenario even more for the Yumi romance if they do break up.

Okay, so, since I’m effectively taking a short break from in-depth character analysis until the opportunity to talk about the few select characters I *do* want to cover later naturally presents itself, I guess it’s time for something a little different. The following is going to be me unabashedly and very passionately gushing about a certain aspect of Lessons in Love that I think is either somewhat underappreciated or simply gets unmentioned due to all of the constant focus on the plot, the characters and so on: namely, what kids these days colloquially refer to as “the vibes”. It’s also going to be a lot less focused than the walls of text I normally produce, so feel free to ignore my post if this subject isn’t really up your alley.

Now, everyone who played LiL as much I as I did knows *exactly* what I’m talking about here: the game has a very, very particular style and mood about it, both of which (as Moonflare, if I’m not mistaken, once pointed out) get strongly established right from the get-go, with the perfection that is “Every Day I Grow Some More”, and then are meticulously maintained throughout the rest of the narrative experience that is this unholy piece of fiction. Selebus’ ability to write extremely engaging prose in addition to his (almost) immaculate choice of music certainly do a lot of the heavy lifting in this regard: tracks like “undersea”, “blue air”, “glasswalker”, “itsingsinitssleep”, “papercity”, “saudade”, the recent “flowersforalgernon” and many others are great for evoking the surreal, retrospective and deeply melancholic tone that permeates Lessons in Love to its very core – but I would also argue that (despite what a certain ignorant friend of mine seems to think) the simple, relatively low-poly Koikatsu visuals *also* play a huge role in this, as the game, IMO, just wouldn’t work nearly as well if it had regular 2D sprites or, alternatively, much more “realistic” 3D graphics.

Furthermore, the “vibes” of LiL remind me a lot of the general atmosphere of Haruki Murakami’s works, or the (frankly, genius) way SHAFT chose to adapt the Monogatari novels: in both cases the underlying surrealism of what is going on is *always* present, affecting how you perceive even otherwise completely commonplace scenes, but rather than intentionally contrasting with the mundane, like it’s usually done within the genre of magical realism, the surreal aspects instead run *in parallel* with the grounded stuff, making it so that the setting feels both normal and abnormal at the same time and you can never be sure if the next thing that is going to happen will have the protagonist filing their taxes or casually encountering God. I guess “liminal” is the best way to describe it, as it is applicable both in the sense of “being on the threshold” (of reality and unreality, with the never-ending struggle of trying to discern which is which) as well as the ever-familiar feeling of constant ambiguity and disorientation that you eventually learn to accept, thrive in and even yearn for.

The thing I like the most about these kinds of stories, however, is the fact that none of them are inherently “scary”. A touch unsettling and mildly creepy, sure, but never to the point where you are supposed to be feeling actual *fear*. Because, yes, going home after school/work like it’s any other day and then suddenly running into a skinwalker or finding yourself in some wacky alien dimension operating on moon logic would *probably* be a very terrifying thing to experience… but it could *also* be a really cool one. Like, who knows? Maybe those “eldritch horrors beyond human comprehension” are actually pretty chill and are just as confused about you as you are about them? That’s not to say that they would instead be openly friendly to you or unable to easily make you bleed from every orifice just by looking at you funny, but there is a huge difference between “do some basic precautions, and you’ll be fine” and having to permanently fear for your life with every action you take.

Just think of how beyond life-changing of an experience it would be to be able to freely explore somewhere like the Great Pareidolia Mall, for example, or any of the Transpacific Sadness Symposium locations, without needing to worry about your personal safety, or getting lost, or anything negative whatsoever – just pure unrestrained curiosity, coupled with the ability to openly meet otherworldly entities that defy all understanding and see the sights that potentially no other human has ever seen? To personally gaze at the same impossible sky Sensei, and Maya, and the rest of RAS see whenever they gather on the school rooftop right before a Reset, or, hell, to just spend even a few days visiting Kumon-mi – a place where there are secrets to find and mysteries to uncover behind every corner?
