Okay, so, since I’m effectively taking a short break from in-depth character analysis until the opportunity to talk about the few select characters I *do* want to cover later naturally presents itself, I guess it’s time for something a little different. The following is going to be me unabashedly and very passionately gushing about a certain aspect of Lessons in Love that I think is either somewhat underappreciated or simply gets unmentioned due to all of the constant focus on the plot, the characters and so on: namely, what kids these days colloquially refer to as “the vibes”. It’s also going to be a lot less focused than the walls of text I normally produce, so feel free to ignore my post if this subject isn’t really up your alley.
Spoiler:
Immaculate vibes, and wanderlust
Now, everyone who played LiL as much I as I did knows *exactly* what I’m talking about here: the game has a very, very particular style and mood about it, both of which (as Moonflare, if I’m not mistaken, once pointed out) get strongly established right from the get-go, with the perfection that is “Every Day I Grow Some More”, and then are meticulously maintained throughout the rest of the narrative experience that is this unholy piece of fiction. Selebus’ ability to write extremely engaging prose in addition to his (almost) immaculate choice of music certainly do a lot of the heavy lifting in this regard: tracks like “undersea”, “blue air”, “glasswalker”, “itsingsinitssleep”, “papercity”, “saudade”, the recent “flowersforalgernon” and many others are great for evoking the surreal, retrospective and deeply melancholic tone that permeates Lessons in Love to its very core – but I would also argue that (despite what a certain ignorant friend of mine seems to think) the simple, relatively low-poly Koikatsu visuals *also* play a huge role in this, as the game, IMO, just wouldn’t work nearly as well if it had regular 2D sprites or, alternatively, much more “realistic” 3D graphics.
Furthermore, the “vibes” of LiL remind me a lot of the general atmosphere of Haruki Murakami’s works, or the (frankly, genius) way SHAFT chose to adapt the Monogatari novels: in both cases the underlying surrealism of what is going on is *always* present, affecting how you perceive even otherwise completely commonplace scenes, but rather than intentionally contrasting with the mundane, like it’s usually done within the genre of magical realism, the surreal aspects instead run *in parallel* with the grounded stuff, making it so that the setting feels both normal and abnormal at the same time and you can never be sure if the next thing that is going to happen will have the protagonist filing their taxes or casually encountering God. I guess “liminal” is the best way to describe it, as it is applicable both in the sense of “being on the threshold” (of reality and unreality, with the never-ending struggle of trying to discern which is which) as well as the ever-familiar feeling of constant ambiguity and disorientation that you eventually learn to accept, thrive in and even yearn for.
The thing I like the most about these kinds of stories, however, is the fact that none of them are inherently “scary”. A touch unsettling and mildly creepy, sure, but never to the point where you are supposed to be feeling actual *fear*. Because, yes, going home after school/work like it’s any other day and then suddenly running into a skinwalker or finding yourself in some wacky alien dimension operating on moon logic would *probably* be a very terrifying thing to experience… but it could *also* be a really cool one. Like, who knows? Maybe those “eldritch horrors beyond human comprehension” are actually pretty chill and are just as confused about you as you are about them? That’s not to say that they would instead be openly friendly to you or unable to easily make you bleed from every orifice just by looking at you funny, but there is a huge difference between “do some basic precautions, and you’ll be fine” and having to permanently fear for your life with every action you take.
Just think of how beyond life-changing of an experience it would be to be able to freely explore somewhere like the Great Pareidolia Mall, for example, or any of the Transpacific Sadness Symposium locations, without needing to worry about your personal safety, or getting lost, or anything negative whatsoever – just pure unrestrained curiosity, coupled with the ability to openly meet otherworldly entities that defy all understanding and see the sights that potentially no other human has ever seen? To personally gaze at the same impossible sky Sensei, and Maya, and the rest of RAS see whenever they gather on the school rooftop right before a Reset, or, hell, to just spend even a few days visiting Kumon-mi – a place where there are secrets to find and mysteries to uncover behind every corner? Some people don’t feel the same wanderlust, don’t seek the strange and the unfamiliar with the same desperate yearning I do, preferring to instead lead a calm and peaceful life of daily monotony – and that is okay! But others…? Others – including me – would *kill* for a chance like that.

but I would also argue that (despite what a certain ignorant friend of mine seems to think) the simple, relatively low-poly Koikatsu visuals *also* play a huge role in this, as the game, IMO, just wouldn’t work nearly as well if it had regular 2D sprites or, alternatively, much more “realistic” 3D graphics.
Click to expand...
Personally I'm not a huge fan of Koikatsu-based games, the character modeling is limited and, truth be told, faces just really look the same for every female character, which is also why every LiL character has their own eye color, hair color and hair style. Which, by the way, and I hope I'm not the only one, makes Halloween events so damn confusing sometimes when they dress up and change their hair style.

Basically, the engine does not offer much on individual traits that help distinguish characters or make them look unique, outside of body proportions. Also adult male models always look like shit (sorry, Akira).
But I do get your point of this simplicity also working well for the game. It has a cute look and emphasizes the more wholesome aspects of the game, while at the same time working as a contrast to the more creepy and outlandish themes within the story.

However, I'm not sure why 2D sprites wouldn't be able to convey something similar, depending on the style. I think that's the main argument here, hand drawn art(i.e. not AI generated, unless someone put a lot of effort into it) would offer a lot of potential detail in what the author wants to depict, set free from the Koikatsu character presets and the assets as well. Sel himself has often commented on the topic of some assets not really fitting in well with the game, but the more humoristic and absurd part of the storytelling often accommodates such discrepancies and inserts rather naturally.
And as a side note, since not everyone might be aware of that, Sel's next game is supposed to include hand drawn 2D anime art as opposed to Koikatsu, or any other 3D engine for that matter, especially since he will be living directly in Japan with supposed contacts to local artists to commission/collaborate with.

That being said, I fully agree with your take that more realistic looking 3D engine models (Daz3D, Unreal etc.) would look out of place and ruin the vibe the game is meant to portray. The more realistic it looked, the more of the surreal and playful whimsy would be lost in the overall atmosphere due to it.

Especially the depiction of the wizards would just look very off-putting in this game. Not that depicting underage girls in a porn game in the first place is inherently wholesome, mind you, but this sort of anime style lends itself to make it fall under the more commonly accepted/tolerated loli-rule I suppose, that kind of makes you separate the individual characters from what they actually are to what they represent in that medium, making it a bit more tolerable in a certain sense, I think. Or in other words, they can more easily pass off as just smaller adults lol. At least more so than any more realistic-looking models would be able to do. Or maybe I'm coping, whatever, sue me.
You also make a great point about the game evoking some form of wanderlust in the player.
Akira himself often points out that he feels like he cannot stand still and has the urge to traverse Kumon-mi and visit different places, which conveniently plays nicely into the gameplay loop. But yeah, exploring new areas, seeing new perspectives from new renders, discovering the mysterious of this strange world and triggering happy events is quite mesmerizing and makes up a lot of the charm of this game.

So much so even, that now that I think about it, I kind of wish someone created a spin off of this game at some point that would essentially be either a 3D mystery sandbox to explore Kumon-mi or at least a 2D point-and-click adventure to collect clues. I'd play the fuck out of a Disco Elysium set in Kumon-mi with the different fucked up gods talking to me and providing live commentary. Fuck, I miss Disco Elysium.
Edit: Also, I just remembered, on the topic of Koikatsu. Is anyone else unable to play other Koikatsu games because of LiL? Maybe not completely unable to, but a lot of the models, whether intentionally or not, look too similar to LiL characters to not have the connection somewhere in the back of my head, breaking the immersion.

spoilers.title: Immaculate vibes, and wanderlust
spoilers.html:
Now, everyone who played LiL as much I as I did knows *exactly* what I’m talking about here: the game has a very, very particular style and mood about it, both of which (as Moonflare, if I’m not mistaken, once pointed out) get strongly established right from the get-go, with the perfection that is “Every Day I Grow Some More”, and then are meticulously maintained throughout the rest of the narrative experience that is this unholy piece of fiction. Selebus’ ability to write extremely engaging prose in addition to his (almost) immaculate choice of music certainly do a lot of the heavy lifting in this regard: tracks like “undersea”, “blue air”, “glasswalker”, “itsingsinitssleep”, “papercity”, “saudade”, the recent “flowersforalgernon” and many others are great for evoking the surreal, retrospective and deeply melancholic tone that permeates Lessons in Love to its very core – but I would also argue that (despite what a certain ignorant friend of mine seems to think) the simple, relatively low-poly Koikatsu visuals *also* play a huge role in this, as the game, IMO, just wouldn’t work nearly as well if it had regular 2D sprites or, alternatively, much more “realistic” 3D graphics.

Furthermore, the “vibes” of LiL remind me a lot of the general atmosphere of Haruki Murakami’s works, or the (frankly, genius) way SHAFT chose to adapt the Monogatari novels: in both cases the underlying surrealism of what is going on is *always* present, affecting how you perceive even otherwise completely commonplace scenes, but rather than intentionally contrasting with the mundane, like it’s usually done within the genre of magical realism, the surreal aspects instead run *in parallel* with the grounded stuff, making it so that the setting feels both normal and abnormal at the same time and you can never be sure if the next thing that is going to happen will have the protagonist filing their taxes or casually encountering God. I guess “liminal” is the best way to describe it, as it is applicable both in the sense of “being on the threshold” (of reality and unreality, with the never-ending struggle of trying to discern which is which) as well as the ever-familiar feeling of constant ambiguity and disorientation that you eventually learn to accept, thrive in and even yearn for.

The thing I like the most about these kinds of stories, however, is the fact that none of them are inherently “scary”. A touch unsettling and mildly creepy, sure, but never to the point where you are supposed to be feeling actual *fear*. Because, yes, going home after school/work like it’s any other day and then suddenly running into a skinwalker or finding yourself in some wacky alien dimension operating on moon logic would *probably* be a very terrifying thing to experience… but it could *also* be a really cool one. Like, who knows? Maybe those “eldritch horrors beyond human comprehension” are actually pretty chill and are just as confused about you as you are about them? That’s not to say that they would instead be openly friendly to you or unable to easily make you bleed from every orifice just by looking at you funny, but there is a huge difference between “do some basic precautions, and you’ll be fine” and having to permanently fear for your life with every action you take.

Just think of how beyond life-changing of an experience it would be to be able to freely explore somewhere like the Great Pareidolia Mall, for example, or any of the Transpacific Sadness Symposium locations, without needing to worry about your personal safety, or getting lost, or anything negative whatsoever – just pure unrestrained curiosity, coupled with the ability to openly meet otherworldly entities that defy all understanding and see the sights that potentially no other human has ever seen? To personally gaze at the same impossible sky Sensei, and Maya, and the rest of RAS see whenever they gather on the school rooftop right before a Reset, or, hell, to just spend even a few days visiting Kumon-mi – a place where there are secrets to find and mysteries to uncover behind every corner? Some people don’t feel the same wanderlust, don’t seek the strange and the unfamiliar with the same desperate yearning I do, preferring to instead lead a calm and peaceful life of daily monotony – and that is okay! But others…? Others – including me – would *kill* for a chance like that.

posts.content_html_raw:
CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Furthermore, the “vibes” of LiL remind me a lot of the general atmosphere of Haruki Murakami’s works, or the (frankly, genius) way SHAFT chose to adapt the Monogatari novels.
Click to expand...
Very good post, and while I agree with it overall, I'd like to add a few things.
Ironically, imo, what makes the adaptation of monogatari better than LiL (excluding the inherent differences of their genres) is that, although both deal with the supernatural, monogatari's supernatural is a tool to make the internal struggles external. Most of the time, there aren't even supernatural elements - but rather what you said: a hyperfocus on an element that makes us reevaluate the ordinary as extraordinary.

Having a black screen between shots is not supernatural, but having one that has "black" written in the middle of it, and then writing "noir" instead of either black in Japanese or English makes you "wake up" and take it as something that needs to be evaluated on its own. This is inherently different from having random gods come talk to Akira (which is actually supernatural).

There is a quote I think explains this that says that "if we were able to look at the world again, as we did when we were young, and everything was new, we'd realise how everything around us has never stopped being magical".

All of this isn't either new or my merit for noticing but a technique in formal literature called "estrangement" = forcing the reader to stop their automatic comprehension, and making them have to evaluate something as unique.

I think Selebus does follow it to some extent, but, again, as I said it is mostly supernatural in essence. If Akira kept wandering towards the noise he would have been deleted, this is not the ordinary being perceived as extraordinary, it is the extraordinary itself.

While Monogatari does have aspects of the supernatural, they are presented as "a girl that has no weight" (because she suffered a trauma so great she gave up her ability to deal with anything), or "a girl that is a stray cat" (because she feels as a stray in a home of people who married her parents, and yet her parents died, and now she lives with a couple of strangers that have no blood ties to her). These supernatural situations and more are not "real" in terms of analysis, but projections of their actual traumas.

If LiL was, as many assumed throughout the years, a manifestation of Akira's inner trauma then it would have a long play by Selebus in which none of the supernatural actually existed, and things would have been more in tone with monogatari - but that isn't the case.

One isn't better than the other just from the tools they choose to use, obviously, but what I mean by considering the monogatari adaptation better is that (to me) actually making the ordinary extraordinary requires more than meshing supernatural elements throughout the ordinary.
They're both great works at the end of the day regardless, just thought I'd add something.

While Monogatari does have aspects of the supernatural, they are presented as "a girl that has no weight" (because she suffered a trauma so great she gave up her ability to deal with anything), or "a girl that is a stray cat" (because she feels as a stray in a home of people who married her parents, and yet her parents died, and now she lives with a couple of strangers that have no blood ties to her). These supernatural situations and more are not "real" in terms of analysis, but projections of their actual traumas.

If LiL was, as many assumed throughout the years, a manifestation of Akira's inner trauma then it would have a long play by Selebus in which none of the supernatural actually existed, and things would have been more in tone with monogatari - but that isn't the case.

One isn't better than the other just from the tools they choose to use, obviously, but what I mean by considering the monogatari adaptation better is that (to me) actually making the ordinary extraordinary requires more than meshing supernatural elements throughout the ordinary.

DeanNoriko said:
A very good post, once again, putting a lot of what I feel when playing the game in terms I wouldn't be able to come up with myself.


Personally I'm not a huge fan of Koikatsu-based games, the character modeling is limited and, truth be told, faces just really look the same for every female character, which is also why every LiL character has their own eye color, hair color and hair style. Which, by the way, and I hope I'm not the only one, makes Halloween events so damn confusing sometimes when they dress up and change their hair style.

Basically, the engine does not offer much on individual traits that help distinguish characters or make them look unique, outside of body proportions. Also adult male models always look like shit (sorry, Akira).
But I do get your point of this simplicity also working well for the game. It has a cute look and emphasizes the more wholesome aspects of the game, while at the same time working as a contrast to the more creepy and outlandish themes within the story.

However, I'm not sure why 2D sprites wouldn't be able to convey something similar, depending on the style. I think that's the main argument here, hand drawn art(i.e. not AI generated, unless someone put a lot of effort into it) would offer a lot of potential detail in what the author wants to depict, set free from the Koikatsu character presets and the assets as well. Sel himself has often commented on the topic of some assets not really fitting in well with the game, but the more humoristic and absurd part of the storytelling often accommodates such discrepancies and inserts rather naturally.
And as a side note, since not everyone might be aware of that, Sel's next game is supposed to include hand drawn 2D anime art as opposed to Koikatsu, or any other 3D engine for that matter, especially since he will be living directly in Japan with supposed contacts to local artists to commission/collaborate with.

That being said, I fully agree with your take that more realistic looking 3D engine models (Daz3D, Unreal etc.) would look out of place and ruin the vibe the game is meant to portray. The more realistic it looked, the more of the surreal and playful whimsy would be lost in the overall atmosphere due to it.

Especially the depiction of the wizards would just look very off-putting in this game. Not that depicting underage girls in a porn game in the first place is inherently wholesome, mind you, but this sort of anime style lends itself to make it fall under the more commonly accepted/tolerated loli-rule I suppose, that kind of makes you separate the individual characters from what they actually are to what they represent in that medium, making it a bit more tolerable in a certain sense, I think. Or in other words, they can more easily pass off as just smaller adults lol. At least more so than any more realistic-looking models would be able to do. Or maybe I'm coping, whatever, sue me.
You also make a great point about the game evoking some form of wanderlust in the player.
Akira himself often points out that he feels like he cannot stand still and has the urge to traverse Kumon-mi and visit different places, which conveniently plays nicely into the gameplay loop. But yeah, exploring new areas, seeing new perspectives from new renders, discovering the mysterious of this strange world and triggering happy events is quite mesmerizing and makes up a lot of the charm of this game.

So much so even, that now that I think about it, I kind of wish someone created a spin off of this game at some point that would essentially be either a 3D mystery sandbox to explore Kumon-mi or at least a 2D point-and-click adventure to collect clues. I'd play the fuck out of a Disco Elysium set in Kumon-mi with the different fucked up gods talking to me and providing live commentary. Fuck, I miss Disco Elysium.
Edit: Also, I just remembered, on the topic of Koikatsu. Is anyone else unable to play other Koikatsu games because of LiL? Maybe not completely unable to, but a lot of the models, whether intentionally or not, look too similar to LiL characters to not have the connection somewhere in the back of my head, breaking the immersion.
Click to expand...
My statement that “the game, IMO, just wouldn’t work nearly as well if it had regular 2D sprites” mostly comes down to two things:

For one, due to the fact that every single in-game image is a screenshot of a static 3D set, LiL has something that no other 2D visual novel (even the greatest ones out there, that I consider masterpieces in their own right) can boast about: actual high-level cinematography. Well, okay, perhaps “cinematography” is not exactly the right word, since we’re ultimately still dealing with unmoving pictures – I just don’t know shit about photography and can’t find any better term to describe it right now, sorry – but my point is that it is extremely clear that Selebus frequently puts *a lot* of thought into the visual composition of his shots: making clever use of camera positioning, playing with perspective, hiding certain things slightly out of frame, etcetera – and this is something that you fundamentally *cannot* do with the traditional set-up of “two-three character portraits overlaid on top of a pre-drawn background image” that all VNs normally use.

Like, generally speaking, when reading almost any scene in a regular visual novel, unless it’s some big high-detailed CG you’re mostly just paying attention to the text bar (the part that *really* matters, obviously) and maybe also the character portraits (their facial expressions, specifically) for some additional context – that’s pretty much the extent of it. LiL, meanwhile, regularly hides small, but still fairly important visual details about its plot/characters purely in the background, never bringing any direct attention to them: you’ll have the “front” of the shot with Sensei talking with one or two girls about something, for example, but then you’ll *also* have a few other girls doing something completely unrelated to that in the “back” of the shot, or perhaps giving away a very brief reaction to just *a single line* of something that was said and then quickly putting their poker face back on the very next screenshot. It’s a “reward” of sorts for actually paying attention to the whole scene, not just what appears to be the main focus of it – and it’s, once again, something that *cannot* be done unless you’re using Selebus’ current method: drawing a billion unique CGs with extremely minor variations in order to achieve a similar result is just too much work for any artist (compared to simply slightly tweaking a 3D model in Koikatsu and then pressing «Print Screen»), and trying to do this with just static portraits and backgrounds makes it *way* too obvious, because you only have three or four important things on the screen at once (once again, compared to a screenshot of a 3D set, where *any* of the dozens small details could potentially be relevant).

And the second reason is that Lessons in Love is very much a twisted unholy chimera of visual styles with a lot of intentional contrast between them – contrast that is frequently meant to convey Sensei coming into contact with forces/entities that are quite literally “not of this world”, which is reflected in the fact that they all look completely alien both in- and out-of-universe – and so shit like “photoshopped real life stock images mixed with distorted 3D models and Paint-drawn scribbles, plus one part of it is pixelated and another has its RGB colors reversed” just wouldn’t have nearly the same “holy shit, what am I even looking at?” striking effect if it was all just 2D in the first place.

Aside from that, yeah, I agree: a mix of LiL and Disco Elysium – or even anything remotely similar – would go hard as fuck.

posts.content_html_raw:
Nodoka is one of my favorite characters simply for the way Selebus writes her dialogue. He uses her in such interesting ways, and this line, I mean wow. That is a banger of a line, and the depth behind it is amazing!

Mini breakdown:

She is directly accusing him of performative repentance, and in such a cutting way. Akira feels guilt, but he also uses that guilt as an excuse. Nodoka is directly telling him that his repentance doesn't negate the harm he does, because his guilt doesn't restrain him, it ENABLES him.

Self absolution(Which Catholicism loves, btw) through suffering! She isn't saying he's faking the guilt, he's not pretending to be sorry. She is telling Akira directly that he needs to feel bad in order to keep going. It's not a "brake", it's his fuel.

His inner torment is reframed as self-serving, which I think we can all agree with.

Nodoka recognizes her place in Akira's emotional transaction. She's symbolic currency in his moral struggle, but she is stripping him of the narrative that he's a tragic sinner seeking redemption.

Through this, and I think this is important to the coming updates:

Selebus is reminding us that Akira is not "Tormented but Noble", that self loathing does not equal accountability, and that suffering does not mean redemption. There is nothing romantic behind Akira's internal struggle with who he is. He may be a 'victim', both of Sekai's and his own actions, but that doesn't change that he is actively doing harm while stumbling through the guilt he feels in retrospect. He is not innocent. This conversation with Nodoka is an indictment against him, using his supposed 'virtue' of 'penance' as evidence against him.

Now, I may be putting more nuance behind this than Selebus actually intended...but after the events of 0.53, Haruka being the worse version of herself, Maki's condemnations...I don't think I am.

I think Selebus is preparing for a real series of events with consequences, and fallout.

I don't quite get the sarcasm or the joke because, out of Ami, your point doesn't really land. And it's unfair to even include Ami because her situation has little to do with literally anyone else. One could also include Maya on that because she's literally a wish.

Sana hasn't fallen to depravity because of him either (it has little to do with him in fact), if anything it's more due to natural tendencies or her absent father's situation.

Uta decides it's okay for him to have the pictures because one day they'll be able to heal together from it. Pedophilia is in both of their pasts, and Akira represents a possibility that she'll be able to share that with her loved one and really not be judged for it/just tolerated.

How does any of this has to do with the Chika situation, other than the obvious "being groomed by the same dude"? What happened to Chika was that she went insane not just when she found out, she went insane years ago by just rejecting reality and that's where the annoyance comes from. Akira's attempts to either tell her about Niki or that he wasn't her boyfriend are from quite early on. Her arc in itself is fine, that it took years is the annoying bit that I referenced.

The sarcastic joke portion was that I was purposefully comparing one situation to another, and ignoring the nuance. I took each heavily nuanced situation into small blurbs that were accurate only from a single POV of a multitude of potential POVs.

However, as I kept naming people, I came to realize that each of the girls I was mentioning did indeed have their own form of lunacy(Caused by Akira or not). It's harder to see the trees(The girls and their individuality), while still stuck in the forest(Playing the game).

It takes a moment of retrospective to really dig into the nuance, much like you did in your reply.

I do still stand by my defense of Chika, so, for your reading pleasure, I present to you...

But in Chika's defense, some people are 100% like that. I did alot of dating in highschool, and early college before I finally found the person that was perfect for me.

The amount of times I've been pursued by someone with an obsessive nature is absurd; but it actually perfectly mirrors how Chika fell apart in a very realistic way. Those girls, including 2 stalkers and someone that literally tried to kill me...were thankfully not stuck in a timeloop with me while I fucked all of their friends, and those friends family members.

I know that as a whole everyone seems to view Chika's obsessiveness in a vein of annoyance, but I also kinda think you guys are forgetting what it's like to be a teenager?

Hormones = BIG emotions
First time feeling certain emotions = BIG EMOTIONS

Imagine if those hormones never get to calm down? You wake up every morning as the worst version of yourself, a literal soup of anxiety, hormones, and never ending horny.

From Chika's POV, Akira IS her savior, a sign of how special she is(Ego), AND(And I don't think this can be expressed enough), her first EVERYTHING.

Do you guys remember your first love? I do, and holy shit I was a fuck up.

Do you guys remember your first break up? I do, and holy shit I was fucked up.

I think the reason I don't see Chika as annoying is a mixture of all of that. I've had experience with girls just like her, and I remember exactly what it was like to experience these kinds of things at her age. I don't blame her for feeling the way she did, for making most of the choices she did. I would think it's fair to say that most people have put up with horrible behavior from loved ones, ignored red flags, and changed themselves fundamentally to keep a hold of someone. Or some mixture of it, atleast.

Kids do stupid things...so imagine the never ending horror of being stuck that way?

She is, after all, a kid stuck in the worst kind of situation(Dead parents, raising her sister, deep poverty, being groomed by the all time greatest groomer that ever groomed apparently). Her rose colored glasses are both in character, and an expectation of everyone at that age.

There is a reason they say you never forget your first love(Even if alot of us may want to later in life. lmao). We all ignore red flags, we all pretend things are one way, even when they are obviously another.

I find it easy to imagine things from Chika's POV...but that's also entirely possible because, at 19, I found myself forced to choose between breaking up with my highschool sweetheart of 3 years, after we had been living together for a year...or agree to her demand to open the relationship.

In this instance I said yes to opening the relationship cause of course she swore it was "Just in case something happened at a party, or while we're out of town, teehee." But, as 99% of 'surprise I want to open the relationship' actually means 'I want to sleep with someone else, have it already planned, but don't want to lose my meal ticket, so forcing the relationship to be open means I'm not cheating teehee', it's easy to imagine how this situation would eventually play out...

Except not cause he turned her down(LOL), and I fucked her best friend(This ends up being one of the stalkers previously mentioned, btw) on Valentines Day while ignoring her calls a week later. Turns out her best friend had a crush on me, convinced her to convince me to open the relationship, all so she could sleep with me. Bitches be crazy!

That I broke up with both of them, and swore off any forms of polygamy should be obvious.

Which in a way kinda mirrors the situation that Chika was forced into. Her first love, her first everything, has put her into a situation where neither choice make her happy. Give up Akira, or find a way to accept the situation. That she cracked as part of this is expected from the amount of stress she lives under, and exactly what Akira meant to her as a whole. Also, most mental illness pop up between 12 and 25 for a reason. It's the most stressful time of your life. Imagine having to navigate Chika's life while stuck under a timeloop and not being able to grow. The stress accumulates.

I think this also makes sense as to why we start to see her healing now, at this point in the story. The world is changing more drastically, and all of the girls are finally growing a bit. That realizing she is ignoring a massive part of her life, and hurting others because of who she has become, is a massive sign of growth that she wasn't really allowed to have prior to this due to the nature of the timeloop, not due to who she is as a person. If that were the case...she wouldn't be growing at all.

In closing; massive TL;DR: Chika is a victim of circumstance, and being stuck in a timeloop as a dumb teenager. I think she deserves a smidge more consideration than being branded as annoying for being broken when the world broke first.

spoilers.title: The Chika Rant
spoilers.html:
But in Chika's defense, some people are 100% like that. I did alot of dating in highschool, and early college before I finally found the person that was perfect for me.

The amount of times I've been pursued by someone with an obsessive nature is absurd; but it actually perfectly mirrors how Chika fell apart in a very realistic way. Those girls, including 2 stalkers and someone that literally tried to kill me...were thankfully not stuck in a timeloop with me while I fucked all of their friends, and those friends family members.

I know that as a whole everyone seems to view Chika's obsessiveness in a vein of annoyance, but I also kinda think you guys are forgetting what it's like to be a teenager?

Hormones = BIG emotions
First time feeling certain emotions = BIG EMOTIONS

Imagine if those hormones never get to calm down? You wake up every morning as the worst version of yourself, a literal soup of anxiety, hormones, and never ending horny.

From Chika's POV, Akira IS her savior, a sign of how special she is(Ego), AND(And I don't think this can be expressed enough), her first EVERYTHING.

Do you guys remember your first love? I do, and holy shit I was a fuck up.

Do you guys remember your first break up? I do, and holy shit I was fucked up.

I think the reason I don't see Chika as annoying is a mixture of all of that. I've had experience with girls just like her, and I remember exactly what it was like to experience these kinds of things at her age. I don't blame her for feeling the way she did, for making most of the choices she did. I would think it's fair to say that most people have put up with horrible behavior from loved ones, ignored red flags, and changed themselves fundamentally to keep a hold of someone. Or some mixture of it, atleast.

Kids do stupid things...so imagine the never ending horror of being stuck that way?

She is, after all, a kid stuck in the worst kind of situation(Dead parents, raising her sister, deep poverty, being groomed by the all time greatest groomer that ever groomed apparently). Her rose colored glasses are both in character, and an expectation of everyone at that age.

There is a reason they say you never forget your first love(Even if alot of us may want to later in life. lmao). We all ignore red flags, we all pretend things are one way, even when they are obviously another.

I find it easy to imagine things from Chika's POV...but that's also entirely possible because, at 19, I found myself forced to choose between breaking up with my highschool sweetheart of 3 years, after we had been living together for a year...or agree to her demand to open the relationship.

In this instance I said yes to opening the relationship cause of course she swore it was "Just in case something happened at a party, or while we're out of town, teehee." But, as 99% of 'surprise I want to open the relationship' actually means 'I want to sleep with someone else, have it already planned, but don't want to lose my meal ticket, so forcing the relationship to be open means I'm not cheating teehee', it's easy to imagine how this situation would eventually play out...

Except not cause he turned her down(LOL), and I fucked her best friend(This ends up being one of the stalkers previously mentioned, btw) on Valentines Day while ignoring her calls a week later. Turns out her best friend had a crush on me, convinced her to convince me to open the relationship, all so she could sleep with me. Bitches be crazy!

That I broke up with both of them, and swore off any forms of polygamy should be obvious.

Which in a way kinda mirrors the situation that Chika was forced into. Her first love, her first everything, has put her into a situation where neither choice make her happy. Give up Akira, or find a way to accept the situation. That she cracked as part of this is expected from the amount of stress she lives under, and exactly what Akira meant to her as a whole. Also, most mental illness pop up between 12 and 25 for a reason. It's the most stressful time of your life. Imagine having to navigate Chika's life while stuck under a timeloop and not being able to grow. The stress accumulates.

I think this also makes sense as to why we start to see her healing now, at this point in the story. The world is changing more drastically, and all of the girls are finally growing a bit. That realizing she is ignoring a massive part of her life, and hurting others because of who she has become, is a massive sign of growth that she wasn't really allowed to have prior to this due to the nature of the timeloop, not due to who she is as a person. If that were the case...she wouldn't be growing at all.

Moonflare said:
It's yet another case of expecting too much out of Selebus, when he has come out multiple times stating that he chooses things "because I felt like it" and "most of it isn't planned at all".
Click to expand...
I mean, as a mental asylum escapee with over 2500 pages of text notes for LiL (that amount to a million of hand-written words, plus individual hyperlinks to about three thousand additional screenshots for further context where necessary), I’ll be the first one to defend my fellow schizo by taking a huff of some high-grade copium and claiming that the validity of these statements is *still* arguably very much up in the air.

The insidious question of just how much of Selebus’ apparent online persona is actually genuine and how much of it is him just simply playing along with the bit (“the game clearly hates you, the player; so why wouldn’t its creator hate you, as well?”) – a thing that isn’t exactly *unheard of* in the wider creative world, especially if we liken Lessons in Love to something like an avant-garde theatre play, with all of us in the audience being just as much a part of the performance as the actors directly present on the stage – has already been brought up multiple times over the years by quite a lot of different people in this thread. That question, in combination with the “I’m almost 99% certain this is ragebait” way Selebus likes to create his tierlists, makes me wonder why more people aren’t willing to at least entertain the idea that the same performative logic could *also* apply to the rest of the shit he regularly posts in the Lilcord. Like, this is clearly his magnum opus – the dude has been pouring his heart and soul into it for a *long* fucking time (as evident by the fact that, as far as I’m aware, the UDH Twitter account predates LiL itself by at least a couple of years) – so I *really* wouldn’t put it past him to go for the long con, because if there is *anything* we know about Selebus with absolute certainty, it’s that he is an insanely committed individual: his absurd work ethic speaks for itself.

(As a side note, I’m not trying to imply that literally *everything* that he says in the Lilcord is a part of him acting “in-character”, but that a lot of it *could* be – the best way to lie is to carefully mix *just a few* select falsehoods among a whole bunch of truths, after all)

So, yeah, while a lot of these more abstract/hidden thematical links in Lessons in Love (like the colors, the characters’ names and so on) *could* theoretically be just a “monkey on a typewriter” situation, where the vast majority of these apparent connections and symbols are effectively pareidolic (ha-ha, get it?) in nature and are a product of pure chance rather than careful planning, the fact that so many of them *do* actually make a great amount sense once you grasp the underlying logic and find the right Rosetta stone to begin decoding the cipher makes me wholeheartedly put my faith in Selebus and his potential Grand Design. And maybe I am a fool for doing that – just a naïve deluded idiot who spends their precious time chasing ghosts and uncovering mysteries that don’t actually exist – but even so, I’d rather be a fool who believes than a skeptic who doesn’t.

As they say: without love, it cannot be seen.

Well, I’ll try because the short and true answer will be I don’t know too. But it’s funny how all this shit is smh relevant.

I started playing LIL, like all others, skipping most of it. And stayed only when I was hooked by the drama (R/C, Mo/R). The game developed, the plot continued to drag on, but I did not receive any single answer.

When I saw the post about Tb as narrator, I recalled that I too had feeling that characters reiterate themselves. Then I got into the code and started looking for patterns. Many have led and continue to lead in the wrong or ambiguous directions. But there are also those that always lead to one point.

The next thought was: the colors must mean something. And it would be nice if they had names. The first was hexcolorpedia, but later I completely settled on hexpot: What’s in a pot, Akira?

What follows is complete speculation, because I don’t know how the colors are applied to the game.
Therefore, I simply took the following as a starting (possibly mistakenly) point:
  1. inversed color – male/female
  2. complementary – mirrored or UD version of character
  3. Square – a window of time
  4. Tetradic – a door to others planes/worlds
Further, if we consider the characters as paints on a canvas, then they can be mixed. This approach did not bring much clarity, but it did produce a lot of funny coincidences, and as we know from the words of M, coincidence is god.

Remember, there was nameless narrator ranting about rocks and how it will be forgotten immediately. Look like it talks about minerals/crystals and the stage of the creation when girls will be associated with mineral rocks.

Chlorite - a dark green mineral consisting of a basic hydrated aluminosilicate of magnesium and iron. It occurs as a constituent of many rocks, typically forming flat crystals resembling mica

Kimberlite-rare, blue-tinged, coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock sometimes containing diamonds, found in South Africa and Siberia

And others scattered through events.


I’m, currently reading Soliloquy (read 0.53, then came back to where I was at 0.45). So, there were a few patterns leads to Osako, and I was confused about it, until I directly jumped into mineral/rocks scene with Osako and all color references became logical.


I still forced myself to read the original - NiB, which further strengthened me in the idea that colors and text are connected.

Best example NiB (as hint to read source):
Nature becomes envious of her beauty and sends a gust of wind to attack us.

Don’t ask me how I came across this: perhaps from the moment I decided to finally read NiB, or perhaps when some kind of database had already been collected, which led to this idea.


Io+Yu= Nature
envious – flowers on Io’s bathrobe
her beauty – Reina’s color
gust of wind - *In every gust of wind, I hear her name. – NN about Sekai?

Saki - Rich Lavender, inversed Enviable , Complementary Apple Orchard,
W+O: Skeletor's Cape, Inverse: Energise, Nature's Delight, Complementary: Enviable




‘Enviable’ mentioned only once during whole 0.54 in Chika(Chiaki?)’s hj to S:
It's so open and honest that it's almost enviable. It lights a fire within me.




It seems that in this game three games LiL, NiB, GOTD are collapsed at once and huge amount of everything else like literature, religious inserted into. And that what is shown relates at once to the present, to the past, and to the future, and also intersect with each other, but you can talk about this much better than me, because I was busy with something else, since the undeveloped plot and the ever-increasing pile of unanswered questions prompted me to play another game: to follow the abundantly scattered bread crumbs.

And since nothing here is what it seems: BJ is kinda analogue to Blue Jay, so it remains to uncover what HJ and sex means for real.

Then the fun continues: Envy =ipurposeful



What follows from this? That Io is UD Yasu, another version of M? Or that Three Halves Make a Whole? I’m not good at analyzing stuff, just raw guesses.

But such a conclusion simply suggests itself: W+O – Yu+Io - on the opposite sides.

By the way iIo=Silver Rust similar to Saki
S=Sooty=iMercury
Io+Mercury=Tactile

And now the question: when Io and S shown to us, is S a male version of Yuki like it’s the past itself shown in the same rendered bodies just to fuck with our brains?

Well, about the cheese.

When I saw this for the first time, I just labeled that shit as a pattern and moved on. Re-reading it completely now, I felt only one thing: “What the fuck was that and for what fucking purpose?” Then I opened Photoshop and went through the colors with an eyedropper. And everything fell into place.


So based on all of the above, I have a strong feeling that Sel is a neurweb, or a dude or a group of dudes, writing a game about colors using a neurweb that spuns the world.

And if you compare him to actual writers that, you know, write for a living - he's not that amazing to justify taking LiL as if it was the next literature classic. Obviously, seldom do people claim any of this, but what has been pointed out, and I agree, is that Selebus has adopted this almost "artistically transgressive genius persona" that's just ridiculous, and a demerit to his work.

On a separate topic, do we have a schedule for the updates beyond Jan 1st?

An idle mind goes a-wandering, and because my job provides no intellectual stimulation, today I came up with my plan for improving Kumon-mi if I ever get isekai'd into it, preferably early on in the story before all most of the awful stuff has happened:
  1. Marry Sara and treat her like she deserves to be treated, hopefully reducing her desire to drink to excess. Stick around, and don't abandon her. Also, if having sex with her, do it out of earshot of Sana.
  2. Become a good father figure to Sana so she doesn't feel the need to act out, and get her to stay her adorable, slightly awkward self. Forbid her to change her hairstyle, or at least lobby her strongly to keep it.
  3. Adopt Chika and Chinami (Yumi can come too if she wants but I doubt it). Get Chinami on some quality health insurance and keep that gem in the world. Get her some proper N95 masks so she doesn't have to suffer with that sweltering dog mask during the oppressive heat. But keep the mask for her to wear occasionally because she's just so darn adorable in it.
  4. Convince Tsubasa to sponsor a grant to open a free after-school community center with programs focusing on recognizing and resisting grooming techniques. Also try to convince the school to look into that weirdo teaching Class A. At night, the center hosts AA and SAA meetings.
  5. Create a petition for the city to conduct thorough, proper testing of the structural engineering of all school buildings and their foundations. Can't be too careful, after all.
  6. Put any leftover grant money into a lobbying group calling for ending the space war and opening the city back up. Hopefully if Haruka gets her husband back, it will help her control her inner freak. Or at least he can keep an eye on her.
  7. Oh, yeah, maybe look into getting the city's name changed. Really, city council, what were you thinking?

In regards to your first point, just to clarify, HOPE’s main divine symbols/attributes are, in no particular order:

– Light (I mean, obviously – it’s in his title: “The Peerless God of Light”);

– Callousness (also in the title, as HOPE’s aspect is “The Callous One”);

– Lust (from his origin story – “the horny ball of light” – which is also reflected in a lot of what the Angels say to Akira in Chapter 1 and many, many instances of HOPE intentionally inducing abnormal arousal in people: just from the top of my head, this happens in Yasu’s “Glossolalia”, Ami’s “No One Can Hear Us”, Touka’s “Come For Me”, and Sana’s “It Comes To Claim Us All” – the latter of which also serves as the trigger/starting point for Sana’s gradual descent into lust-fueled depravity);

– Summer (HOPE’s season, when he is the most active);

– Heat (logically follows from HOPE being related to both light and summer, as the natural opposition to Tenchou’s cold/winter, in addition to the fact that all of the aforementioned lust-induced episodes are *also* accompanied by at least one of the participants mentioning how “the air suddenly feels extremely heated and humid”);

– The sun (now this one is, admittedly, not something that’s ever been directly confirmed, I don’t think, but the combination of “light + summer + heat” makes also associating HOPE with the sun a fairly obvious next logical step; plus there were a lot of pretty suspicious examples of narration mentioning the sun “watching over people” in early Chapter 3, as well as the “Second Sun” Happy Event, which I believe to be a pun on “sun/son”, since the event itself is very HOPE-focused, has at least one direct allusion to Sensei’s past in relation to Nozomu, and, well, Akira literally being the “second son”);

– Eyes (HOPE is repeatedly called “the many-eyed one” by multiple characters, including Yasu, the Angels and the narrator of “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus”, and there is also that whole strange myth/story Yasu tells Sensei in “Sakura Season” explaining why she and the rabbits who serve HOPE occasionally wear blindfolds);

– Feathers (kinda; HOPE himself occasionally refers to himself as “the thing with feathers”, which is, in turn, a reference to the line “Hope is the thing with feathers” from one of Emily Dickinson’s poems – that also gets directly quoted by Makoto in “Bluejay”; plus, Pegasus, who has feathered wings, has many noticeable similarities with HOPE: from his general appearance, to how he speaks, him being very lust-driven in relation to how he approaches Sana, the potential Sara connection, etcetera – so there is that too, I guess);

– Worms (from the book that relates to him in “A Life of Prizes”, HOPE mentioning worms during his first (?) appearance in “Window of the Waking Mind”, and worms in general being something that gets repeatedly brought up in relation to the Arakawa family – mainly Ami – in “Worry Not, The Mason Jar”, “Della” and so on);

That’s pretty much all of them, provided I haven’t missed anything among my pages upon pages of notes. So, as you can see, aside from HOPE’s smile – and *maybe* the whole three-colored moon business relating to how red/green/blue appear to individually symbolize each member of the Trinity, though none of this is in any way conclusive as of right now – HOPE isn’t really associated with red the way you seem to believe he is, or at least not to the same extent as all of his other attributes.

You know who *is* strongly associated with the color red, though? Sekai. An entity who is very much *not* on HOPE’s side (judging from Yasu’s reaction in “Fruits of Torment”) – and that’s not even touching upon whatever the fuck was going on between them while they were both still alive, since we know that Nozomu had a habit of frequently beating (and maybe even raping, if that’s what that one part of “Second Sun” was alluding to) Sekai, while she clearly despised the guy for what he had done to Akira and only stayed married to him for Akira’s sake (or otherwise due to currently undisclosed reasons). Thus, “red is bad”, indeed.

And, yes, Pareidolia is the third God, the “concerned” one: he repeatedly states so himself during many of his appearances throughout the game, like when he takes control of Terminal 23 in “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus”, or in “Friends”, where he responds with “I was far too concerned” when Akira asks why Pareidolia always refused to leave him alone prior to that point. The “changing faces” thing is just something that he randomly does in early Chapter 4, likely just exercising his newfound freedom as the one in charge by flexing his powers over perception (since that’s kinda his whole thing), before eventually getting bored of it and going back to how he originally looked – I believe there is even a scene where this is directly said, but I couldn’t quickly find it, sorry.

For Tenchou it’s:

– Trees/roots/wires (as well as basically anything technology-related, like computers, TV static, machines and science in general);

– Darkness/winter/cold (in direct opposition to HOPE’s light/summer/heat);

– The feeling of “calm” (his main attribute);

– Order (as maintaining the “natural” way of things is stated to be Tenchou’s primary directive as a deity, according to “There is Nothing”);

– Exerting direct control over others and making “visual alterations” (both of which are also listed in “There is Nothing” as the main examples of his powers).

In regards to the former, it’s worth noting that Tenchou’s abilities in this regard greatly surpass those of the other two Gods: while HOPE is seemingly forced to manually “assume control” of people in order to affect their actions, like he does with Yasu, and Pareidolia can only manipulate what you *say*, but not what you *think*, Tenchou is infinitely more insidious about it, being able to effectively cut off Akira’s free will at a moment's notice and replace it with a pre-programmed behavior pattern of Tenchou’s own choosing – like the “auto-pilot” thing that frequently happens to Tsuneyo, forcing her to behave like a robot in accordance with her programming of “maintain the façade of normality in Tojo Ramen at all costs” – except in Tsuneyo’s case it’s always fairly obvious whenever that happens, while with Sensei you can easily go for half a scene before realizing that he’s not actually acting like his normal self.

As for the latter, it can be seen with Ami (during that very scene in “There is Nothing”), Kaori (in “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)”) and Sana (in “The Complete Absence of Everything”). Also, Tenchoi is apparently capable of “deleting viruses like depression or bipolarity” (once again, “There is Nothing”), which likely explains Makoto magically getting better after a Reset both times she experienced her “sad girl arc”.

– The Old Town (obviously, since that entire area is his main domain where he’s the strongest), and, less obviously, the abandoned school with the cross (it’s always snowing near that school, regardless of the current season, and the one narrating backwards at the end of “Arms Bent Back” is almost 100% Tenchou);

– Noodles (this includes the dish itself, considering the whole thing about him being the owner of Tojo Ramen and also the fact that “tori shio ramen” appears to be a code phrase of sorts: the only people who ever order/mention tori shio ramen are those who are “in the know” about what is actually going on, like Sekai and Youdidit, and Tsuneyo says that her father never truly taught her how to make it, always taking care of the clients who ordered it by himself – and also the bird Tsuneyo effectively adopted, because Noodles seems to actively serve as Tenchou’s agent when it comes to information gathering or delivering urgent messages);

– And, finally, roaches (from Tenchou’s book in “A Life of Prizes” – though this one *is* pretty strange, all things considered, because outside of that one mention I honestly struggle to meaningfully connect Tenchou to roaches in any way, shape or form: that’s more of a Youdidit/Moyo thing, and those two are generally considered to be HOPE-affiliated, through their own admittance in “Second Sun”);

As for Pareidolia, being shifty and untrustworthy as fuck about anything he does is his entire M.O – with him being on the record of potentially impersonating the other members of the Trinity and whatnot, not to mention whatever the hell happened at the end of 0.44 with his apparent sacrifice (which instead resulted in Tenchou’s deletion, while this fucking guy just relocated into Yumi’s head and has been chilling inside her for almost a year at this point) – but the few things that we *do* know are related to him are:

– Perception (from “Word of the Day”; plus, I mean, “pareidolia” – it is literally in the name);

– Being “concerned” for someone or about something (his main attribute);

– Edit: Whoops, I forgot the most obvious fucking one: spring. Lol.

– Spiders (once again, Pareidolia’s book in “A Life of Prizes”; not to mention, y’know, Kaori being his main “vessel”), and also probably frogs (the giant frog that apparently lives at the center of the Great Pareidolia Mall + Pareidolia randomly calling Akira “frog boy” a few times in early Chapter 4, which then culminates in him saying

“Only the spiders can save you now, Frog Boy. May you find yourself in their web and be tucked tightly into your final sleeping bag.”

in a TTS at the end of “Perfect Harmony”.);

There are also a few things that do technically fit multiple Gods, like the fact that Pareidolia’s book in “A Life of Prizes” is called “The Dark” – something that is otherwise pretty exclusively used to refer to Tenchou – or how, despite my earlier statement about HOPE clearly embodying the scorching summer sun, *the entire Trinity* has already been repeatedly represented via moon-related symbolism on multiple occasions throughout the last two Chapters (“All That's Left Are Stars” being the most recent one). This overlap does not necessarily contradict anything and *can* theoretically be handwaved away using the same “three Gods, but also one God” and “all of us do everything” explanation both Maya and Pareidolia express to Sensei on two separate occasions (in “Trinity Pt. I: Stations of the Cross” and “Paranoid”, respectively), but it *does* make my job of analyzing Trinity as individuals through thematical/symbolic lens a lot more difficult – thanks, Selebus.

And I’m going to express the exact opposite opinion to the one Moonflare gave earlier and say that, from my perspective, nothing that has been revealed recently really contradicts or negates any of the earlier stuff, so if you’re someone who finds this theological/mystical side of LiL especially engaging, you absolutely *should* replay the entire VN from the very beginning and pay a lot more attention to all of the divine-related scenes this time around – I did it (three times), and, personally speaking, it was 100% worth it. Or, if not, then, sure: waiting for a few months/years for the entire picture to become much more cohesive and clearly defined is *also* something that you can do.

In regards to the former, it’s worth noting that Tenchou’s abilities in this regard greatly surpass those of the other two Gods: while HOPE is seemingly forced to manually “assume control” of people in order to affect their actions, like he does with Yasu, and Pareidolia can only manipulate what you *say*, but not what you *think*, Tenchou is infinitely more insidious about it, being able to effectively cut off Akira’s free will at a moment's notice and replace it with a pre-programmed behavior pattern of Tenchou’s own choosing – like the “auto-pilot” thing that frequently happens to Tsuneyo, forcing her to behave like a robot in accordance with her programming of “maintain the façade of normality in Tojo Ramen at all costs” – except in Tsuneyo’s case it’s always fairly obvious whenever that happens, while with Sensei you can easily go for half a scene before realizing that he’s not actually acting like his normal self.

As for the latter, it can be seen with Ami (during that very scene in “There is Nothing”), Kaori (in “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)”) and Sana (in “The Complete Absence of Everything”). Also, Tenchoi is apparently capable of “deleting viruses like depression or bipolarity” (once again, “There is Nothing”), which likely explains Makoto magically getting better after a Reset both times she experienced her “sad girl arc”.

– The Old Town (obviously, since that entire area is his main domain where he’s the strongest), and, less obviously, the abandoned school with the cross (it’s always snowing near that school, regardless of the current season, and the one narrating backwards at the end of “Arms Bent Back” is almost 100% Tenchou);

– Noodles (this includes the dish itself, considering the whole thing about him being the owner of Tojo Ramen and also the fact that “tori shio ramen” appears to be a code phrase of sorts: the only people who ever order/mention tori shio ramen are those who are “in the know” about what is actually going on, like Sekai and Youdidit, and Tsuneyo says that her father never truly taught her how to make it, always taking care of the clients who ordered it by himself – and also the bird Tsuneyo effectively adopted, because Noodles seems to actively serve as Tenchou’s agent when it comes to information gathering or delivering urgent messages);

– And, finally, roaches (from Tenchou’s book in “A Life of Prizes” – though this one *is* pretty strange, all things considered, because outside of that one mention I honestly struggle to meaningfully connect Tenchou to roaches in any way, shape or form: that’s more of a Youdidit/Moyo thing, and those two are generally considered to be HOPE-affiliated, through their own admittance in “Second Sun”);

spoilers.title: Pareidolia's symbology
spoilers.html:
– Perception (from “Word of the Day”; plus, I mean, “pareidolia” – it is literally in the name);

– Being “concerned” for someone or about something (his main attribute);

– Edit: Whoops, I forgot the most obvious fucking one: spring. Lol.

– Spiders (once again, Pareidolia’s book in “A Life of Prizes”; not to mention, y’know, Kaori being his main “vessel”), and also probably frogs (the giant frog that apparently lives at the center of the Great Pareidolia Mall + Pareidolia randomly calling Akira “frog boy” a few times in early Chapter 4, which then culminates in him saying

“Only the spiders can save you now, Frog Boy. May you find yourself in their web and be tucked tightly into your final sleeping bag.”

in a TTS at the end of “Perfect Harmony”.);

spoilers.title: Mixed symbols
spoilers.html: There are also a few things that do technically fit multiple Gods, like the fact that Pareidolia’s book in “A Life of Prizes” is called “The Dark” – something that is otherwise pretty exclusively used to refer to Tenchou – or how, despite my earlier statement about HOPE clearly embodying the scorching summer sun, *the entire Trinity* has already been repeatedly represented via moon-related symbolism on multiple occasions throughout the last two Chapters (“All That's Left Are Stars” being the most recent one). This overlap does not necessarily contradict anything and *can* theoretically be handwaved away using the same “three Gods, but also one God” and “all of us do everything” explanation both Maya and Pareidolia express to Sensei on two separate occasions (in “Trinity Pt. I: Stations of the Cross” and “Paranoid”, respectively), but it *does* make my job of analyzing Trinity as individuals through thematical/symbolic lens a lot more difficult – thanks, Selebus.

posts.content_html_raw:
I agree but there's a counterpoint: "what was the point of 10 years of LiL?"

Yumi and Rin happy endings. Can you imagine Himawari Yamaguchi and Himawari Rokuhara? (or their actual names, which I doubt will be Himawari, cause I hope these two have better sense than letting Akira name their children).

That being said, I have been developing another perspective towards the ten year thing which might be helpful. That is centered around the question of "what has really happened in these 5 years of story?" And, well, almost nothing - if you look at the actual world. I'll give an example.
As some know, I've been writing/developing a game for the past 6 months, and, unlike Selebus, I plan the entire thing in advance. But, well, I have to - because my story has events in which the player changes the "world" around the characters, and events in which the "world" changes the game around the player. "You didn't help the village with their food crisis? Well, after the next time skip they'll be fucking dead." "You thought your life was settled? Well, the hints that the geopolitical stuation was about to change come true, and now you have to rethink your next steps".

The difference between writing a story that is mostly centered around characters interactions towards one another, and one where it is between the relation of the main cast and the world (in a back and forth) is that you don't really need a long ass story for the first. If I were to tell my story in a short game it would either turn into a glossary of exposition or a really dumbed down version of events where things happen just because. But LiL could be a short game. Think back to the world around Akira, are we so distant from where we began? I'd say no.

The company treats TERMINAL 23 in mostly the exact same way, the only big difference is that Himawari got reassigned. Everything that happened only has to do with either finding out what already was the status quo (hidden from us through a thick layer of misdirection and convoluted white noise), or the interaction between Akira and the cast. The reason LiL is so long is not because of the story it's telling, but because of the number of characters.

Were we to have a story with only Akira's original class, LiL would be over by now. It's amazing that we have so many characters, but it is also one of the misgivings people have pointed out over the years - arcs sometimes take too long because they can't advance too much before other arcs have been given their time with the current Akira's circumstances. Hell, we're likely looking at a period of two/three years just for individual endings for 35 girls. That's insane.

So, at the end of the day, in terms of wordcount, LiL is a story about its characters interactions with each other, much more than any supernatural/mystery story. Think about Steins;Gate, no one would say it's a story about the lab members interactions with one another, it's clearly about time travel. But could we say the same about LiL? Is it really a story about the resets? Or are the resets just the setting in which the character interactions happen?
So, "why did LiL take/will take 10 years?" Because it has 35 "main" characters (by which I mean with their individual arcs). The actual story could be told in one single chapter with time to spare. All of this being said, I also hope everything Akira is answered by the end.

I agree with your assessment.

But I'm also fine with the dynamic of the story. Unlike in other stories, like in some TV shows where it is common to produce filler episodes to prolong the length of the series, LiL benefits from this "filler" by adding wholesome, interesting, obscure, funny etc. side stories to follow. I prefer a game where there are a lot of smaller story arcs intertwined with each other, while the grander story is pushed to the background to a game that is just about the main story with superficial character developments or a very small cast.
Not that there aren't "filler" updates in LiL necessarily cough Drom Wars cough, but I interpret them more so as Sel's opportunity for a creative breather. Considering he is churning out update after update each month, I think it's fine if not every update is a banger and I don't think it's intentional per se.

Credit where credit is due, Selebus is a great character writer, he would rob himself of his strengths were he to focus on a convoluted mystery story and put the individual protagonists on the back seat.

And on a side note, a game developed by Moonflare with time skips?

Everything that happened only has to do with either finding out what already was the status quo (hidden from us through a thick layer of misdirection and convoluted white noise), or the interaction between Akira and the cast. The reason LiL is so long is not because of the story it's telling, but because of the number of characters.

Were we to have a story with only Akira's original class, LiL would be over by now. It's amazing that we have so many characters, but it is also one of the misgivings people have pointed out over the years - arcs sometimes take too long because they can't advance too much before other arcs have been given their time with the current Akira's circumstances. Hell, we're likely looking at a period of two/three years just for individual endings for 35 girls. That's insane.

So, at the end of the day, in terms of wordcount, LiL is a story about its characters interactions with each other, much more than any supernatural/mystery story. Think about Steins;Gate, no one would say it's a story about the lab members interactions with one another, it's clearly about time travel. But could we say the same about LiL? Is it really a story about the resets? Or are the resets just the setting in which the character interactions happen?

But, well, I have to - because my story has events in which the player changes the "world" around the characters, and events in which the "world" changes the game around the player. posts.content_html_raw:
Hi everyone. This is going to be a long and rambling post about Ami: did she always know about the resets from the start, or not?

I finished replaying Chapter 2 and have started Chapter 3, trying to focus specifically on her appearances. At the same time, I was also replaying the game just to enjoy it, so it’s not like I had the discipline to analyze every single detail — nor am I smart enough to do so anyway. I also know that many of the things I’m about to say have already been discussed at length, and I’m sure I’ll miss or forget things since I haven’t replayed the entire game yet. Still, I wanted to give it a try.

TL;DR: In the first two chapters, the evidence for Ami either knowing or not knowing about the resets is deeply conflicting. Personally, I’d be fine with Selebus eventually revealing either option as true — or even a mix of both (which is what I currently believe).

Start of the game: Ami’s very first appearance puts her in the famous “Monika pose” from the ending of DDLC (Doki Doki Literature Club). This could be a coincidence, a homage, or an intentional clue. DDLC spoilers:
Monika is a character who mirrors Ami in the sense that she knows far more about the world than she lets on, but keeps that knowledge hidden.

Before the first reset: Throughout most of Chapter 1, Ami seems very accustomed to how the world works. She reacts to Akira in a way that suggests both prior experience with him as a broken person and familiarity with him as an endlessly resetting being — especially if you consider how relaxed she is about Sensei losing his memories.
As aramaug noted a few posts earlier, in the event “Della” she appears to repeat the game’s introduction as if it were a rehearsed scene she has played out countless times.

As many have pointed out before, it often feels like Ami doesn’t care about Sensei as a specific individual. She doesn’t seem interested in finding his “true” iteration; instead, she’s in love with the 'idea' of Sensei. Each Sensei is equivalent to all the others, as long as she gets her way with him every time.

At the same time, her easygoing attitude in Chapter 1 could simply be another example of the failsafe acceptance that all the other students exhibit — something Maya explains later. Her sense of having called Sensei that for “so long” could also mirror how, later in the game, all the girls feel like they’ve had him as a teacher for years, when in reality it’s only been a few months.

So, let’s assume for a moment that Ami doesn’t remember past cycles during Chapter 1. What does she remember at the start of the game?

Everything.

She would be in a situation similar to New Maya’s: treating the present as the natural continuation of the past as she always perceived it. She remembers being raised by Sensei, remembers his memory issues — or rather, how easily influenced he is when reminded of the past. She remembers meeting Maya in middle school, and she definitely remembers Maya sleeping with Sensei in their house ever since — until, from her perspective, it suddenly stopped a few months earlier, with Maya now seemingly hating Sensei for unknown reasons.

One of the most frustrating events for me to analyze is “Something Darker.” In it, Ami clearly wants Sensei to act on her, to take her, fully believing that they can’t hurt each other. When Sensei resists and leaves the room, Ami’s reaction — “what the heck just happened?” — can be read in two completely opposite ways.
Either she’s shocked that her seduction attempt almost worked, something that — if she had no memory of past resets — had never happened before… or she’s shocked that it didn’t work, surprised that Sensei managed to stop himself, which would imply knowledge of previous cycles.


First Reset: “Everlasting Love” event: Ami is clearly worried about the world ending and makes explicit references to everyone disappearing, just like during the resets. She asks Sensei not to leave her alone.
In the following scene (which I can’t seem to find in the replays), Ami is sitting on the sofa with an annoyed, almost unfazed expression, while glitching smiley faces appear over her face. She looks like she understands what’s about to happen — and she’s clearly not happy about it.

“There Is Nothing” event: The reset begins. Ami feels like she’s melting from the inside; she’s in pain, literally crumbling while still alive. She knows she’s experiencing the end of the world. My guess is that the gods/caretakers were “trying something new” on her during this reset. She’s essentially being tortured — which doesn’t feel like something Himawari would do, but more likely the work of another caretaker.

I don’t think Sensei later asking Himawari whether it’s possible for Ami to be tortured during a reset was a coincidence. Ami being tortured across multiple resets, as part of attempts to “change” her, feels like something Ami Prime will eventually use to guilt-trip someone. And honestly, I can understand why she wouldn’t want to be found by the caretakers during resets, if she remembers how much they can make her suffer.

Chapter 2
"heaven for human blood" event: Ami seems both 'possessed' during this event and genuinely troubled as she tries to piece together parts of the past she hadn’t even questioned before Noriko entered her life. Noriko makes her rethink Sensei’s tutoring years — his hidden past relationship with Maya, and the fact that he knew Maya even before Ami introduced her to him in middle school.
Ami also admits that both of them have “blackouts” due to their past experiences. This makes me lean toward the idea that, at the start of Chapter 2, Ami didn’t have full memories of past resets — otherwise, she would have already known these things in some way.

In the early chapters, she also doesn’t act like a fully self-aware, manipulative, billion-years-old incest gremlin. I mean, she is still an incest gremlin — but a naive one. She’s clearly a girl who has never had a normal life.

one for me and one for you,
the wonders of what god can do
a different one for each of us
we pray the same, but struggle thus.

She shows Maya what are likely nude photos from Maya’s youth, photos Sensei had kept hidden in a secret folder at home (as revealed in the next reset).
Maya believed none of those photos still existed, and she’s then absolutely terrified by the idea of an impending factory reset of herself — something we know will later happen, creating Nu Maya, and which has probably happened multiple times before. Ami then gaslights her into thinking she imagined everything.
Maya takes a few days for herself and comes back without ever confronting Ami directly, but now fully aware that she might not be as eternal as she once believed. Maya also admits that she has seen people “disappear” during resets before, and that it’s always horrifying — which suggests she may have witnessed Ami being “tortured” in past cycles.
Still, the fact that Ami claims she only put “some scary movies and stuff” in the Scary Room — along with other events — makes me think she created the room during a brief resurgence of past memories, possibly with the help of USER2 (or 1?), and then immediately forgot doing so.
I suspect that if anyone other than Maya had entered the Scary Room, they would have seen exactly what Ami described. The Scary Room feels like a place that only “evil” Ami — with divine assistance — can truly access.
Because of this, I still think it’s possible that at this point in the story Ami’s memories are driven more by instinct and subconscious perception of past resets rather than full, conscious recollection like she has now.
Even without remembering past resets, I think Ami has always known and remembered Maya having sex with Sensei. As I said before, I believe she thought Maya and Sensei had broken up somehow, but remained deeply suspicious of both of them.

Ami openly acknowledges that she wants to be more like Maya, already aware that Maya has always been Sensei’s favorite.
