She reacts to Akira in a way that suggests both prior experience with him as a broken person and familiarity with him as an endlessly resetting being — especially if you consider how relaxed she is about Sensei losing his memories.
As aramaug noted a few posts earlier, in the event “Della” she appears to repeat the game’s introduction as if it were a rehearsed scene she has played out countless times.

As many have pointed out before, it often feels like Ami doesn’t care about Sensei as a specific individual. She doesn’t seem interested in finding his “true” iteration; instead, she’s in love with the 'idea' of Sensei. Each Sensei is equivalent to all the others, as long as she gets her way with him every time.

At the same time, her easygoing attitude in Chapter 1 could simply be another example of the failsafe acceptance that all the other students exhibit — something Maya explains later. Her sense of having called Sensei that for “so long” could also mirror how, later in the game, all the girls feel like they’ve had him as a teacher for years, when in reality it’s only been a few months.

So, let’s assume for a moment that Ami doesn’t remember past cycles during Chapter 1. What does she remember at the start of the game?

Everything.

She would be in a situation similar to New Maya’s: treating the present as the natural continuation of the past as she always perceived it. She remembers being raised by Sensei, remembers his memory issues — or rather, how easily influenced he is when reminded of the past. She remembers meeting Maya in middle school, and she definitely remembers Maya sleeping with Sensei in their house ever since — until, from her perspective, it suddenly stopped a few months earlier, with Maya now seemingly hating Sensei for unknown reasons.

One of the most frustrating events for me to analyze is “Something Darker.” In it, Ami clearly wants Sensei to act on her, to take her, fully believing that they can’t hurt each other. When Sensei resists and leaves the room, Ami’s reaction — “what the heck just happened?” — can be read in two completely opposite ways.
Either she’s shocked that her seduction attempt almost worked, something that — if she had no memory of past resets — had never happened before… or she’s shocked that it didn’t work, surprised that Sensei managed to stop himself, which would imply knowledge of previous cycles.


First Reset: “Everlasting Love” event: Ami is clearly worried about the world ending and makes explicit references to everyone disappearing, just like during the resets. She asks Sensei not to leave her alone.
In the following scene (which I can’t seem to find in the replays), Ami is sitting on the sofa with an annoyed, almost unfazed expression, while glitching smiley faces appear over her face. She looks like she understands what’s about to happen — and she’s clearly not happy about it.

My guess is that the gods/caretakers were “trying something new” on her during this reset. She’s essentially being tortured — which doesn’t feel like something Himawari would do, but more likely the work of another caretaker.

I don’t think Sensei later asking Himawari whether it’s possible for Ami to be tortured during a reset was a coincidence. During the second Halloween (the first sigh of frying threads event), Ami realizes that Maya is warming up to Sensei again — and she’s clearly unhappy about it. Short answer: we don’t know for sure.

“Slightly” longer answer:

Aside from Himawari’s comment in “Wind Chime” about how, quote, “anything we’d do to her to affect her memories would only be temporary”, implying that, even though Ami is not *immune* to the memory erasure stuff, she always regains at least *some* of her meta-knowledge in one way or another – though Himawari doesn’t clarify whether this recollection simply happens on its own with the passage of time (as in, the longer the cycle goes on, the more stuff Ami becomes aware of, thus potentially explaining why the longest Chapter yet with the longest period between Resets has her acting completely off-the-wall), or if there is a trigger of some kind (accidental or intentionally set-up by “Ami Prime”) that greatly expedites this process – it mostly depends on which one of the two main “Ami theories” you personally subscribe to and find the most convincing/reasonable.

The main dividing factor between these theories is whether you believe that “Nu Ami” (the ditzy, naïve, airheaded girl from Chapters 1 and 2) and “Ami Prime” (the callous, manipulative and remorseless psycho from the second half of Chapter 3 and all of Chapter 4) are two separate entities, with the latter somehow replacing the former: maybe through a “mind-virus” of some kind, like a few people theorized; maybe due to being directly influenced by Sekai after her revival; maybe as a natural consequence of Ami simply regaining all of her memories; or perhaps through some Umineko-like “assuming manual control of your Piece on the Game Board” process, where our Ami’s consciousness has been directly switched with an “ascended” version of her – or, alternatively, that there is only one Ami (specifically, “Ami Prime”) and that “Nu Ami” was simply a mask that she wore for one reason or another, pretending to be pure and innocent all that time when in reality she was anything but.

Personally, I already made my thoughts on Ami’s situation perfectly clear (post № 61315 on December 13, if I’m not mistaken – you can find my long-ass Ami analysis there), so I won’t repeat them here. Moonflare also had a lot of great posts relating to this topic about a year ago, I believe, made in the few months following the release of 0.45 – you can try searching for them, as well. Either way, though, there is a lot of evidence that supports *both* interpretations of her character – including the “Lamb Legs” Happy Scene that very few people ever mention, surprisingly – so, in the wise words of the late (but never forgotten) Plant #2:

“Bro, this is Lessons in Love. Anything is possible.”

Monika is a character who mirrors Ami in the sense that she knows far more about the world than she lets on, but keeps that knowledge hidden.
Before the first reset:
Throughout most of Chapter 1, Ami seems very accustomed to how the world works. She reacts to Akira in a way that suggests both prior experience with him as a broken person and familiarity with him as an endlessly resetting being — especially if you consider how relaxed she is about Sensei losing his memories.
As aramaug noted a few posts earlier, in the event “Della” she appears to repeat the game’s introduction as if it were a rehearsed scene she has played out countless times.
As many have pointed out before, it often feels like Ami doesn’t care about Sensei as a specific individual. She doesn’t seem interested in finding his “true” iteration; instead, she’s in love with the 'idea' of Sensei. Each Sensei is equivalent to all the others, as long as she gets her way with him every time.
At the same time, her easygoing attitude in Chapter 1 could simply be another example of the failsafe acceptance that all the other students exhibit — something Maya explains later. Her sense of having called Sensei that for “so long” could also mirror how, later in the game, all the girls feel like they’ve had him as a teacher for years, when in reality it’s only been a few months.
So, let’s assume for a moment that Ami doesn’t remember past cycles during Chapter 1. What does she remember at the start of the game?
Everything.
She would be in a situation similar to New Maya’s: treating the present as the natural continuation of the past as she always perceived it. She remembers being raised by Sensei, remembers his memory issues — or rather, how easily influenced he is when reminded of the past. She remembers meeting Maya in middle school, and she definitely remembers Maya sleeping with Sensei in their house ever since — until, from her perspective, it suddenly stopped a few months earlier, with Maya now seemingly hating Sensei for unknown reasons.
One of the most frustrating events for me to analyze is “Something Darker.” In it, Ami clearly wants Sensei to act on her, to take her, fully believing that they can’t hurt each other. When Sensei resists and leaves the room, Ami’s reaction — “what the heck just happened?” — can be read in two completely opposite ways.
Either she’s shocked that her seduction attempt almost worked, something that — if she had no memory of past resets — had never happened before… or she’s shocked that it didn’t work, surprised that Sensei managed to stop himself, which would imply knowledge of previous cycles.
First Reset: “Everlasting Love” event:
Ami is clearly worried about the world ending and makes explicit references to everyone disappearing, just like during the resets. She asks Sensei not to leave her alone.
In the following scene (which I can’t seem to find in the replays), Ami is sitting on the sofa with an annoyed, almost unfazed expression, while glitching smiley faces appear over her face. She looks like she understands what’s about to happen — and she’s clearly not happy about it.
“There Is Nothing” event:
The reset begins. Ami feels like she’s melting from the inside; she’s in pain, literally crumbling while still alive. She knows she’s experiencing the end of the world. My guess is that the gods/caretakers were “trying something new” on her during this reset. She’s essentially being tortured — which doesn’t feel like something Himawari would do, but more likely the work of another caretaker.
I don’t think Sensei later asking Himawari whether it’s possible for Ami to be tortured during a reset was a coincidence. Ami being tortured across multiple resets, as part of attempts to “change” her, feels like something Ami Prime will eventually use to guilt-trip someone. And honestly, I can understand why she wouldn’t want to be found by the caretakers during resets, if she remembers how much they can make her suffer.
Chapter 2
"heaven for human blood" event: Ami seems both 'possessed' during this event and genuinely troubled as she tries to piece together parts of the past she hadn’t even questioned before Noriko entered her life. Noriko makes her rethink Sensei’s tutoring years — his hidden past relationship with Maya, and the fact that he knew Maya even before Ami introduced her to him in middle school.
Ami also admits that both of them have “blackouts” due to their past experiences. This makes me lean toward the idea that, at the start of Chapter 2, Ami didn’t have full memories of past resets — otherwise, she would have already known these things in some way.
In the early chapters, she also doesn’t act like a fully self-aware, manipulative, billion-years-old incest gremlin. I mean, she is still an incest gremlin — but a naive one. She’s clearly a girl who has never had a normal life.
This can be interpreted in two ways: either the appearance of the “real” Sensei has disrupted a billion-year-old script so much that even a fully aware Ami is experiencing genuinely new story branches, or Ami simply doesn’t have all — or any — memories of past cycles.
Whatever the caretakers tried on her during the last reset doesn’t seem to have worked, or only worked temporarily. During the first dorm war, she’s the one who suggests the courage challenge to Maya, and in “The Scary Room” she outright mind-tortures her. She shows Maya what are likely nude photos from Maya’s youth, photos Sensei had kept hidden in a secret folder at home (as revealed in the next reset).
Maya believed none of those photos still existed, and she’s then absolutely terrified by the idea of an impending factory reset of herself — something we know will later happen, creating Nu Maya, and which has probably happened multiple times before. Ami then gaslights her into thinking she imagined everything.
Maya takes a few days for herself and comes back without ever confronting Ami directly, but now fully aware that she might not be as eternal as she once believed. Maya also admits that she has seen people “disappear” during resets before, and that it’s always horrifying — which suggests she may have witnessed Ami being “tortured” in past cycles.
Still, the fact that Ami claims she only put “some scary movies and stuff” in the Scary Room — along with other events — makes me think she created the room during a brief resurgence of past memories, possibly with the help of USER2 (or 1?), and then immediately forgot doing so.
I suspect that if anyone other than Maya had entered the Scary Room, they would have seen exactly what Ami described. The Scary Room feels like a place that only “evil” Ami — with divine assistance — can truly access.
Because of this, I still think it’s possible that at this point in the story Ami’s memories are driven more by instinct and subconscious perception of past resets rather than full, conscious recollection like she has now.
Even without remembering past resets, I think Ami has always known and remembered Maya having sex with Sensei. As I said before, I believe she thought Maya and Sensei had broken up somehow, but remained deeply suspicious of both of them.
During the second beach trip, Ami is genuinely surprised and awed when she meets Niki, and she cries when she sees Rin and Otoha get together. She doesn’t act at all like present-day Ami. If she does have memories of past cycles at this point, then maybe none of those cycles ever included Niki.
During the second Halloween (the first sigh of frying threads event), Ami realizes that Maya is warming up to Sensei again — and she’s clearly unhappy about it. She accuses Maya of having ulterior motives when she calls Ami cute, as if Maya is forcing herself to keep Ami happy while Ami already knows that Sensei will always take Maya’s side.
Ami openly acknowledges that she wants to be more like Maya, already aware that Maya has always been Sensei’s favorite.
What really puts me in a state of confusion is how Ami genuinely seems to meet many of the newly introduced characters for the first time, acting completely clueless about who they are. At this point, she still can’t see Sekai’s ghost, and she doesn’t know Maki either (the first Maki home invitation).
We know Ami is a good actress, but she’s not that good — especially considering the lies and inconsistencies she starts making from Chapter 3 onward. Because of that, I find it very unlikely that she never met Maki in previous cycles if she truly had full memories, and that she’s faking ignorance during Maki’s first visit.
“Fair and Square” event:
Ami implies that she has a third “mode” (besides helpful and horny), which Sensei half-jokingly labels as “worrying.”
“Sisters” event:
Ami opens up to Niki and Noriko, saying that Sensei is her whole life. She claims she can accept others being with Sensei, as long as those others also accept that Ami will always be there with him — glossing over the fact that, in her mind, “being there” also means she will remain sexually involved with him.
She makes it very clear how protective she is of him, and how she’ll be “very unkind” to anyone who hurts him in any way.
“My Life With You” event:
By the end of Chapter 2, things start to deviate from Ami’s usual routine. She feels that something is different than normal, and this shift seems to begin when she starts reading her mom’s poems.

one for me and one for you,
the wonders of what god can do
a different one for each of us
we pray the same, but struggle thus.
spiders! bugs! and arthropods!
which ones squirm and which one’s god,
many? some? none? a few?
i can’t help but fall in love with you.
During the happy event “Lamb Legs”, “nomal” Ami briefly reappears at the end, telling Sensei that she would never hurt him, and that whatever is happening around him is not the “real” Ami.
To me, this feels like one of the strongest hints that a different iteration of Ami is beginning to replace the one we know.
That’s it for now. I’m going to replay both Chapters 3 and 4 before making another post like this about Ami. I really hope for the story too soon open up about Ami’s own story, because she truly is one of the more present and important character, yet one of the less explored, by author’s choice.
Click to expand...
Short answer: we don’t know for sure.
“Slightly” longer answer:
Spoiler:
Ami stuff
Aside from Himawari’s comment in “Wind Chime” about how, quote, “anything we’d do to her to affect her memories would only be temporary”, implying that, even though Ami is not *immune* to the memory erasure stuff, she always regains at least *some* of her meta-knowledge in one way or another – though Himawari doesn’t clarify whether this recollection simply happens on its own with the passage of time (as in, the longer the cycle goes on, the more stuff Ami becomes aware of, thus potentially explaining why the longest Chapter yet with the longest period between Resets has her acting completely off-the-wall), or if there is a trigger of some kind (accidental or intentionally set-up by “Ami Prime”) that greatly expedites this process – it mostly depends on which one of the two main “Ami theories” you personally subscribe to and find the most convincing/reasonable.
The main dividing factor between these theories is whether you believe that “Nu Ami” (the ditzy, naïve, airheaded girl from Chapters 1 and 2) and “Ami Prime” (the callous, manipulative and remorseless psycho from the second half of Chapter 3 and all of Chapter 4) are two separate entities, with the latter somehow replacing the former: maybe through a “mind-virus” of some kind, like a few people theorized; maybe due to being directly influenced by Sekai after her revival; maybe as a natural consequence of Ami simply regaining all of her memories; or perhaps through some Umineko-like “assuming manual control of your Piece on the Game Board” process, where our Ami’s consciousness has been directly switched with an “ascended” version of her – or, alternatively, that there is only one Ami (specifically, “Ami Prime”) and that “Nu Ami” was simply a mask that she wore for one reason or another, pretending to be pure and innocent all that time when in reality she was anything but.
Personally, I already made my thoughts on Ami’s situation perfectly clear (post № 61315 on December 13, if I’m not mistaken – you can find my long-ass Ami analysis there), so I won’t repeat them here. Moonflare also had a lot of great posts relating to this topic about a year ago, I believe, made in the few months following the release of 0.45 – you can try searching for them, as well. Either way, though, there is a lot of evidence that supports *both* interpretations of her character – including the “Lamb Legs” Happy Scene that very few people ever mention, surprisingly – so, in the wise words of the late (but never forgotten) Plant #2:
Spoiler:
Eternal words of wisdom
“Bro, this is Lessons in Love.
Anything
is possible.”

spoilers.title: Ami stuff
spoilers.html:
Aside from Himawari’s comment in “Wind Chime” about how, quote, “anything we’d do to her to affect her memories would only be temporary”, implying that, even though Ami is not *immune* to the memory erasure stuff, she always regains at least *some* of her meta-knowledge in one way or another – though Himawari doesn’t clarify whether this recollection simply happens on its own with the passage of time (as in, the longer the cycle goes on, the more stuff Ami becomes aware of, thus potentially explaining why the longest Chapter yet with the longest period between Resets has her acting completely off-the-wall), or if there is a trigger of some kind (accidental or intentionally set-up by “Ami Prime”) that greatly expedites this process – it mostly depends on which one of the two main “Ami theories” you personally subscribe to and find the most convincing/reasonable.

The main dividing factor between these theories is whether you believe that “Nu Ami” (the ditzy, naïve, airheaded girl from Chapters 1 and 2) and “Ami Prime” (the callous, manipulative and remorseless psycho from the second half of Chapter 3 and all of Chapter 4) are two separate entities, with the latter somehow replacing the former: maybe through a “mind-virus” of some kind, like a few people theorized; maybe due to being directly influenced by Sekai after her revival; maybe as a natural consequence of Ami simply regaining all of her memories; or perhaps through some Umineko-like “assuming manual control of your Piece on the Game Board” process, where our Ami’s consciousness has been directly switched with an “ascended” version of her – or, alternatively, that there is only one Ami (specifically, “Ami Prime”) and that “Nu Ami” was simply a mask that she wore for one reason or another, pretending to be pure and innocent all that time when in reality she was anything but.

posts.content_html_raw:
Okay, so… This is an interpretation that I had been wanting to share with others for a *long* fucking time – pretty much ever since I first started reading Lessons in Love, so more than a year in the making – and I guess the recent discussion about "what was the point of 10 years of LiL?" and the perspectives shared by Moonflare and DeanNoriko (that I almost completely agree with, for the record) have finally given me enough motivation to actually put my thoughts into words. Plus, it’s Christmas (currently; who the fuck knows whether this is still going to be the case by the time I finish writing this shit), so I have a perfect excuse for being a bit more whimsical and emotionally open during this singular day of the year.

There is just one more thing that should be said before I properly dive into it – which is also going to serve as a hell of an opening statement for my following thesis:
I don’t really agree with the idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei” that gets endlessly repeated to every new unfortunate soul who visits this thread and dares to ask questions about getting into LiL. The way I see it, what you’re *actually* not supposed to do is *self-insert* into him – which, yeah, makes sense: Akira is a fully established character with his own beliefs, goals and motivations, not just a bland vessel for you to pilot (plus, I’m sure he would be positively thrilled at the idea of anyone trying to insert *anything* into him) – but *relating* to Sensei, as fucked up as it is, is something that is very much encouraged by the narrative and, dare I say it, extremely integral to what I consider to be the “true LiL experience”.

As always, this is going to be fairly out there, deeply introspective and decently personal – not to mention *extremely* fucking long – so, y’know, the usual disclaimers apply: “this is just my perspective on things”, “feel free to ignore this post if it isn’t something you’re interested in reading”, “abandon hope, all ye who enter here”, etcetera.

In the very first post I ever made in this thread, I stated that one of the main thematical pillars of Lessons in Love is the idea of “nature vs nurture”, and how the game is an exploration of how much the person you ultimately end up becoming in life depends on your surrounding vs on who you truly are inside, especially when it comes to assigning labels such as “the victim” or “the abuser”. That much is still true – in my eyes, anyway – but, of course, I wouldn’t specify “pillars”, multiple, if LiL only had one of them. Because *another* unifying trait that is shared by pretty much every single character in the game, including the Trinity and other Wishing Well affiliated parties, is their incessant pursuit of happiness, in the best way they know how – with a notable caveat that all of these characters are fucked up in the head, broken by their circumstances, openly depraved, or some combination of the three, and so their “best way” is not exactly what most “normal” human beings would consider good or acceptable.

Akira seeks happiness by alternating between yearning for genuine connection and trying to drown himself in (mostly) teenage pussy, because he is an immature teenage boy puppeteering a corpse of the older version of himself who never actually got to be. Likewise, Sekai could only be happy while she was together with him (for a multitude or reasons), regardless of how deplorable their relationship was seen to be from an outside perspective, and Maya just wishes to be Akira’s own personal cum-receptacle, because she was literally created to be this way. Chika, Ayane, Ami and Sara all yearn for a proper family and/or the joys of motherhood, while others, like Rin (and Rika), Noriko, Kirin and Niki mostly try to complete themselves through romance, focusing only on their partner. Futaba wants to stop hating herself; Yumi, Molly, Uta and Io want to be understood and accepted by someone, with all their flaws and imperfections; Haruka wants to escape her crushing loneliness at any cost (and also prey on some sweet-sweet teenagers); Tsukasa wants to not be a failsafe anymore; Himawari wants to have her mother and father back; the Trinity want to achieve their own “happy endings” – the list goes on. “This is a happy game” and “Remember to Smile” are some of the first lines you see upon starting this game, after all, so it’s no surprise that this idea of endlessly trying to pursue your personal happiness becomes an ever-present constant that permeates the entirety of Lessons in Love and its various aspects.

Now, in what will probably seem like a complete non sequitur (though not really, since I already mentioned her earlier in the title of this thesis), I would like to briefly talk about a certain favorite character of mine, Nodoka Nagasawa, and one of the main ways in which we are extremely similar: namely, our inherent, almost instinctual fascination with the concept of “authenticity”. Nodoka, like me, doesn’t measure the world in terms like “good” or “bad”, “right” or “wrong”, “moral” or “immoral” – instead, the only real metric she uses to determine her feelings about something is whether that thing is “authentic” or not: if it is, she likes it, and if it isn’t, then she couldn’t care less. This desire to see and uncover things as they truly are, to witness the pure unfiltered truth that lies inside everybody’s soul, regardless of whether that truth is beautiful or ugly, virtuous or depraved, is, alongside her boundless sense of intellectual curiosity and filial duty towards Kyoko, one of the main driving forces that pushes Nodoka to do literally everything that she does: from writing her books about the insanity that is going on in Class 1-A to organizing multiple Nodokathons – and why the two controversial events (“Matador” into “Things That Hurt”) that caused most other people to begin strongly hating Nodoka have instead made me fall in love with her in the first place, because the speech she gives to Sensei both during and after blackmailing Yumi made me to finally recognize this weird incest-obsessed girl as not just someone I casually relate to on a surface level, but a true kindred spirit.

I bring all of this up because, with that long-ass preamble out of the way, I am *finally* ready to get to my main point – the perspective that stuck with me ever since I finished my first “full” read-through of LiL (which was up to version 0.45): how Lessons in Love, if I were to try and describe the main “goal” of it all, is effectively an experimental group therapy session for both the characters *and* the reader, except with someone like Nodoka as a therapist – a person who doesn’t want you to “get better”, necessarily, but is instead much more interested in having you deeply analyze your own inner thoughts and desires, without pushing you one way or the other in regards to what the actual outcome of that self-reflection is ultimately going to be.

So if healing/redemption is something that you *genuinely* wish for, having come to this “group therapy” with every intention to become a better individual by the end of it, then, sure – LiL will fully support your decision and give you many sincere words of encouragement by showing you multiple characters like Chika, or Yumi, or Kirin, or Maki slowly (and, hopefully, successfully) walking down that exact path. But it will *also* accept your choice if you instead decide to wholeheartedly indulge in your dark nature rather than renouncing it (which is the “good/moral” thing to do), eagerly following in the footsteps of Sekai, or Sana, or Haruka – because both results are equally *authentic*, and that’s the only thing the aforementioned Nodoka-esque therapist really cares for.

The story constantly asks its characters a single, simple question: “What does ‘living happily’ mean for you?” – and then urges them to *actually* think about the deeper implications of their answer: whether what they *believe* will bring them happiness actually will (a lot of Chapter 1 and 2 scenes with Sana, Rin, Miku and Kirin revolve around this topic, with all four girls initially pushing for things that they later realize won’t actually make them happy), whether they are prepared to deal with the potential consequences of pursuing their goal (Niki’s promise to stay with Akira no matter what that she made while having no fucking clue what she just signed herself up for), whether “crossing the line” is truly worth it (if their answer contained something immoral and/or illegal, like it does for many characters), etcetera.

Which, in turn, brings me back to the apparent idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei”, because *every single one* of the aforementioned questions is *also* ideally supposed to be directed at YOU, the one reading the novel – which doesn’t fucking work if you *don’t* relate to Akira in any way, shape or form and *don’t* share at least some of his personal failings: his attraction to teenagers/wizards, knowing what it feels like to be blatantly manipulate people and string them along for your own benefit, using sex (or something similar) as a currency and a coping mechanism to circumvent having to actually open up to people, easily falling to temptation – hell, just being a flat-out bad person, for fuck’s sake.

Like, I genuinely cannot imagine what the experience of reading Lessons in Love must be like from the perspective of people who are fundamentally unable to put themselves in Akira’s shoes and have an intimate understanding of the same forbidden attraction, the same self-destructive impulses, the same lack of willpower and the same habit of coping with all of your deep-rooted problems through avoidance and escapism he constantly exhibits and struggles with over the course of the story. The people who see the Chinami/Tsukasa plotlines as *just* a horror show in the making, who believe that Sekai was *just* an abuser to Akira whose relationship with him had no positive aspects whatsoever, and for whom Sensei is *just* a morally bankrupt predator rather than a dark, alternative version of themselves from a twisted mirror world in which they made many of the same mistakes and bad decisions – one of the worst possible versions, no doubt about it, but still not an *impossible* one.

It must all look like such a fucking freak circus to them, with both the protagonist and many other characters being objectively irredeemable monsters who belong either behind bars or in a mental asylum. That’s not how *I* see it, obviously, but I’d also fit right in with the general cast of LiL (if I was a cute teenage girl or a hot MILF – alas, I am neither), so that’s not really saying much: it takes one to know one, as they say.

My finishing thought, if I were to leave one, would probably be this: I’m not really judging anyone who strongly disagrees with me and *does* share the same “moral” perspective on the events and characters of this game that I (somewhat exaggeratedly) described earlier, but it *does* make me wonder which one of us is closer to the intended “Lessons in Love audience” Selebus writes this story for. Specifically, how much of LiL is supposed to resonate with “normal” people, who would see Akira as a creep and his life as a fate worse than death, compared to the fellow abyss-dwellers (like myself) who thrive in the darkness and can find the underlying beauty in even some of the ugliest possible things.

The way I see it, what you’re *actually* not supposed to do is *self-insert* into him – which, yeah, makes sense: Akira is a fully established character with his own beliefs, goals and motivations, not just a bland vessel for you to pilot (plus, I’m sure he would be positively thrilled at the idea of anyone trying to insert *anything* into him) – but *relating* to Sensei, as fucked up as it is, is something that is very much encouraged by the narrative and, dare I say it, extremely integral to what I consider to be the “true LiL experience”.
As always, this is going to be fairly out there, deeply introspective and decently personal – not to mention *extremely* fucking long – so, y’know, the usual disclaimers apply: “this is just my perspective on things”, “feel free to ignore this post if it isn’t something you’re interested in reading”, “abandon hope, all ye who enter here”, etcetera.
Spoiler:
To Live Happily, or Nodoka Nagasawa’s group therapy theory
In the very first post I ever made in this thread, I stated that one of the main thematical pillars of Lessons in Love is the idea of “nature vs nurture”, and how the game is an exploration of how much the person you ultimately end up becoming in life depends on your surrounding vs on who you truly are inside, especially when it comes to assigning labels such as “the victim” or “the abuser”. That much is still true – in my eyes, anyway – but, of course, I wouldn’t specify “pillars”, multiple, if LiL only had one of them. Because *another* unifying trait that is shared by pretty much every single character in the game, including the Trinity and other Wishing Well affiliated parties, is their incessant pursuit of happiness, in the best way they know how – with a notable caveat that all of these characters are fucked up in the head, broken by their circumstances, openly depraved, or some combination of the three, and so their “best way” is not exactly what most “normal” human beings would consider good or acceptable.
Akira seeks happiness by alternating between yearning for genuine connection and trying to drown himself in (mostly) teenage pussy, because he is an immature teenage boy puppeteering a corpse of the older version of himself who never actually got to be. Likewise, Sekai could only be happy while she was together with him (for a multitude or reasons), regardless of how deplorable their relationship was seen to be from an outside perspective, and Maya just wishes to be Akira’s own personal cum-receptacle, because she was literally created to be this way. Chika, Ayane, Ami and Sara all yearn for a proper family and/or the joys of motherhood, while others, like Rin (and Rika), Noriko, Kirin and Niki mostly try to complete themselves through romance, focusing only on their partner. Futaba wants to stop hating herself; Yumi, Molly, Uta and Io want to be understood and accepted by someone, with all their flaws and imperfections; Haruka wants to escape her crushing loneliness at any cost (and also prey on some sweet-sweet teenagers); Tsukasa wants to not be a failsafe anymore; Himawari wants to have her mother and father back; the Trinity want to achieve their own “happy endings” – the list goes on. “This is a happy game” and “Remember to Smile” are some of the first lines you see upon starting this game, after all, so it’s no surprise that this idea of endlessly trying to pursue your personal happiness becomes an ever-present constant that permeates the entirety of Lessons in Love and its various aspects.
Now, in what will probably seem like a complete non sequitur (though not really, since I already mentioned her earlier in the title of this thesis), I would like to briefly talk about a certain favorite character of mine, Nodoka Nagasawa, and one of the main ways in which we are extremely similar: namely, our inherent, almost instinctual fascination with the concept of “authenticity”. Nodoka, like me, doesn’t measure the world in terms like “good” or “bad”, “right” or “wrong”, “moral” or “immoral” – instead, the only real metric she uses to determine her feelings about something is whether that thing is “authentic” or not: if it is, she likes it, and if it isn’t, then she couldn’t care less. This desire to see and uncover things as they truly are, to witness the pure unfiltered truth that lies inside everybody’s soul, regardless of whether that truth is beautiful or ugly, virtuous or depraved, is, alongside her boundless sense of intellectual curiosity and filial duty towards Kyoko, one of the main driving forces that pushes Nodoka to do literally everything that she does: from writing her books about the insanity that is going on in Class 1-A to organizing multiple Nodokathons – and why the two controversial events (“Matador” into “Things That Hurt”) that caused most other people to begin strongly hating Nodoka have instead made me fall in love with her in the first place, because the speech she gives to Sensei both during and after blackmailing Yumi made me to finally recognize this weird incest-obsessed girl as not just someone I casually relate to on a surface level, but a true kindred spirit.
I bring all of this up because, with that long-ass preamble out of the way, I am *finally* ready to get to my main point – the perspective that stuck with me ever since I finished my first “full” read-through of LiL (which was up to version 0.45): how Lessons in Love, if I were to try and describe the main “goal” of it all, is effectively an experimental group therapy session for both the characters *and* the reader, except with someone like Nodoka as a therapist – a person who doesn’t want you to “get better”, necessarily, but is instead much more interested in having you deeply analyze your own inner thoughts and desires, without pushing you one way or the other in regards to what the actual outcome of that self-reflection is ultimately going to be.
So if healing/redemption is something that you *genuinely* wish for, having come to this “group therapy” with every intention to become a better individual by the end of it, then, sure – LiL will fully support your decision and give you many sincere words of encouragement by showing you multiple characters like Chika, or Yumi, or Kirin, or Maki slowly (and, hopefully, successfully) walking down that exact path. But it will *also* accept your choice if you instead decide to wholeheartedly indulge in your dark nature rather than renouncing it (which is the “good/moral” thing to do), eagerly following in the footsteps of Sekai, or Sana, or Haruka – because both results are equally *authentic*, and that’s the only thing the aforementioned Nodoka-esque therapist really cares for.
The story constantly asks its characters a single, simple question: “What does ‘living happily’ mean for you?” – and then urges them to *actually* think about the deeper implications of their answer: whether what they *believe* will bring them happiness actually will (a lot of Chapter 1 and 2 scenes with Sana, Rin, Miku and Kirin revolve around this topic, with all four girls initially pushing for things that they later realize won’t actually make them happy), whether they are prepared to deal with the potential consequences of pursuing their goal (Niki’s promise to stay with Akira no matter what that she made while having no fucking clue what she just signed herself up for), whether “crossing the line” is truly worth it (if their answer contained something immoral and/or illegal, like it does for many characters), etcetera.
Which, in turn, brings me back to the apparent idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei”, because *every single one* of the aforementioned questions is *also* ideally supposed to be directed at YOU, the one reading the novel – which doesn’t fucking work if you *don’t* relate to Akira in any way, shape or form and *don’t* share at least some of his personal failings: his attraction to teenagers/wizards, knowing what it feels like to be blatantly manipulate people and string them along for your own benefit, using sex (or something similar) as a currency and a coping mechanism to circumvent having to actually open up to people, easily falling to temptation – hell, just being a flat-out bad person, for fuck’s sake.
Like, I genuinely cannot imagine what the experience of reading Lessons in Love must be like from the perspective of people who are fundamentally unable to put themselves in Akira’s shoes and have an intimate understanding of the same forbidden attraction, the same self-destructive impulses, the same lack of willpower and the same habit of coping with all of your deep-rooted problems through avoidance and escapism he constantly exhibits and struggles with over the course of the story. The people who see the Chinami/Tsukasa plotlines as *just* a horror show in the making, who believe that Sekai was *just* an abuser to Akira whose relationship with him had no positive aspects whatsoever, and for whom Sensei is *just* a morally bankrupt predator rather than a dark, alternative version of themselves from a twisted mirror world in which they made many of the same mistakes and bad decisions – one of the worst possible versions, no doubt about it, but still not an *impossible* one.
It must all look like such a fucking freak circus to them, with both the protagonist and many other characters being objectively irredeemable monsters who belong either behind bars or in a mental asylum. That’s not how *I* see it, obviously, but I’d also fit right in with the general cast of LiL (if I was a cute teenage girl or a hot MILF – alas, I am neither), so that’s not really saying much: it takes one to know one, as they say.
My finishing thought, if I were to leave one, would probably be this: I’m not really judging anyone who strongly disagrees with me and *does* share the same “moral” perspective on the events and characters of this game that I (somewhat exaggeratedly) described earlier, but it *does* make me wonder which one of us is closer to the intended “Lessons in Love audience” Selebus writes this story for. Specifically, how much of LiL is supposed to resonate with “normal” people, who would see Akira as a creep and his life as a fate worse than death, compared to the fellow abyss-dwellers (like myself) who thrive in the darkness and can find the underlying beauty in even some of the ugliest possible things.

As to how the game makes sense to you, that's an interesting perspective. But then, when you question the validity of people's interactions with the story, and even compare that to Selebus' intent with it, you lose me.
What I find ironic is that you do recognize that it's not just Akira, every character in the story has "lessons in love" to deal with. And yet you choose to fix on Akira. I have never been abused as a child, nor groomed by a predator, nor had any desire whatsoever to have sex with minors. I have fucked up many times in my life, and yet I didn't wallow in them forever - sometimes I managed to apologise for my actions, sometimes I moved on, more damaged than before, but still here. I have issues, lots of them, but they're not in Akira's character. That doesn't mean that I wouldn't be able to empathize with someone for their conditions, even though I am so foreign to them - but since you pointed that out from your perspective, I'm telling mine. I do not have a link to Akira, and I'd prefer that he was a much more active character and fuck up that way - because that's closer to who I am.

Now, obviously LiL's subject matter is the cycle of grooming and Akira is central to that. There's no arguing this. But that doesn't mean that it's for the cycle of grooming. Or for darker aspects of the human psyque. I'd argue that what it does is to more accurately represent the intricacies of these aspects. Akira's not just a predator, nor is Sekai, nor anyone that does anything bad in this game. Does this mean that because a situation is more complicated that Selebus is saying that you cannot condemn them, or have to put yourself in their shoes? I'd vehemently disagree. Kirin blackmailed Ayane into sexual assault and that's unforgivable to me. What right do you have (or anyone else) to tell me my reaction to this is "less right" than what the creator intended? It's a situation that he put there. It happened in the story and affected me. I think that is the intent. If you felt empathy for all this stuff at the end of it, great. If someone felt revulsion, I think it's equally great. What matters is that people enjoyed the effort put in the details of the situation.

I hope Akira does have a happy ending, but by the same token, how dare I tell someone that they can't wish for Akira to end up in a mental hospital, or jailed (or even dead)? I mean, I have done this - but from a story standpoint. Never in telling them that how they feel about it is "less right" in terms of what Selebus intended. While I can say that the story doesn't seem to be going towards a big tragedy (in terms of structure), that has nothing to do with personal feelings towards each character. The big issue for me is that you tackled all of this from an emotional standpoint. Empathy and "putting yourself in someone's shoes" isn't something that I'd try to argue with people about them feeling or not.

I think LiL is a story with at least 36 characters, and Akira is but one of them. The difference is that he's also the means by which we experience the story. And he can be quite annoying. At rare times it even feels like he becomes a mouthpiece to the author, and I can see Selebus rambling in his thoughts. Nevertheless, I'd like to point out two things. First is that, as I mentioned, there are other characters in this story. Sure, if the player empathizes with none of them they'd have stopped playing by now. But it doesn't have to be Akira, nor the aspects of Akira that you brought up. I have talked a lot about "stomachache", and there are aspects there both from Akira and Io that resurfaced some stuff from me - even though, as I have said, I rarely identify with Akira. My point here is that there is a difference between identifying/empathizing with Akira as a norm, and empathizing with specific situations in which he's in.

And my second and final point is that LiL is much more than Akira. If Selebus even has an intended objective of whom he's writing for (cause I think it's just himself), I'd say that it's probably people that can appreciate the complicated tragedy of such a topic, being explored to its inconvenient details. To presume he wants to close in on what such people must conclude of his spectacle is antithetical, in my opinion, to everything he has shown thus far in how he writes.
Lastly, I think there's a danger here of taking "you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei" way out of context. Usually this is said towards someone that thinks they are the protagonist, upon starting the game. I haven't ever seen someone say that here meaning "you aren't supposed to relate to anything this character says, does or any situation he's in ever". But I'm presuming you used it as an excuse to write your post, which was interesting tbf.

Regardless of what he says (and what he expects in a profit way), I don't think Sel actually intended this game for the general public, doesn't feel like it is the target audience. Also, your entire post made me think of both that one Umineko quote (turn on subtitles if you open it), and the protagonist from My Teen Romantic Comedy SNAFU who pretty much was searching for something genuine.
I say that, if you're already deep into reading LiL and didn't get filtered by how LiL it is, you're already relating in some way with the game. And as 今 said, Sensei isn't the protagonist, so you don't have to relate to Sensei to truly experience LiL. I believe it's all about the word of the day, so if you're already commited to the game, what you get out of it is the genuine experience that the game offered you. Though, on a meta level, since this story revolves around him, whether you see him as the pov or as someone you relate to, he's the vehicle by which you experience it, so some crossover is somewhat expected considering his internal thoughts also form part of the story.
He ain't batting for that team, buddy.
Click to expand...
First of all, just to dispel any doubts:
yes, I am very familiar with both Umineko and OreGairu light novels and hold these two stories in very high regard (theme-wise and in terms of character writing, especially), so any similarities you see between them and my personal worldview (which is partially reflected in this very analysis) are completely on the mark, because I was 100% influenced by both of these stories during my late teens and early adulthood years.

Second of all, while I’m not sure if I agree with taking what Nao/The Xoanon says to Akira in “Mother’s Milk” completely at face value, because there is a lot of additional (and not yet understood) meta-context to their statements that severely muddles the water, your point about how “you're already deep into reading LiL and didn't get filtered by how LiL it is, you're already relating in some way with the game” is undoubtedly correct. However, the question of whether or not there is a “right” and “wrong” way to experience Lessons in Love *is* very much a complicated one, since it directly ties into the greater argument of authorial intent vs “Death of The Author” – and, specific to this thread in particular, the whole “Green Path Chads vs Red Path Virgins” (or vice versa, depending on who you ask) endless debate that still keeps happening to this very day (though not as of late, admittedly).

So while, yes, a theoretical person who, for the sake of my extra-specific example, played the entire game on mute (following the guide mod or looking up answers to the puzzles they couldn’t solve on their own), skipped every single event that could be skipped, changed every instance of Akira’s name to “Marty” in the game files and also hated his guts whenever he was on screen did *technically* have an “authentic” experience with LiL of some kind, I can’t wholeheartedly agree with the notion that their experience is in *any* way comparable (not even talking about “good vs bad” comparable – just comparable, period) with what *I* experienced during my own original playthrough of Lessons in Love, neither emotionally nor thematically. At that point we just have to concede that we’re both pretty much reading through two entirely different visual novels with only passing surface-level similarities, so, like, what could the two of us – me and that theoretical weird person –even talk about in relation to LiL? The name of the VN? Koikatsu visuals? Kumon-mi as the setting?

Once again, to reiterate: I am *not* pushing for the idea that “my way is the correct one, and everyone else just didn’t get it”. The point I was trying to make was more about our ability to discuss and connect over our shared experiences as readers, since if there *are* no shared experiences (due to us having viewed every single scene/character in the game through diametrically opposed lenses), then none of our arguments would mean anything to the other side and we would, effectively, just be talking past each other. Hence me wondering whether this divide in perspectives was in any way intentional, and which outlook – “moral” or “immoral” – is closer to the one personally shared by Selebus.

And finally, if it wasn’t already super-obvious,
“I’m sure he would be positively thrilled at the idea of anyone trying to insert *anything* into him” was meant to be extremely sarcastic, since I *just* recently made a huge post pointing out that exact apprehension of Akira’s.

posts.content_html_raw:
CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Okay, so… This is an interpretation that I had been wanting to share with others for a *long* fucking time – pretty much ever since I first started reading Lessons in Love, so more than a year in the making – and I guess the recent discussion about "what was the point of 10 years of LiL?" and the perspectives shared by Moonflare and DeanNoriko (that I almost completely agree with, for the record) have finally given me enough motivation to actually put my thoughts into words. Plus, it’s Christmas (currently; who the fuck knows whether this is still going to be the case by the time I finish writing this shit), so I have a perfect excuse for being a bit more whimsical and emotionally open during this singular day of the year.

There is just one more thing that should be said before I properly dive into it – which is also going to serve as a hell of an opening statement for my following thesis:
I don’t really agree with the idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei” that gets endlessly repeated to every new unfortunate soul who visits this thread and dares to ask questions about getting into LiL. The way I see it, what you’re *actually* not supposed to do is *self-insert* into him – which, yeah, makes sense: Akira is a fully established character with his own beliefs, goals and motivations, not just a bland vessel for you to pilot (plus, I’m sure he would be positively thrilled at the idea of anyone trying to insert *anything* into him) – but *relating* to Sensei, as fucked up as it is, is something that is very much encouraged by the narrative and, dare I say it, extremely integral to what I consider to be the “true LiL experience”.

As always, this is going to be fairly out there, deeply introspective and decently personal – not to mention *extremely* fucking long – so, y’know, the usual disclaimers apply: “this is just my perspective on things”, “feel free to ignore this post if it isn’t something you’re interested in reading”, “abandon hope, all ye who enter here”, etcetera.

In the very first post I ever made in this thread, I stated that one of the main thematical pillars of Lessons in Love is the idea of “nature vs nurture”, and how the game is an exploration of how much the person you ultimately end up becoming in life depends on your surrounding vs on who you truly are inside, especially when it comes to assigning labels such as “the victim” or “the abuser”. That much is still true – in my eyes, anyway – but, of course, I wouldn’t specify “pillars”, multiple, if LiL only had one of them. Because *another* unifying trait that is shared by pretty much every single character in the game, including the Trinity and other Wishing Well affiliated parties, is their incessant pursuit of happiness, in the best way they know how – with a notable caveat that all of these characters are fucked up in the head, broken by their circumstances, openly depraved, or some combination of the three, and so their “best way” is not exactly what most “normal” human beings would consider good or acceptable.

Akira seeks happiness by alternating between yearning for genuine connection and trying to drown himself in (mostly) teenage pussy, because he is an immature teenage boy puppeteering a corpse of the older version of himself who never actually got to be. Likewise, Sekai could only be happy while she was together with him (for a multitude or reasons), regardless of how deplorable their relationship was seen to be from an outside perspective, and Maya just wishes to be Akira’s own personal cum-receptacle, because she was literally created to be this way. Chika, Ayane, Ami and Sara all yearn for a proper family and/or the joys of motherhood, while others, like Rin (and Rika), Noriko, Kirin and Niki mostly try to complete themselves through romance, focusing only on their partner. Futaba wants to stop hating herself; Yumi, Molly, Uta and Io want to be understood and accepted by someone, with all their flaws and imperfections; Haruka wants to escape her crushing loneliness at any cost (and also prey on some sweet-sweet teenagers); Tsukasa wants to not be a failsafe anymore; Himawari wants to have her mother and father back; the Trinity want to achieve their own “happy endings” – the list goes on. “This is a happy game” and “Remember to Smile” are some of the first lines you see upon starting this game, after all, so it’s no surprise that this idea of endlessly trying to pursue your personal happiness becomes an ever-present constant that permeates the entirety of Lessons in Love and its various aspects.

Now, in what will probably seem like a complete non sequitur (though not really, since I already mentioned her earlier in the title of this thesis), I would like to briefly talk about a certain favorite character of mine, Nodoka Nagasawa, and one of the main ways in which we are extremely similar: namely, our inherent, almost instinctual fascination with the concept of “authenticity”. Nodoka, like me, doesn’t measure the world in terms like “good” or “bad”, “right” or “wrong”, “moral” or “immoral” – instead, the only real metric she uses to determine her feelings about something is whether that thing is “authentic” or not: if it is, she likes it, and if it isn’t, then she couldn’t care less. This desire to see and uncover things as they truly are, to witness the pure unfiltered truth that lies inside everybody’s soul, regardless of whether that truth is beautiful or ugly, virtuous or depraved, is, alongside her boundless sense of intellectual curiosity and filial duty towards Kyoko, one of the main driving forces that pushes Nodoka to do literally everything that she does: from writing her books about the insanity that is going on in Class 1-A to organizing multiple Nodokathons – and why the two controversial events (“Matador” into “Things That Hurt”) that caused most other people to begin strongly hating Nodoka have instead made me fall in love with her in the first place, because the speech she gives to Sensei both during and after blackmailing Yumi made me to finally recognize this weird incest-obsessed girl as not just someone I casually relate to on a surface level, but a true kindred spirit.

I bring all of this up because, with that long-ass preamble out of the way, I am *finally* ready to get to my main point – the perspective that stuck with me ever since I finished my first “full” read-through of LiL (which was up to version 0.45): how Lessons in Love, if I were to try and describe the main “goal” of it all, is effectively an experimental group therapy session for both the characters *and* the reader, except with someone like Nodoka as a therapist – a person who doesn’t want you to “get better”, necessarily, but is instead much more interested in having you deeply analyze your own inner thoughts and desires, without pushing you one way or the other in regards to what the actual outcome of that self-reflection is ultimately going to be.

So if healing/redemption is something that you *genuinely* wish for, having come to this “group therapy” with every intention to become a better individual by the end of it, then, sure – LiL will fully support your decision and give you many sincere words of encouragement by showing you multiple characters like Chika, or Yumi, or Kirin, or Maki slowly (and, hopefully, successfully) walking down that exact path. But it will *also* accept your choice if you instead decide to wholeheartedly indulge in your dark nature rather than renouncing it (which is the “good/moral” thing to do), eagerly following in the footsteps of Sekai, or Sana, or Haruka – because both results are equally *authentic*, and that’s the only thing the aforementioned Nodoka-esque therapist really cares for.

The story constantly asks its characters a single, simple question: “What does ‘living happily’ mean for you?” – and then urges them to *actually* think about the deeper implications of their answer: whether what they *believe* will bring them happiness actually will (a lot of Chapter 1 and 2 scenes with Sana, Rin, Miku and Kirin revolve around this topic, with all four girls initially pushing for things that they later realize won’t actually make them happy), whether they are prepared to deal with the potential consequences of pursuing their goal (Niki’s promise to stay with Akira no matter what that she made while having no fucking clue what she just signed herself up for), whether “crossing the line” is truly worth it (if their answer contained something immoral and/or illegal, like it does for many characters), etcetera.

Which, in turn, brings me back to the apparent idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei”, because *every single one* of the aforementioned questions is *also* ideally supposed to be directed at YOU, the one reading the novel – which doesn’t fucking work if you *don’t* relate to Akira in any way, shape or form and *don’t* share at least some of his personal failings: his attraction to teenagers/wizards, knowing what it feels like to be blatantly manipulate people and string them along for your own benefit, using sex (or something similar) as a currency and a coping mechanism to circumvent having to actually open up to people, easily falling to temptation – hell, just being a flat-out bad person, for fuck’s sake.

Like, I genuinely cannot imagine what the experience of reading Lessons in Love must be like from the perspective of people who are fundamentally unable to put themselves in Akira’s shoes and have an intimate understanding of the same forbidden attraction, the same self-destructive impulses, the same lack of willpower and the same habit of coping with all of your deep-rooted problems through avoidance and escapism he constantly exhibits and struggles with over the course of the story. The people who see the Chinami/Tsukasa plotlines as *just* a horror show in the making, who believe that Sekai was *just* an abuser to Akira whose relationship with him had no positive aspects whatsoever, and for whom Sensei is *just* a morally bankrupt predator rather than a dark, alternative version of themselves from a twisted mirror world in which they made many of the same mistakes and bad decisions – one of the worst possible versions, no doubt about it, but still not an *impossible* one.

It must all look like such a fucking freak circus to them, with both the protagonist and many other characters being objectively irredeemable monsters who belong either behind bars or in a mental asylum. That’s not how *I* see it, obviously, but I’d also fit right in with the general cast of LiL (if I was a cute teenage girl or a hot MILF – alas, I am neither), so that’s not really saying much: it takes one to know one, as they say.

My finishing thought, if I were to leave one, would probably be this: I’m not really judging anyone who strongly disagrees with me and *does* share the same “moral” perspective on the events and characters of this game that I (somewhat exaggeratedly) described earlier, but it *does* make me wonder which one of us is closer to the intended “Lessons in Love audience” Selebus writes this story for. Specifically, how much of LiL is supposed to resonate with “normal” people, who would see Akira as a creep and his life as a fate worse than death, compared to the fellow abyss-dwellers (like myself) who thrive in the darkness and can find the underlying beauty in even some of the ugliest possible things.

This desire to see and uncover things as they truly are, to witness the pure unfiltered truth that lies inside everybody’s soul, regardless of whether that truth is beautiful or ugly, virtuous or depraved, is, alongside her boundless sense of intellectual curiosity and filial duty towards Kyoko, one of the main driving forces that pushes Nodoka to do literally everything that she does: from writing her books about the insanity that is going on in Class 1-A to organizing multiple Nodokathons – and why the two controversial events (“Matador” into “Things That Hurt”) that caused most other people to begin strongly hating Nodoka have instead made me fall in love with her in the first place, because the speech she gives to Sensei both during and after blackmailing Yumi made me to finally recognize this weird incest-obsessed girl as not just someone I casually relate to on a surface level, but a true kindred spirit.
I bring all of this up because, with that long-ass preamble out of the way, I am *finally* ready to get to my main point – the perspective that stuck with me ever since I finished my first “full” read-through of LiL (which was up to version 0.45): how Lessons in Love, if I were to try and describe the main “goal” of it all, is effectively an experimental group therapy session for both the characters *and* the reader, except with someone like Nodoka as a therapist – a person who doesn’t want you to “get better”, necessarily, but is instead much more interested in having you deeply analyze your own inner thoughts and desires, without pushing you one way or the other in regards to what the actual outcome of that self-reflection is ultimately going to be.
So if healing/redemption is something that you *genuinely* wish for, having come to this “group therapy” with every intention to become a better individual by the end of it, then, sure – LiL will fully support your decision and give you many sincere words of encouragement by showing you multiple characters like Chika, or Yumi, or Kirin, or Maki slowly (and, hopefully, successfully) walking down that exact path. But it will *also* accept your choice if you instead decide to wholeheartedly indulge in your dark nature rather than renouncing it (which is the “good/moral” thing to do), eagerly following in the footsteps of Sekai, or Sana, or Haruka – because both results are equally *authentic*, and that’s the only thing the aforementioned Nodoka-esque therapist really cares for.
The story constantly asks its characters a single, simple question: “What does ‘living happily’ mean for you?” – and then urges them to *actually* think about the deeper implications of their answer: whether what they *believe* will bring them happiness actually will (a lot of Chapter 1 and 2 scenes with Sana, Rin, Miku and Kirin revolve around this topic, with all four girls initially pushing for things that they later realize won’t actually make them happy), whether they are prepared to deal with the potential consequences of pursuing their goal (Niki’s promise to stay with Akira no matter what that she made while having no fucking clue what she just signed herself up for), whether “crossing the line” is truly worth it (if their answer contained something immoral and/or illegal, like it does for many characters), etcetera.
Which, in turn, brings me back to the apparent idea that “you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei”, because *every single one* of the aforementioned questions is *also* ideally supposed to be directed at YOU, the one reading the novel – which doesn’t fucking work if you *don’t* relate to Akira in any way, shape or form and *don’t* share at least some of his personal failings: his attraction to teenagers/wizards, knowing what it feels like to be blatantly manipulate people and string them along for your own benefit, using sex (or something similar) as a currency and a coping mechanism to circumvent having to actually open up to people, easily falling to temptation – hell, just being a flat-out bad person, for fuck’s sake.
Like, I genuinely cannot imagine what the experience of reading Lessons in Love must be like from the perspective of people who are fundamentally unable to put themselves in Akira’s shoes and have an intimate understanding of the same forbidden attraction, the same self-destructive impulses, the same lack of willpower and the same habit of coping with all of your deep-rooted problems through avoidance and escapism he constantly exhibits and struggles with over the course of the story. The people who see the Chinami/Tsukasa plotlines as *just* a horror show in the making, who believe that Sekai was *just* an abuser to Akira whose relationship with him had no positive aspects whatsoever, and for whom Sensei is *just* a morally bankrupt predator rather than a dark, alternative version of themselves from a twisted mirror world in which they made many of the same mistakes and bad decisions – one of the worst possible versions, no doubt about it, but still not an *impossible* one.
It must all look like such a fucking freak circus to them, with both the protagonist and many other characters being objectively irredeemable monsters who belong either behind bars or in a mental asylum. That’s not how *I* see it, obviously, but I’d also fit right in with the general cast of LiL (if I was a cute teenage girl or a hot MILF – alas, I am neither), so that’s not really saying much: it takes one to know one, as they say.

First of all, just to dispel any doubts:
yes, I am very familiar with both Umineko and OreGairu light novels and hold these two stories in very high regard (theme-wise and in terms of character writing, especially), so any similarities you see between them and my personal worldview (which is partially reflected in this very analysis) are completely on the mark, because I was 100% influenced by both of these stories during my late teens and early adulthood years.

Second of all, while I’m not sure if I agree with taking what Nao/The Xoanon says to Akira in “Mother’s Milk” completely at face value, because there is a lot of additional (and not yet understood) meta-context to their statements that severely muddles the water, your point about how “you're already deep into reading LiL and didn't get filtered by how LiL it is, you're already relating in some way with the game” is undoubtedly correct. However, the question of whether or not there is a “right” and “wrong” way to experience Lessons in Love *is* very much a complicated one, since it directly ties into the greater argument of authorial intent vs “Death of The Author” – and, specific to this thread in particular, the whole “Green Path Chads vs Red Path Virgins” (or vice versa, depending on who you ask) endless debate that still keeps happening to this very day (though not as of late, admittedly).

So while, yes, a theoretical person who, for the sake of my extra-specific example, played the entire game on mute (following the guide mod or looking up answers to the puzzles they couldn’t solve on their own), skipped every single event that could be skipped, changed every instance of Akira’s name to “Marty” in the game files and also hated his guts whenever he was on screen did *technically* have an “authentic” experience with LiL of some kind, I can’t wholeheartedly agree with the notion that their experience is in *any* way comparable (not even talking about “good vs bad” comparable – just comparable, period) with what *I* experienced during my own original playthrough of Lessons in Love, neither emotionally nor thematically. At that point we just have to concede that we’re both pretty much reading through two entirely different visual novels with only passing surface-level similarities, so, like, what could the two of us – me and that theoretical weird person –even talk about in relation to LiL? The name of the VN? Koikatsu visuals? Kumon-mi as the setting?
