Well, I'm not overly criticizing the post because it's clearly made from an emotional and personal place. But I will point out that maybe you're losing sight of your arguments here and there. As to how the game makes sense to you, that's an interesting perspective. But then, when you question the validity of people's interactions with the story, and even compare that to Selebus' intent with it, you lose me.
What I find ironic is that you do recognize that it's not just Akira, every character in the story has "lessons in love" to deal with. And yet you choose to fix on Akira. I have never been abused as a child, nor groomed by a predator, nor had any desire whatsoever to have sex with minors. I have fucked up many times in my life, and yet I didn't wallow in them forever - sometimes I managed to apologise for my actions, sometimes I moved on, more damaged than before, but still here. I have issues, lots of them, but they're not in Akira's character. That doesn't mean that I wouldn't be able to empathize with someone for their conditions, even though I am so foreign to them - but since you pointed that out from your perspective, I'm telling mine. I do not have a link to Akira, and I'd prefer that he was a much more active character and fuck up that way - because that's closer to who I am.

Now, obviously LiL's subject matter is the cycle of grooming and Akira is central to that. There's no arguing this. But that doesn't mean that it's for the cycle of grooming. Or for darker aspects of the human psyque. I'd argue that what it does is to more accurately represent the intricacies of these aspects. Akira's not just a predator, nor is Sekai, nor anyone that does anything bad in this game. Does this mean that because a situation is more complicated that Selebus is saying that you cannot condemn them, or have to put yourself in their shoes? I'd vehemently disagree. Kirin blackmailed Ayane into sexual assault and that's unforgivable to me. What right do you have (or anyone else) to tell me my reaction to this is "less right" than what the creator intended? It's a situation that he put there. It happened in the story and affected me. I think that is the intent. If you felt empathy for all this stuff at the end of it, great. If someone felt revulsion, I think it's equally great. What matters is that people enjoyed the effort put in the details of the situation.

I hope Akira does have a happy ending, but by the same token, how dare I tell someone that they can't wish for Akira to end up in a mental hospital, or jailed (or even dead)? I mean, I have done this - but from a story standpoint. Never in telling them that how they feel about it is "less right" in terms of what Selebus intended. While I can say that the story doesn't seem to be going towards a big tragedy (in terms of structure), that has nothing to do with personal feelings towards each character. The big issue for me is that you tackled all of this from an emotional standpoint. Empathy and "putting yourself in someone's shoes" isn't something that I'd try to argue with people about them feeling or not.

I think LiL is a story with at least 36 characters, and Akira is but one of them. The difference is that he's also the means by which we experience the story. And he can be quite annoying. At rare times it even feels like he becomes a mouthpiece to the author, and I can see Selebus rambling in his thoughts. Nevertheless, I'd like to point out two things. First is that, as I mentioned, there are other characters in this story. Sure, if the player empathizes with none of them they'd have stopped playing by now. But it doesn't have to be Akira, nor the aspects of Akira that you brought up. I have talked a lot about "stomachache", and there are aspects there both from Akira and Io that resurfaced some stuff from me - even though, as I have said, I rarely identify with Akira. My point here is that there is a difference between identifying/empathizing with Akira as a norm, and empathizing with specific situations in which he's in.

And my second and final point is that LiL is much more than Akira. If Selebus even has an intended objective of whom he's writing for (cause I think it's just himself), I'd say that it's probably people that can appreciate the complicated tragedy of such a topic, being explored to its inconvenient details. To presume he wants to close in on what such people must conclude of his spectacle is antithetical, in my opinion, to everything he has shown thus far in how he writes.
Lastly, I think there's a danger here of taking "you aren’t supposed to self-identify with Sensei" way out of context. Usually this is said towards someone that thinks they are the protagonist, upon starting the game. I haven't ever seen someone say that here meaning "you aren't supposed to relate to anything this character says, does or any situation he's in ever". But I'm presuming you used it as an excuse to write your post, which was interesting tbf.
Click to expand...

Thank you once again for your detailed thoughts. I already clarified some of my original goals/intentions in my reply to SlidingSubject (which you seemingly disagreed with, but that's okay), so I won’t repeat them here. Aside from that, I mostly agree with all of your counterarguments, and the few ones I *do* fundamentally disagree with are worded in a way where I can still fully understand where you’re coming from (which means that it’s all good). So the only real point that still needs clarification is why I decided to specifically focus on Akira – when, as we both pointed out, LiL is so much bigger than just him:

Well, the answer to that is quite simple, actually: it’s because, regardless of the size/quality of the rest of its cast, Akira is still the main (and only) protagonist of Lessons in Love – and that title is not something that I take lightly.

Traditional theory of storytelling dictates that – provided the author knows that they’re doing (which Selebus 100% is, in my opinion) and that they didn’t employ any particular twists or subversions related to this topic (like multiple parallel protagonists, protagonist switch, etcetera – which, since we are now 150+ hours into the game, I would say *extremely* unlikely) – a character being selected as “the protagonist of a story” carries a very clear, very specific implication of their basically uncontested level of thematic and narrative significance within said story, in addition to the unwritten promise (from the author to the audience) that they are going to be *continually upheld* to that status throughout their entire narrative journey.

The only real exception to that is the modern “self-insert” approach that, sadly, plagues many stories that were created in the last few decades (not to be confused with the “audience surrogate” trope, like Dr. Watson in the Sherlock Holmes novels), but aside from those fucking narrative abominations it is practically a given that the protagonist of a story is going to be extremely important to its every major theme and plot beat that happens within it, because they were *specifically* selected for that very purpose – if there was a different character better suited for that role, *they* would have been chosen as the protagonist instead.

So just because Lessons in Love has 35+ other extremely well-written characters, each of whom also directly ties into the overarching narrative/themes in some way and can potentially be personally relatable to you, or me, or anyone else (which is just how stories are normally supposed to work: it’s not exactly some unique crowning achievement special to LiL), their individual contributions to the grand thematical canvas, comprised of all of the main ideas/concepts the story is interested in exploring, completely pale in comparison to Akira’s lion’s share of the same exact canvas – Akira, who consistently serves as a focal point for each and every one of these major themes.

– *Akira* is the one almost all of these narrative questions about “being happy” are directly addressed to, to a much greater extent than literally any other character in the game: “whether what you seek will actually bring you happiness”, “whether you’re prepared to deal with the consequences of trying to be happy”, “whether it is worth it to cross the moral/legal line to get what you want” – these are *all* about him, first and foremost.

– *Akira* is the one who most strongly embodies the conflict of “nature vs nurture”, both having experienced the (arguably) harshest level/amount of trauma among anyone else in Kumon-mi (Saki + Nozomu + Sekai is an *insane* fucking combo to live through – Io, Yumi and Yasu got off easy compared to him, though their circumstances are also nothing to sneeze at) while also being one of the most realistically depraved and disgusting characters I’ve ever seen in fiction, due to *a lot* more than just the environment he grew up in.

– *Akira* is the one who most frequently waxes poetic about the nature of love and its various forms: familial (parental, sisterly, brotherly, filial in general), romantical, sexual, unconditional, fake, pure, toxic – another main theme of the game.

– *Akira* is the one who overall serves as our “window” into the world of Lessons in Love and connects all of its varied aspects by the sheer virtue of his own existence: “meta” elements of the story, slice of life scenes, interpersonal drama, erotica, comedy, philosophical musings – all of them primarily flow through him, with Akira being the general focus of the decent 60% events in the entire game (especially the first three Chapters). Not to mention how throughout the entire story he also constantly colors our perspective on people, events and concepts by expressing his own (personal and biased) opinions about them, the effectiveness of which varies based on how much you *already* share Akira’s cynical and depressing worldview (which becomes much easier when you personally understand where he is coming from, having experience with using the same deflections and self-justifications Sensei repeatedly resorts to).

– And, finally (and not that importantly in the grand scheme of things, but I still felt like mentioning it here nonetheless), there is also a certain realization that I already brought up in one of my earliest posts: the fact that Sensei’s callous behavior and extremely detached, almost mechanical approach he had towards girls in early Chapter 1, treating them less like actual people and more like targets to be conquered, almost perfectly matches with an “honest” mindset of an average male eroge player, who only cares about female characters in the games he plays in terms of obtaining their CGs – something that from the very beginning is meant to quickly establish a deliberate (if surface-level) connection between Akira, the protagonist, and you, the reader, because I would assume that most people who stumbled upon Lessons in Love already had a pretty decent familiarity with the “date sim” genre and various character/narrative tropes it constantly employs, which is exactly the same thing Selebus counted on when writing Chapter 1 of LiL.

So, yeah, I hope that answers your question of why I so strongly fixated on him in my original theory/analysis: because from my perspective, the difference between “being able to personally relate to Akira” and “being unable to do that” is fucking *astronomical*, and no other character in the game even comes close to being on the same level of narrative complexity and thematical importance as him. There is nothing wrong with only really relating to other characters that are *not* Akira, like Io, Ayane, Rin or anyone else – I love them too, *a lot* – but, once again, at that point it is almost a completely different experience.

spoilers.title: Why the central focus on Sensei?
spoilers.html:
Well, the answer to that is quite simple, actually: it’s because, regardless of the size/quality of the rest of its cast, Akira is still the main (and only) protagonist of Lessons in Love – and that title is not something that I take lightly.

Traditional theory of storytelling dictates that – provided the author knows that they’re doing (which Selebus 100% is, in my opinion) and that they didn’t employ any particular twists or subversions related to this topic (like multiple parallel protagonists, protagonist switch, etcetera – which, since we are now 150+ hours into the game, I would say *extremely* unlikely) – a character being selected as “the protagonist of a story” carries a very clear, very specific implication of their basically uncontested level of thematic and narrative significance within said story, in addition to the unwritten promise (from the author to the audience) that they are going to be *continually upheld* to that status throughout their entire narrative journey.

The only real exception to that is the modern “self-insert” approach that, sadly, plagues many stories that were created in the last few decades (not to be confused with the “audience surrogate” trope, like Dr. Watson in the Sherlock Holmes novels), but aside from those fucking narrative abominations it is practically a given that the protagonist of a story is going to be extremely important to its every major theme and plot beat that happens within it, because they were *specifically* selected for that very purpose – if there was a different character better suited for that role, *they* would have been chosen as the protagonist instead.

So just because Lessons in Love has 35+ other extremely well-written characters, each of whom also directly ties into the overarching narrative/themes in some way and can potentially be personally relatable to you, or me, or anyone else (which is just how stories are normally supposed to work: it’s not exactly some unique crowning achievement special to LiL), their individual contributions to the grand thematical canvas, comprised of all of the main ideas/concepts the story is interested in exploring, completely pale in comparison to Akira’s lion’s share of the same exact canvas – Akira, who consistently serves as a focal point for each and every one of these major themes.

– *Akira* is the one almost all of these narrative questions about “being happy” are directly addressed to, to a much greater extent than literally any other character in the game: “whether what you seek will actually bring you happiness”, “whether you’re prepared to deal with the consequences of trying to be happy”, “whether it is worth it to cross the moral/legal line to get what you want” – these are *all* about him, first and foremost.

– *Akira* is the one who most strongly embodies the conflict of “nature vs nurture”, both having experienced the (arguably) harshest level/amount of trauma among anyone else in Kumon-mi (Saki + Nozomu + Sekai is an *insane* fucking combo to live through – Io, Yumi and Yasu got off easy compared to him, though their circumstances are also nothing to sneeze at) while also being one of the most realistically depraved and disgusting characters I’ve ever seen in fiction, due to *a lot* more than just the environment he grew up in.

– *Akira* is the one who most frequently waxes poetic about the nature of love and its various forms: familial (parental, sisterly, brotherly, filial in general), romantical, sexual, unconditional, fake, pure, toxic – another main theme of the game.

– *Akira* is the one who overall serves as our “window” into the world of Lessons in Love and connects all of its varied aspects by the sheer virtue of his own existence: “meta” elements of the story, slice of life scenes, interpersonal drama, erotica, comedy, philosophical musings – all of them primarily flow through him, with Akira being the general focus of the decent 60% events in the entire game (especially the first three Chapters). Not to mention how throughout the entire story he also constantly colors our perspective on people, events and concepts by expressing his own (personal and biased) opinions about them, the effectiveness of which varies based on how much you *already* share Akira’s cynical and depressing worldview (which becomes much easier when you personally understand where he is coming from, having experience with using the same deflections and self-justifications Sensei repeatedly resorts to).

– And, finally (and not that importantly in the grand scheme of things, but I still felt like mentioning it here nonetheless), there is also a certain realization that I already brought up in one of my earliest posts: the fact that Sensei’s callous behavior and extremely detached, almost mechanical approach he had towards girls in early Chapter 1, treating them less like actual people and more like targets to be conquered, almost perfectly matches with an “honest” mindset of an average male eroge player, who only cares about female characters in the games he plays in terms of obtaining their CGs – something that from the very beginning is meant to quickly establish a deliberate (if surface-level) connection between Akira, the protagonist, and you, the reader, because I would assume that most people who stumbled upon Lessons in Love already had a pretty decent familiarity with the “date sim” genre and various character/narrative tropes it constantly employs, which is exactly the same thing Selebus counted on when writing Chapter 1 of LiL.

So, yeah, I hope that answers your question of why I so strongly fixated on him in my original theory/analysis: because from my perspective, the difference between “being able to personally relate to Akira” and “being unable to do that” is fucking *astronomical*, and no other character in the game even comes close to being on the same level of narrative complexity and thematical importance as him. There is nothing wrong with only really relating to other characters that are *not* Akira, like Io, Ayane, Rin or anyone else – I love them too, *a lot* – but, once again, at that point it is almost a completely different experience.

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Thank you once again for your detailed thoughts. I already clarified some of my original goals/intentions in my reply to SlidingSubject (which you seemingly disagreed with, but that's okay), so I won’t repeat them here. Aside from that, I mostly agree with all of your counterarguments, and the few ones I *do* fundamentally disagree with are worded in a way where I can still fully understand where you’re coming from (which means that it’s all good). So the only real point that still needs clarification is why I decided to specifically focus on Akira – when, as we both pointed out, LiL is so much bigger than just him:

Well, the answer to that is quite simple, actually: it’s because, regardless of the size/quality of the rest of its cast, Akira is still the main (and only) protagonist of Lessons in Love – and that title is not something that I take lightly.

Traditional theory of storytelling dictates that – provided the author knows that they’re doing (which Selebus 100% is, in my opinion) and that they didn’t employ any particular twists or subversions related to this topic (like multiple parallel protagonists, protagonist switch, etcetera – which, since we are now 150+ hours into the game, I would say *extremely* unlikely) – a character being selected as “the protagonist of a story” carries a very clear, very specific implication of their basically uncontested level of thematic and narrative significance within said story, in addition to the unwritten promise (from the author to the audience) that they are going to be *continually upheld* to that status throughout their entire narrative journey.

The only real exception to that is the modern “self-insert” approach that, sadly, plagues many stories that were created in the last few decades (not to be confused with the “audience surrogate” trope, like Dr. Watson in the Sherlock Holmes novels), but aside from those fucking narrative abominations it is practically a given that the protagonist of a story is going to be extremely important to its every major theme and plot beat that happens within it, because they were *specifically* selected for that very purpose – if there was a different character better suited for that role, *they* would have been chosen as the protagonist instead.

So just because Lessons in Love has 35+ other extremely well-written characters, each of whom also directly ties into the overarching narrative/themes in some way and can potentially be personally relatable to you, or me, or anyone else (which is just how stories are normally supposed to work: it’s not exactly some unique crowning achievement special to LiL), their individual contributions to the grand thematical canvas, comprised of all of the main ideas/concepts the story is interested in exploring, completely pale in comparison to Akira’s lion’s share of the same exact canvas – Akira, who consistently serves as a focal point for each and every one of these major themes.

– *Akira* is the one almost all of these narrative questions about “being happy” are directly addressed to, to a much greater extent than literally any other character in the game: “whether what you seek will actually bring you happiness”, “whether you’re prepared to deal with the consequences of trying to be happy”, “whether it is worth it to cross the moral/legal line to get what you want” – these are *all* about him, first and foremost.

– *Akira* is the one who most strongly embodies the conflict of “nature vs nurture”, both having experienced the (arguably) harshest level/amount of trauma among anyone else in Kumon-mi (Saki + Nozomu + Sekai is an *insane* fucking combo to live through – Io, Yumi and Yasu got off easy compared to him, though their circumstances are also nothing to sneeze at) while also being one of the most realistically depraved and disgusting characters I’ve ever seen in fiction, due to *a lot* more than just the environment he grew up in.

– *Akira* is the one who most frequently waxes poetic about the nature of love and its various forms: familial (parental, sisterly, brotherly, filial in general), romantical, sexual, unconditional, fake, pure, toxic – another main theme of the game.

– *Akira* is the one who overall serves as our “window” into the world of Lessons in Love and connects all of its varied aspects by the sheer virtue of his own existence: “meta” elements of the story, slice of life scenes, interpersonal drama, erotica, comedy, philosophical musings – all of them primarily flow through him, with Akira being the general focus of the decent 60% events in the entire game (especially the first three Chapters). Not to mention how throughout the entire story he also constantly colors our perspective on people, events and concepts by expressing his own (personal and biased) opinions about them, the effectiveness of which varies based on how much you *already* share Akira’s cynical and depressing worldview (which becomes much easier when you personally understand where he is coming from, having experience with using the same deflections and self-justifications Sensei repeatedly resorts to).

– And, finally (and not that importantly in the grand scheme of things, but I still felt like mentioning it here nonetheless), there is also a certain realization that I already brought up in one of my earliest posts: the fact that Sensei’s callous behavior and extremely detached, almost mechanical approach he had towards girls in early Chapter 1, treating them less like actual people and more like targets to be conquered, almost perfectly matches with an “honest” mindset of an average male eroge player, who only cares about female characters in the games he plays in terms of obtaining their CGs – something that from the very beginning is meant to quickly establish a deliberate (if surface-level) connection between Akira, the protagonist, and you, the reader, because I would assume that most people who stumbled upon Lessons in Love already had a pretty decent familiarity with the “date sim” genre and various character/narrative tropes it constantly employs, which is exactly the same thing Selebus counted on when writing Chapter 1 of LiL.

So, yeah, I hope that answers your question of why I so strongly fixated on him in my original theory/analysis: because from my perspective, the difference between “being able to personally relate to Akira” and “being unable to do that” is fucking *astronomical*, and no other character in the game even comes close to being on the same level of narrative complexity and thematical importance as him. There is nothing wrong with only really relating to other characters that are *not* Akira, like Io, Ayane, Rin or anyone else – I love them too, *a lot* – but, once again, at that point it is almost a completely different experience.

– And, finally (and not that importantly in the grand scheme of things, but I still felt like mentioning it here nonetheless), there is also a certain realization that I already brought up in one of my earliest posts: the fact that Sensei’s callous behavior and extremely detached, almost mechanical approach he had towards girls in early Chapter 1, treating them less like actual people and more like targets to be conquered, almost perfectly matches with an “honest” mindset of an average male eroge player, who only cares about female characters in the games he plays in terms of obtaining their CGs – something that from the very beginning is meant to quickly establish a deliberate (if surface-level) connection between Akira, the protagonist, and you, the reader, because I would assume that most people who stumbled upon Lessons in Love already had a pretty decent familiarity with the “date sim” genre and various character/narrative tropes it constantly employs, which is exactly the same thing Selebus counted on when writing Chapter 1 of LiL.
So, yeah, I hope that answers your question of why I so strongly fixated on him in my original theory/analysis: because from my perspective, the difference between “being able to personally relate to Akira” and “being unable to do that” is fucking *astronomical*, and no other character in the game even comes close to being on the same level of narrative complexity and thematical importance as him. There is nothing wrong with only really relating to other characters that are *not* Akira, like Io, Ayane, Rin or anyone else – I love them too, *a lot* – but, once again, at that point it is almost a completely different experience.

As much as we all rag on Selebus; The man does deliver, most often on time, and they all seem to have roughly the same amount(Or more!) of content. So many people abandon their games, even when being paid for it. He clearly treats this as his full time job, which I appreciate. Some content creators make it to the point where they can quit their main job...and don't move to making their creative content as their full time job.

If we assume that he wrote the 55k words from the last update, till now...that's the length of the average science fiction novel. Every month. For years.

I'm an author; that shit is hard! At the height of my popularity, I was lucky to manage 15k words a month. I wasn't being paid nearly as much, never enough to replace my full time job, but even then I don't think I could have pulled another 40k words to save my life. That's simply ALOT of writing.

Fahrenheit 451: 46k words
Slaughterhouse-Five: 50k words
The Martian: 105k words

The guy is simply VERY productive, and I do appreciate that. If I have to wait a month for my next fix, I need it to be worth it.

Click to expand...
I agree, I have said it before but as much as we guys hate on him, he is reliable. He is certainly no George R.R. Martin of the degenerate visual novels, to put it that way

The comparison with other (actual) novels is interesting, but of course you can't really compare these works to something like this.
I just recently re-read Slaughterhouse Five and the truth is that it is not the longest book in the world (but as you mentioned, many famous book are of that length), however, they still manage to tell a whole story. They are concise, the authors carefully choose which topics to cover and how deep to go into the story.
Funnily enough, exactly in this book the author openly states that he intended a much longer book more closely following the war, but ended up just writing his experiences into a sci-fi novel that left out a lot, intentionally.

What I'm trying to say is that a classic book that is published and sold in book stores goes through a completely different completion process. It gets rewritten, changed completely, revised by an editor, restructured, etc. until the finished product is (ideally) in perfect shape.
A typical VN can't do that. Maybe Sel would want to (though I have my doubts), maybe the product would be amazing if he just sat down 5 years and trimmed the whole plot down to a single story from start to finish. But that doesn't pay his bills.
The way these types of games work is that you publish update after update. And if the author does decide to change it halfway through (which occasionally happens, you might know some example) the customers provide a shitstorm and his financial backing is in danger. So obviously most people just stick by it and ride it through. Some even blatantly milk it. Don't hate the player, hate the game, I guess.
Which, again, also highlights how much better he is at delivering good and rich content on a regular basis compared to many, many other developers.

Tl:dr: Yes it's impressive, but to some extent, it's just the nature of the medium.

The comparison with other (actual) novels is interesting, but of course you can't really compare these works to something like this.
I just recently re-read Slaughterhouse Five and the truth is that it is not the longest book in the world (but as you mentioned, many famous book are of that length), however, they still manage to tell a whole story. They are concise, the authors carefully choose which topics to cover and how deep to go into the story.
Funnily enough, exactly in this book the author openly states that he intended a much longer book more closely following the war, but ended up just writing his experiences into a sci-fi novel that left out a lot, intentionally.
What I'm trying to say is that a classic book that is published and sold in book stores goes through a completely different completion process. It gets rewritten, changed completely, revised by an editor, restructured, etc. until the finished product is (ideally) in perfect shape.
A typical VN can't do that. Maybe Sel would want to (though I have my doubts), maybe the product would be amazing if he just sat down 5 years and trimmed the whole plot down to a single story from start to finish. But that doesn't pay his bills.
The way these types of games work is that you publish update after update. And if the author does decide to change it halfway through (which occasionally happens, you might know some example) the customers provide a shitstorm and his financial backing is in danger. So obviously most people just stick by it and ride it through. Some even blatantly milk it. Don't hate the player, hate the game, I guess.
Which, again, also highlights how much better he is at delivering good and rich content on a regular basis compared to many, many other developers.
Tl:dr: Yes it's impressive, but to some extent, it's just the nature of the medium.

Alright I finally sat down and read the update v0.54 and wow its um well its something. Here is my immediate thoughts for anyone interested.

Idgaf about Chika, I was so bored reading her stuff. I dont know when it happened because I used to really like her character but man she's just a bore. Honestly she might be a victim of the general tone shift of Lil in the recent chapters, focusing more about timey fucky and wacky godly hijinks. A terrible description but it gets my general frustrations out.

Kirin, boo fucking hoo. I mean that sucks yeah, but her character is also a bit of a meh for me. The scene is the symposium being an allegory for how some girls must feel about being pressured to perform (while literally being pressured to perform) is a bit on the nose. Good but meh

Maya is just the best character of the main cast. There was a time I didn't see it, like she was always top 5 for sure. However the more updates that come out the more I realize this game is just made for her.

Haruka haruka haruka, no plot armor for you. Her story and the consequences of what she did I hope is further explored sooner rather than later. Its the natural progression of her character (if you pick that route) but depending on how Selebus chooses to continue could be either interesting or just bad.

Nadoka update. Its fine. I like her character but she's just... A plot device? Idk just like she feels like nothing. I think her talking about her feeling a bit more is a step in the right direction but then its just shoved to the side. Guess that's fitting bc its what Akira literally does when she wants to talk but its a bit disappointing. I think she could be more interesting outside of T23 related stuff. I mean one of my favorite scenes is when she talks about a world without color, or when she was talking about the moat. As a matter of fact her best scenes are when she ISNT involved in T23 stuff (for me at least)

Not enough to write about these girls so speed run
Yasu - Great you got screen time. Oh its kinda interesting your character is progressing? Oh and shes gone. Bye Yasu.
Maki - I get your point but why are you making it? Context just ruins her point.
Futaba - Oh and we're just gonna hand wave Futabas parents... ok. Futaba you're gonna let Otaha stop you from helping your friend... ok. Futaba are you gonna do anything ever... ok.
NO TOUKA MEANS F TIER UPDATE jk

Coming off the back of what may the best update (in isolation) is hard to do. This one is fine?

I might write another time to get other peoples thoughts on it as I have yet to gather properly my own thoughts about this topic.
At this point I think the length of the VN may be doing it a disservice. What I believe is a strength may also be its biggest flaw. Its hard to describe but the thing that drew me in was the character work and as more time passes it feels like its degrading or the payoffs are maybe too far between. Like we get good development for a character then its kicked like a can down the street to be picked up and kicked again half a year later OR LONGER. This is only the surface level of my feelings on it though.

No. It's only similar in the way that it happens in a school and there are supernatural elements. The story of Crimson High is that you're an actual investigator, with connections to the police, trying to uncover a murder in a highschool.

This develops into a harem of supernatural girls from all over, kind of like mythic manor, but with way more "myths". "Crimson" High comes from the center of the plot being about vampires but, again, there's all sorts of girls. My favorites are catgirls (obviously) and Okami (wolf girl).

The story is mostly lighthearted, there isn't that much sex, and the plot varies from mid to really bad (but those are rare moments). I recommend giving it a try if there's nothing to do, but it's not that good that I'd rate it high on the recommendation list. Definitely better than any LiL clones though.

I know it's been a while, but first, there are too many spoilers in the thread, so I'm avoiding it until I finish current content. Accidentaly learned about Molly rape and Ayane "pregnancy", when I was looking for totally something else. Secondly, I'm on the beginning of third chapter and there wasn't anything I could consider as something worse than in other porn games. Yeah, MC is a scumbag who in real world would be one of the worst kind of people, even if we take aside age of LIs*, but for now, storywise thing that I hate mostly is... changing Rins hair

*If we don't, he'd be gangraped in prison for being ch**d rapist. I mean, in my country it's an age of consent, but yeah, he'd be gangraped in prison.

The story is interesting, not into my taste, if it comes to settings (had hope to learn more about space war and having it more storywise instead of being just something convenient), but I like it. Wish only that MC try to find and fight a lil bit more against his blacking out. Dialogues and relationships buiilding are one of best I've met and even after over 80hrs of playing I'm not bored with LIs. There are many technical flaws like lack of animations in non repeatable events or poor sandbox desing, but writing and reading experience is very high.

About reactions you mentioned... I'm kind of tired of depressing inside monologues and TBH I'm reading only 1/3 of words, when it comes to them. He's losing connection either to server or reality and for now game suggests he's one of the users that plays this protagonist. I kinda hate it there's no kind of minigame that let us fight over control of his body and let us fight more actively. I usually prefer when games don't have many choices with huge branches, but I'd love it here, if we could chose to play good or bad path. Also I've feeling that at the end MC will wake up in a "room without handles" or it's all going to only be a Maya dream after MCs suicide.

Btw. Huge thanks to everyone who convinced me to play with Guide mod

Edit:

Btw2: I still don't regret changing MCs name

Finally we get a missable scene as a result of Stomachache-skip. This should theoretically solidify Green path as the canon and optimal route hands down since we actually get some sexual progress, no? I'm still not convinced that there isn't significant narrative weight and intent behind Stomachache skip however...

Especially considering how the events that happen in its route are specifically mentioned and alluded to in Green path, as well as an interesting question about choosing the route and which one would technically be "better."



Meanwhile in Red path aka Stomachache-skip, you miss her trying to grow (like has been discussed before), but it's very significant that she does appear...genuinely happy and enamored in red path. Which is odd, because that is fairly atypical for red path.




Even in Red path, there is still some sort of growth happening albeit more idealistic instead of realistic. It's just that her past physical trauma isn't being dealt with directly as it is in Green path. But that harkens back to the monologue before about which answer really IS the right one? It certainly does seem like for the first time, Green path is the noticeable winner for Io here, but I still can't shake the question in the back of my mind asking, "is this really the best for her?" Either way, I love how interestingly Selebus keeping both options in mind and am looking forward to seeing how it plays it out for her character (even if it does end up in tragedy or disappointment on either side.)

Finally, a very interesting point between the two routes: In Red path (Stomachache-skip) Io gains MORE affection (+5) compared to Green path (only +2)

posts.content_html_raw:
Kirin's (VII)
Her TSS is so lightheartedly comical that it's actually difficult to put my finger on it.

Because of the presence of Maya(s) and her recent death at the time, the first two TSSs give us a feeling that we are peeking into something neither we or our girls are supposed to. However, that feeling dwindles as more TSSs come out and the feeling gradually shifts to merely addressing each girl's recent burden in an incomprehensibly surreal way, and that's it. Maybe this is more about expressionism and less about being a viable digging spot for lore.

This unexciting feeling peaks when it's Kirin's turn because, to me, her TSS cements the idea that all TSSs are merely divine solicitations (in true weeb sense, 勧誘) particularly but perhaps not limited to lesser gods. A concept introduced by Himawari, and vaguely represented by all these TSSs. In other words, TSSs aren't temporary dimensional tears where you get a glimpse at any sweet secret. Instead, TSSs represent gods outside of our dimensions having fun with residents inside Kumon-mi that is their ant farm, fish tank, or cell culture petri dish; all TSSs are like that, and especially TSS7 with seemingly a sole focus that is reemphasizing this part of the world building. We either see gods in actions, or the aftermaths after gods having their ways with a certain somebody. I suspect most TSSs are the former and I suspect Noriko's TSS being the latter as TSS1 is still quite unique with it being the only one that isn't really tied to Noriko herself. Although I'd still have no solid idea why some girls are "not required to attend TSS" if this interpretation is correct. Would it because any solicitation from any divine party at the moment is not allowed? not effective? or is this line of thought completely wrong?

Rin's (VIII)
Her TSS is back to the exciting side for obvious reasons. For one, we get to see Maya again (and I'm glad that Rin recognizes her due to perv power). More importantly, we also get to see what I can only surmise as " the result of a version of Rin that caved to a HOPE's solicitation" and this is a potential support to my current interpretation of TSSs: we see our Rin facing a lesser god's temptation and we see an unfortunate version of her that loses to HOPE's temptation. And by extension, this might be an indirect confirmation of the culprit that took away Maya Prime, who has tormented "several types" of Maya but thankfully has not taken interest in our Rin yet. Perhaps what we are seeing here is the beginning of Maya, although being visually fuzzy and speaking in hex but with tones and actual name familiar to us, turning into amiokay as she rots in the room of clock and under HOPE's influence.

Yeah, it's hard to justify her (lack of) actions. As far as consequences go (or, again, lack of) it pretty much mirrors Niki after her whole "being NTR'd by my sister" thing in terms of consequences and it's already looking like both are headed the same way. We've already seen Sara allow herself to be gaslit into acceptance too so it's easy to imagine things winding up similarly for Maki.

But with Niki and Sara even if their reactions were disappointing to a degree there's at least a logic to them from their POV - Niki's bogged down by her history with Akira and Sara's bogged down by her upbringing, by being groomed herself and by being mind-raped by divine beings, all of which her daughter takes advantage of in order to manipulate her. They both have very warped perspectives on the situation to begin with so it makes sense that they would be hesitant to take any real action.

Maki's just got a smart daughter and some self doubt, though. She obviously goes about the initial confrontation in a bizarre way so she's not totally on point lol but she recognises everything going on around her, the fact that she's not the one being weird and the fact that she's been and is being gaslit by everyone around her.

And even her self-loathing doubts only account for half the equation because they're entirely focused on Makoto. Like yeah, sure, "Makoto's mature and I'm a bad mom and bla bla bla" but none of that applies to her all-but-adopted daughter Miku who, if you want to be as generous as you possibly can, is borderline retarded. Her knowledge of and perception of sex stems entirely from being groomed by Akira and the first major step of that process was him full-on molesting her at a point in the story where she was less capable of informed consent than Todd. There are multiple birds in the story more intelligent than Miku, there's no salient argument for her knowing what's best for herself in this situation.

I don't follow the same train of thought some seem to here that 'no death = no consequence' so I haven't felt that a lack of consequence has been too big an issue of the story so far but yeah, there needs to at least be some logical reason why she would decide not to take action.

posts.content_html_raw:
Holy hell another good update, we got a streak goin. Banger after banger event. Rika and Maki easy stars, with Maki's confrontations being everything you could have hoped for. Not much in the way of main plot advancement, but we get a ton of character drama.

Rika - What a slew of great lines. Lesbian puns are funny. Holes within Holes within Holes. She is so much fun, just a chaotic ball energy. Future Rinoyakudon is confirmed in the best way possible.

Imani - Her plan with Rika was hilarious failing right off the bat. The rising tide of "awareness" regarding Akira's preferences is raising all ships. Including the ones that happen in gym showers.

Osako - What an absolute gut punch. We go right from joyous poetry to THE fork in the road for them as a couple. I'm terrified that Wakana's "Oh" implies how its going to end, especially given what Ayane was about to say in the dorms. Or maybe getting Wakana to agree is the catalyst to Osaka's confidence finally growing? It would be quite an accomplishment, and took a TON of bravery to say in the moment. Its nice seeing her get some meaningful depth from her start as Karate Lady.

Ayane - Good to see a little progress on the melancholic sadness. She might be unfortunately right regarding the Osako/Wakana kids situation. It wouldn't be the first in relationship history to end on that note. I don't think we'll get much Ayane for a good long while after .53 and Yasu's unlucky reminder, she's got some recovering to do.

Touka - Momma Mia she is getting aggressive. Hand holding? Without receiving explicit consent? Goodness me. Even Yasu was scandalized.

We get pretty much a full outline of Tsubasa's plan as far as what literally needs to happen, but we don't know that crucial why. Maybe even beyond the marriage problem, are Yasu's ramblings about receiving Akira's "light" are true? Maybe to save them from the world/Hope that needs to happen? Not sure.

Also her first time absolutely should be up against a vending machine. Future call backs would be hilarious.

Maki -Fucking Brutal. Personally I loved everything about it. There could not have been a more on the nose way to immediately put Akira in the vice. His terrified face said it all, going into mind-numbing panic mode. Makoto then comes in with fucking haymakers, god she can be such a great bitch.

Miku's desperate lie doesn't work for even a moment, as Maki later tells Akira. In fact, it probably second-hand confirmed everything being way worse then Maki feared. Even when Maki directly confronts at the apt, Akira finds a way to weasel out of it. He chooses not to answer, but that is an answer too. Maki doesn't literally hear it, but she acknowledges it as obvious.

The stakes for this bomb are not literal in that the police were ever gonna be involved. Its gonna be pure relationship effects. Maki may not have been a great mother figure, but she does care and try. We do see that it seems to cut Sensei to the bone, as even his soft attempt at apology is violently rejected. So obviously he immediately calls Makoto over after Maki leaves. Way to take back that control Akira.

The next time we see Maki and Makoto it'll be matter of factly haymakers rather than the screaming ones we saw this time. Maki's gonna get even more depressed when Sara eventually tries to comfort her with a "Hey so now we have something in common". Maki really will be Gone for a while. Poor Maki.

Io - Some great comfort development for Green Path Io. Her "You already have" line was one of my favorites. I think the bath scene shows support for the Green path in that we're seeing growth from Io. She doesn't get a stomachache from some pretty overt sexual acts, and she even allows Makoto to join them on a future expedition! Go Io!

The great big hole scene was creepy, but I don't think there's any more immediate relevance beyond it being the "edge of the world" or something like that. Is her "Mother?" line literal or more metaphoric in that capacity? IDK.

Rin - Well that was weird. Chika escapades aside, her TSS opens up some questions. Is that a previous version of Rin that succumbed to whatever temptation Hope offered? I think its hinted that Rin's birth mom may have been another of Nozomu's victims. We don't get much in the way of concrete evidence.

On a side note, Rin's ability to instantly realize things is always awesome. She's actually very clear headed and emotionally intelligent in that way. Her mom beating her to the Akira punch was a great gafaw.

Chika - Our ignorant slut is not yet back to normal but much more normal then before. Also she deserved some of that emotional terrorism from Rin. Not a good homie move by Rin but a justified one.

All in all it wasn't up to the level of 53 but I'd say a good 8.5/10. I really enjoyed it, starting off with the funny before hitting with the feels later.

Welp... I made the latest update and... oh damn, why so much humor? Okay, I might be ultra bitter, but god. Such a concentration of humor has annoy me. Maybe not annoy, it's a bit harsh, but... I don't know? Anyway, especially while, next to it, there were some frankly interesting things.

Anyhow, get ready, the reading will probably be long (as always) :

First, I'm going to eliminate the worst of all, Rika.
Just... why? Okay, she's «simple», I get that... but was it necessary to mark it explicitly?


Because it's... crude. And to tell you the truth, I started the update with that scene... if it was the only one, I'm not saying, but it accumulates!
Let's take this, for example :
My first thought was: set a trap? tail him? put a spyware in the girl's phone to see everything she says and does?
But since humor was the point :
And when I say humor, it's not so much about the number of stupid things said, but about the montage itself. I really felt like there was continuous slapstick humor.


But, on the subject of humor, that, that made me smile:
Because yes, Rika, it's literally your whole character. You exist and that's all!


Well, for Io now.
She really threw me off, but in the good sense of the term. Less humor, already (finally!), and above all... a huge evolution! Thank you!

There's the moment where Sensei explains he doesn't want to become the predator and risk to wound her, and Io responds with this :

I... I have nothing to add. It was both fair and violent. And I am largely disappointed that this sentence was quickly replaced by this :

Io... stop sending atomic bombs at my face, I'll end up liking y...
Well... uh... the rest? Yes, the rest.


The case of Maki, then. And it's even more frustrating because I know it won't involve anything. Because she knows now. And, I hope she also understood for Miku, but I don't have much fate about that.

However, during the whole confrontation scene (after watching the weird porn movie and Makoto arriving), Selebus finally turned Sensei into a manipulator and a bad guy. Thanks. Well, it destroys the empathy I could have had for the character, which is none, but at least it's set : Sensei is an asshole.

So, thank you Maki. Even if nothing gonna really change.
See you in 2-3 updates!


Osako, now. And I'm going to thank her for this:
Because, good God, it feels good. Even if I know it won't change anything (do I need to express my frustration?).

Also, the meal with Wakana... I don't know if it was well written, if it was cliché or if I'm just a big jerk who likes chaos, but... I'll give you the scene as I had it in my head:

- She's going to refuse...

- She will refuse so hard.

- Wakana, you're screwed...

- Wakana, stop with your monologue, it's dead!

- I told you.

However, the "I want children" bit, though expected (the discussion with Ayane was going to lead to this), surprised me a little. Anyway. The result is the same. Wakana is bisexual, so she'll join the harem. And Osako was an obstacle, so Selebus get rid of her.


Now, Touka!
So, she starts in a creepy way:
Okay, she's a teenager, but damn, what are these manners? By the way, thanks for reminding us of Sensei's apartment, I was afraid Selebus had forgotten it.

Also, uh... so much erotism, I can't resist:

Just kidding, but there was this dialogue that really disturbed me:
I... I'm not sure I like the innuendo behind this comparison. However, and it's clear and straightforward, Touka is just as weird as her mother.

Okay? What should I conclude? That all those that go into the TSS are replaced because they deviated from their archetypes?

Moonflare said:
Maybe I'll be back to talk in depth about the update, but for now I'd just like to comment a bit on a problem I've been having:
I don't know if anyone will be able to relate to me on this, but I just find the entire Maki situation kind of pointless?

Selebus created this world that is ever-repeating, and then confirmed to us that the entire thing is a wish from Maya, who's also a wish (from Akira), and that created this entire world for him.

Furthermore, Akira knows this. Himawari didn't take that knowledge away. And then you have an entire update more or less focused on "we're a bunch of adults that have a predator friend", and I'm like...

So? None of this matters. What are you going to do? go to the police? Hah, good luck with that. Kill him? Kill yourself? There's absolutely no stakes whatsoever in all of this discussion.
I'm not saying this kills the story, it's not like I'm rolling my eyes at the screen... but this specific part of the plot is also not doing it for me. I can't get really invested with a "problem" that isn't a problem at all from the lack of any actual possible consequences.

Maki will be away for a while, and that's really all that could have possibly happened. Does anyone care? Akira clearly doesn't and neither do I.
Click to expand...
I think what you’re describing *is* the point of that scene – or, well, maybe not the entire point, but definitely a significant part of it – because LiL has always been about this strange mix of extremely realistic scenarios juxtaposed against extremely unrealistic ones (which is a separate topic that I’m currently writing an entire mega-essay about, but that’ll have to wait for at least a week), and the underlying “meaninglessness” of it all is something that is always looming in the background, casting its shadow onto how everything else in the game is perceived.

Kumon-mi is, fundamentally, a place that denies change; an eternal playground that resists progress, ignores accountability and laughs in the face of meaningful consequences. It’s heaven on earth if you just want to live your life however you want and fully indulge in all your depraved desires, laws and morals be damned, but the actual *worst* place to be if you care about personal growth or “trying to do the right thing”. Because while the ants in the ant farm might *believe* that their actions have meaning, that they’re doing something of actual value, we – the ones holding the ant farm, occasionally shaking it up for our own amusement – know just how pointless and ephemeral the notion of “progress” really is.

This is what that makes the story of Lessons in Love so unique and interesting: it’s not *just* a bunch of inter-personal drama about various characters trying to achieve happiness and deal with their deep-rooted issues and traumas, but *also* a “man vs world” situation, in which the universe itself directly conspires to prevent any of it from happening – they are effectively playing against the House, and the House, unfortunately, always wins.

Because while the ants in the ant farm might *believe* that their actions have meaning, that they’re doing something of actual value, we – the ones holding the ant farm, occasionally shaking it up for our own amusement – know just how pointless and ephemeral the notion of “progress” really is.
This is what that makes the story of Lessons in Love so unique and interesting: it’s not *just* a bunch of inter-personal drama about various characters trying to achieve happiness and deal with their deep-rooted issues and traumas, but *also* a “man vs world” situation, in which the universe itself directly conspires to prevent any of it from happening – they are effectively playing against the House, and the House, unfortunately, always wins.
So whenever Akira – or anyone else – tries to apply “real world” logic/morals to the current situation and approach it in a way that is congruent with how things *should* work IRL – which normally results in drastic, irreversible consequences – they are *immediately* hit with the ever-looping nature of Kumon-mi, or divine interference, or some other very convenient excuse/justification that absolves them of most of their sins and severely muddles the waters. It repeatedly hammers in the idea that choosing to draw one-to-one parallels between certain events/characters in LiL and their real-life equivalents is an exercise in futility, as the absurdist/surreal nature of the narrative ensures that it will *never* work – you inherently aren’t supposed to do this. Because, yeah, 10/10 explanations such as “your honor, God made me do it” and “I know she physically looks fifteen, but her mental age is much greater than that” wouldn’t ever fly in a real-life court of law, yet both of these things *have been* undeniably confirmed as true in the context of Lessons in Love – which, in turn, begs the obvious question of *why* is it written in such a way, if not to deliberately criticize/comment on the very real dark things that happen all over the world?
The answer to that question lies in what I already mentioned earlier in this post: the “man vs world” part. It’s to make the characters perpetually doubt themselves; to place as many potential roadblocks in front of them and hinder their path to progress – roadblocks that will either push these characters towards regressing back to their original state, or at the very least force them to run in circles rather than actually moving forward. Unfortunately, only a few select people (Akira, mostly, and I guess also Maya Prime) are explicitly aware that this is happening, while everyone else is mostly kept in the dark: exempt from the depressing realization about the meaninglessness of their aspirations towards self-improvement, but *not* exempt from being affected by the same pushback force.
Spoiler:
Conclusion
Thus, Maki’s situation – as well the situations of Sara, or Niki, or all of the other members of the cast who are similarly stuck in the “narrative limbo” – makes perfect sense to me personally, because they all can be explained with the very same thing: this ever-present… mental compulsion, I guess you could call it, that Kumon-mi exerts on every single one of its inhabitants, inhibiting all of their attempts to intentionally disturb the status quo. It functions the same way as Akira’s unnatural charisma that compels all of the women around Sensei to treat him favorably and eventually fall in love with him – something that even he himself does not properly understand and repeatedly calls out, finding it to be a cruel curse masquerading as a blessing. Both of these things act like baseline “laws of reality” that dictate the main lines of thought and behavior all of the characters follow and cannot deviate from: they *will* come to like Akira, one way or another, just as they *will* participate in maintaining the status quo, regardless of their personal feelings on the matter.
So Maki *wants to* put a definitive end to Akira’s relationship with Makoto, but is effectively mind-controlled by the universe (through exploiting her countless fears and insecurities and lack of self-confidence) into instead acting complacent and only *kind of* confronting him about it. Likewise, Niki can only distance herself from Akira after the whole debacle of 0.50, but not cut him off outright or prevent him from continuing to fuck Noriko – because trying to do the latter would be the equivalent of attempting to fight gravity (spoiler alert: you’ll fucking lose) – and Sara has Sana to masterfully leverage her weaknesses against herself and force the poor woman to do whatever “the plot” demands her to do.
These are the only outcomes that *can* happen, as long as the aforementioned “laws of reality” stay in place – or, to put it another way, as long as the Wishing Well “simulation” continues to (mostly) function as intended. Which is why I believe that this part of the story is directly focused on highlighting all of the “static” aspects of Kumon-mi and intentionally stalling all of the main conflict resolutions, because we’re soon going to be approaching the point of no return where the world finally breaks, and breaks irreversibly – causing the Dark Route (which was confirmed by Selebus to be something “completely different”, potentially implying that these “rules” will no longer apply), which will then lead into Purity Routes and eventual True Route.

I mean, it *will* lead to something (or at least I sure hope so) – just not right now.

My understanding of LiL’s general structure, based on a few past comments Selebus apparently made in the Lilcord – namely, his claim that the Harem Route 100% won’t lead to the true ending – is that the entirety of Harem Route (meaning, the whole game thus far) effectively serves as nothing more than a bunch of slow, but nonetheless extremely necessary set-up: the final preparations for the huge-ass Sword of Damocles hanging above Akira’s head to finally drop X updates from now, heralding Chapter 6 and the beginning of the Dark Route – the proper “climax” of the story, with every loaded Chekhov's gun shooting Akira in unison like a trained firing squad – which then, in turn, is going to lead into the *actual* resolution of all of the remaining themes and plot threads during the Purity Routes, culminating in the true ending.

So what’s happening now is only “meaningless” if you don’t have enough patience and/or can’t find other things to appreciate about the story in the meantime: a perspective that I don’t personally share, for the record, but can still fully understand how it can be an issue for some people – everyone has different sensibilities when it comes to art, after all.

As for the upcoming essay,
it’s going to be my second magnum opus: an *insanely* long analysis (divided into three main sub-topics) that centers around one specific aspect of Selebus’ writing style – his favorite trick, so to speak – and how it manifests itself in pretty much every single aspect of the story, from characters to the plot structure. The essay itself is about 75% done as of right now and will probably be complete in just a few more days (rather than a week), but I simply don’t want to interfere with people (including myself) passionately analyzing the contents of the long-awaited 0.55 update by suddenly introducing a completely separate topic of discussion that is either going to take away from the original subject or ends up being mostly ignored by everyone – both options being bad in their own way. So I’ll rather hold onto my writings for now, until a much better time to post them inevitably presents itself – a week or so should be more than sufficient for that.

So what’s happening now is only “meaningless” if you don’t have enough patience and/or can’t find other things to appreciate about the story in the meantime: a perspective that I don’t personally share, for the record, but can still fully understand how it can be an issue for some people – everyone has different sensibilities when it comes to art, after all.

The essay itself is about 75% done as of right now and will probably be complete in just a few more days (rather than a week), but I simply don’t want to interfere with people (including myself) passionately analyzing the contents of the long-awaited 0.55 update by suddenly introducing a completely separate topic of discussion that is either going to take away from the original subject or ends up being mostly ignored by everyone – both options being bad in their own way. So I’ll rather hold onto my writings for now, until a much better time to post them inevitably presents itself – a week or so should be more than sufficient for that.
